The Software Essentialist — Study Guide

Mental models, frameworks and practices from all 95 lessons, organised by topic. Fluff removed. Every point cites its source lesson. Generated 2026-09-29.

Cheat Sheet: The 10% Worth 1000x

The course's highest-leverage mental models and frameworks, one screen per topic. Kent Beck's framing: 90% of skills dropped to zero, and the leverage of the remaining 10% went up 1000x. Everything below is that 10%. Each item cites its lessons, and → jumps to the deep-dive topic. L3 L13 L91

The Core Loop in One Picture L82 L93 L15

2 mental models

Abstraction: the what, separated from the how. Feedback loop: everything is a guess. Systems thinking ties them together, and “that is the entire course really.” L90 L91 →

Systems thinking

Every thing is input → process → output, moving state A to state B: a function, an app, a business, you. L9 →

Value creation system

Move people from pain to benefit by giving back or enriching time. Go theoretical → physical, left to right. Score, then score faster, without shipping negative value (bugs). L10 L85 →

3 roles, 4 pillars

User, customer and developer must all win at once, and that is what scalability means. The four pillars (architecture, design, testing, strategy) are what make it possible. L11 L12 →

“Never start a project without these four words clearly understood”: who, why, what, how.L82

They are stats you level up, and you need all 12. Any question you have maps to one metaphysical essential plus one theoretical or physical essential. L82 L85 →

FA²STR: Six Steps, Input → Output L27 L52

  1. Find: problem statement → responsibilities (doing / knowing), concrete examples, and the starting guess point. At higher levels the output is role, why and capabilities, then features, stories, acceptance criteria and examples. L52 L27
  2. Architect: responsibilities + examples → the subject under test. At higher levels: patterns, components, the testing strategy and a broad-stroke architecture. L52
  3. Automate: SUT + examples → a test harness and scripts that also run in the pipeline. Success criteria are defined before any code. L52
  4. Specify: one example → a failing spec (red). At feature level this is the outer-loop acceptance test. L52
  5. Test: failing spec → passing code, written with AAA and made green by fake it or the obvious implementation. Commit. L52
  6. Refine: passing code → refactored code once duplication appears three times. Commit, then loop back to Specify. L52
Remember
  • Upfront design = Find + Architect + Automate. Emergent design = Specify + Test + Refine. L52 L87
  • It works at any level. Start anywhere and drill in with n loops. L86 →
  • Everything is a doing or a knowing. Most tests are one doing with many knowings. L52
  • More than about four collaborating pieces? Go to paper and run RDD. L52

Full method → · worked example →

Ideal Developer Workflow: Outer & Inner Loop L26 L87 L40

  1. Clarify the theoretical guesses (Find): vision → role → goal → capabilities → concrete examples. Non-negotiable. L26
  2. Broad-stroke architecture (Architect): patterns, components, testing strategy, and how tests plug into the pipeline. L26 L81
  3. Walking skeleton (Automate): a testable architecture, a tiny deployed slice and a pipeline. L26 L87
  4. Feature work, n loops (Specify/Test/Refine): outer-loop and inner-loop tests, then fill the remaining ~20% and ship. L26

Outer loop · customer

A failing E2E acceptance test at level 5, written in the user's language. One per feature, shared by every platform. Result verification only. L87

Inner loop · developer

A failing use-case test at level 3 for each scenario (one success, many failures). About 80% of the time goes here. Recurse into levels 2 and 1 as new concepts appear. L87

Close it out

Adapter tests (levels 4 and 6), then hook up the view, then deploy. Infrastructure tests come last. L81 L87

Numbers to remember E2E: the happy path plus one or two sad paths. Then about 12–20 parameterized high-value tests. Roughly 1 E2E test to ~10 high-value unit tests, and those unit tests give ~80% of the confidence. L81 L28

The workflow is the same for an MVP and a mature product. Only the time, the effort and the quality of your guesses change. L40 → · MVP →

Testing Rules of Thumb L31

Rules
  • AAA backwards: assert → act → arrange. Start with the most complex example and program by wishful thinking. “Vagueness does not compile.” L51 →
  • Commit on green, never on red, and say whether the commit is new functionality or a refactor. Flip the switch to prove the test can fail. L44 →
  • Red for the right reason: export a stub first, so the test fails on logic and not on a missing import. L45 L49
  • Fake it until duplication forces a change. Use the obvious implementation only when you're confident. L45 L47
  • Rule of three: refactor on the third repeat. Never add examples during a refactor, and keep each step a refactor XOR a transformation. L44 L49
  • TPP: nil → constant → scalars → single statement → conditionals → mutation. If you need a variable or a mutation, question your transformation. L60 →
  • One example per loop, one it / one expect. L47 L55
  • Name tests as responsibilities (a doing or a knowing, e.g. “knows that …”). Keep examples concrete, in it.each rows that hold the input and expected output together. L56 L59 →
  • 3 verification types: result, state, communication. Pick by guess point. State or communication checks at E2E are bad practice. L20 L53 L87
  • Hand-written fakes and spies implement the contract. Keep library mocks for trivial stubs such as a logger. L73 L81 →
  • Contract tests for every fake: run one spec against every implementation. “You're testing the contract, not the implementation.” L81 →
  • Builders for fixtures: a fixture is the initial state. Give well-known states names. L78 →
  • Comments say why, never what. L48
  • Choose the strategy by ROI. There's no perfect strategy, and E2E-only or unit-only always fails. L64 L87 →

Design & Architecture Rules of Thumb L32 L88

Rules
  • Stereotypical architecture: CQS read/write paths, event-based, layers of concerns, the dependency rule. It's the same on frontend, backend and desktop. L32 L87 →
  • Dependency rule: domain → application → adapter → infrastructure. Inner layers never know infrastructure directly, and use cases depend on contracts. L32 L84
  • Classify code by what it touches, not where it comes from. new Date() is infrastructure, so inject a Clock. L84 L88
  • Feature-first folders: modules/<capability>/<feature> for the customer, shared/ for the developer, and tests/ mirroring the features. L92 L29 →
  • Composition root: one place wires dependencies and holds the environment checks. Move to a DI container only when that gets messy. L19 L93 →
  • Temporal decoupling via events: end the slice at its own state change (“order placed”), let a coordinator dispatch, and model success first, then failure. L18 L82 →
  • George Clooney test: “Who else is going to play this role?” Abstract only when there is more than one actor. Start with an interface, and move to an abstract class only after the rule of three. L79 L84 →
  • Object stereotypes: information holder, structurer, service provider, coordinator, controller, interfacer. Lean into each object's dominant role. Controllers get called; they don't subscribe. L94 L95 →
  • Invariants live in domain objects: private constructor + static create, validation in value objects, expected failures returned rather than thrown. The domain stays pure. L77 L74 →
  • Small aggregates: the minimum data a command needs, which is its transaction boundary. Reference other aggregates by ID. L88 L89 →
  • Own the control center: if you need React to test a feature, React is doing the coordinating. L87 L94 →
  • Default shape: a modular monolith with an event bus. Fewer components means fewer guesses. L71 L84 →

Theoretical Design Checklist (Before Any Code) L65 L88

  1. Who / why / what before how: actor → role → goal → capabilities. Exit when you can say who you help, what they achieve, and why it's worthwhile. L21 L66 →
  2. Concrete examples: start state, end state, what the person does, what they see. L68 →
  3. Subdomains: brain-dump the problem categories and stop when you run out. L66 →
  4. Bounded contexts: group by shared language (“be Aristotle”), classify core / supporting / generic, decide build vs buy, draw the context map. L67 L68 →
  5. Event storm one scenario: past-tense events → imperative commands → actors → aggregates → boundaries. Be wary of same-context event chains. L69 →
  6. Add views and tally the I/O data for each command–event pair. L70 →
  7. State machines: states, transitions, events and invariants. One state change per step, per context. L74 L70 →
  8. Architecture: modules, deployable units, event bus, and tools chosen by responsibility and NFR. L71 L92 →
  9. Go physical: pipeline → E2E in a production-like environment → level-3 tests. L72 →
Khalil's standard reply “Do you have clarity on the theoretical guesses first?” L21 “You never want to be making physical guesses unless you have your theoretical guesses sorted.” L88

Anti-Patterns to Catch in Review

Flag these
  • Package by infrastructure (routes/, controllers/), which hides the features. L16 L88
  • Fat controllers / anemic domain: HTTP, rules and SQL in one handler, or this.repo.save in a controller. L84 L93
  • Environment checks everywhere and imports pulled in “willy nilly”. L19
  • Mocks that lie: fakes with no contract tests (“we're only testing our mocks”), or inline library-mock soup. L81 L73
  • Implementation-detail test names such as “sets result to true and error to null…”. L56
  • else-if chains instead of early-return ifs. L47
  • Big-bang commits, commits on red, or design done off-screen in one jump. L46 L63
  • Code-first / DB-first / API-first design: thinking in endpoints, not features. L8 L82
  • Awaited side effects appended to a command: one failure strands the rest (the makePurchase script). L18 L88
  • Components for weeks, deploy last, which ends in “all these weird CORS errors”. L24 L81
  • Premature interfaces: “You George Clooney'd it.” L79
  • Everything is a “service”, and React is the control center. L94 L87
  • E2E-only or unit-only strategies, and state/communication checks at E2E. L87
  • Husky as the only quality gate, or manual walkthroughs as features grow. L25
  • Modelling the domain before the theoretical guesses, or learning DDD on a project with no real value. L65 L93
  • Rewriting legacy code from scratch instead of pinning it with characterization tests first. L81 L92
  • Comments that restate the code. L48

Mindset One-Liners L3 L4

Clarity beats anxiety

Anxiety at work means you lack clarity. Fix your mental models; don't push harder. L89 L4 →

Purpose beats boredom

Tie the work to something that matters. Use the trail of whys until you reach an emotional charge. L4 L6 →

Essentialism loop

Observe & evaluate → eliminate → execute in a straight line. Learn “topics for problems”. L5 L85 L91 →

Think backwards

Name the end state first, then let it “carve the pieces moving back”. This is the idea behind TDD. L75 L3 →

Right action

At quantum moments (“how do I start this project?”) you act on what you value. Value code and you get code; value value and you get value. L85 →

Refinement

Is it working and doing what we need? Then move on. Kill your designs and design it twice. L3 L63 →

No more “it depends”

Run the scenario: theoretical → physical → which guesses → time budget. That's what it depends on. L91

Zoom out when stuck

Stuck in a change-fail loop? Stop, draw it, clarify the responsibilities, then descend one level. L82 →

Using This with AI Coding Agents Added by Copilot

The course's own take: AI “crunches down” some state-change and decision logic, and the skill left to you is knowing the inputs, outputs and goalpost L89. The first milestone had ChatGPT write the code from a pasted grading checklist L42. The checklist below maps the course frameworks onto how you spec and review agent output.

AI-era lens · Copilot
  • Spec = Find output. Give the role, goal, feature, acceptance criteria and a concrete-examples table. A vague prompt is vagueness that won't compile. →
  • Add Architect + Automate. Name the guess point, the subject under test, the contracts it may depend on, the target folder (modules/<capability>/<feature>) and the exact test command.
  • Demand tests first, AAA-backwards. One example per loop, named as responsibilities. Check that the test fails for the right reason before accepting any code.
  • Ask for red-green-refactor commits labelled as new functionality or refactor, so you review a story of commits and not a big-bang diff.
  • Review with the kata checklist and the anti-pattern list. Else-if chains, what-comments, fake names and premature interfaces are common in generated code. →
  • Guard layer boundaries. No new Date() or Math.random() in the domain, no repo calls in controllers, no environment checks outside the composition root. Consider enforcing this with architecture tests (the course mentions TS-Arch L68).
  • Every generated fake needs a contract test. Reject mocks of your own roles that have no parity with the real implementation.
  • Keep the theoretical guesses human. An agent can draft an event storm, but only users and domain experts validate value, and KPIs close the loop.

Course Map & The Big Picture

The course trains one skill: problem decomposition, backed by metacognition and a small set of mental models. The structure goes from why to how: the Metaphysics plants the seeds, the 12 Essentials give the 80/20, the Phases of Craftship drill them, and the Value-First tools (guess points, FA²STR, the ideal developer workflow) put them together so you can decompose any design problem. L1 L7 L91

The Main Skill: Problem Decomposition + Metacognition L1

Pain being solved: the nagging "am I doing this right?" feeling. Developers lack full confidence in their design, architecture, testing and strategy decisions. Requirements keep changing, so they need bespoke approaches, and memorized recipes aren't enough. L1

Definitions
  • Problem decomposition — "the main skill": breaking a problem into steps you can act on. It applies to front end, back end, desktop, and new or existing code, "because it's all just about problem decomposition." L1
  • Metacognition — awareness of your own thinking. You know how you solve problems and can refine that process. "Great programmers, like philosophers, have metacognition." L1
  • Guess points — the catalog of steps in the problem-decomposition process, and "our problem decomposition technique." L1 L7
  • The course is organized around mental models, not topics. It touches psychology, philosophy, strategy and subjectivity. L1 In Khalil's words it is "in essence, a philosophy and metaphysical course… just a course about thinking." L85
  • Design is hard to teach because it is "about you having awareness of how you think and how you learn." L85
  • The course sits one level of abstraction above DDD, testing or FP. It gives you mental models "so that when you're ready to go deeper on those things, you know what to look for." L91
“How to use systems thinking, stereotypical architecture, FA²STR and the ideal developer workflow to work consistently and confidently decompose any design problem.” (the main value of the course, stated as a lesson title)L91
AI-era lens · Copilot

Lesson 3 opens with Kent Beck: “The value of 90% of my skills just dropped to zero. The leverage for the remaining 10% went up 1000x.” L3 Problem decomposition and metacognition belong in that 10%. Agents can write the code. You still have to split the work into verifiable steps (guess points, acceptance tests) and check whether the agent's reasoning holds up, not only whether the code runs. See Mindsets.

What the Course Promises (and What It Demands) L2

Goal

Write scalable code in any context: any language, framework or platform, front or back end, greenfield or existing project, new feature. L2

Content

The 80/20 of software design, testing and architecture, compiled into 12 essentials ("the 80/20 of what I've learned studying all of the greats"). L1 L2

Only 4 things matter

Architecture, testing, design and strategy, "whether there's AI, whether there's not AI". The 12 essentials are small, implementable pieces of these four. L82

Built on

DDD, TDD, BDD, object design, architectural principles and architectural styles. L2

Demand

"Drill it, drill it, drill it." Skill works like a muscle: stress it consistently. Expect lots of code and lots of design. L2

Expect non-linearity

Design feels non-linear. Starting over from scratch is a sign of progress, and it's what makes design feel like an art form. L2
Principles over tools (the woodworker parable)

A woodworker who mastered the plane and drill but never learned which wood to use couldn't build the table when it counted. Tools, techniques and patterns matter, but principles are "thinking tools upon which you can orient yourself." The course aims at phronesis (practical mastery), not just sophia (knowledge). L13

  • Clarity → boredom → creativity: the aim is so much clarity that you're "probably bored". That kind of boredom is good because creativity replaces stress. L2
  • Prerequisites: you're comfortable building front end or back end, you can learn new tech and debug technical snags, and professional experience helps because it gives you more reference experiences. L1 OOP basics (abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism) are assumed. L85
  • Foundational questions first: What is software? Why do we write it? For whom? What is scalability, and what's stopping you from getting it? Without clarity on these, scalable code isn't reachable. L1

The Phases of Craftship L1 L91

The phases describe the natural levels developers pass through. Each one is a different value system for answering "how do I start this project?" L85 Khalil reverse-engineered them from about 6–7 years of his own study and practice. L1 L91

PhaseProblem it answersWhat you learnEnd state
Code-First"Just build something and make it work." L91Being full stack L1. The mindset is problem → code, with anemic models L85A couple of endpoints. Typical flaws: manual curl testing, thinking in endpoints not features, a DB on the local machine L82
Best-Practice-FirstManual testing is bad. The code is a "big clumpy mess" L91Refactor code-first work using many of the essentials L1. Encapsulate infrastructure: composition root, Docker, four-layer E2E test infra, three-tier backend, project structure L82 L91A deployed walking skeleton, front end + back end with E2E tests L91
Pattern-FirstYou need fast high-value unit tests L91Front-end and back-end patterns L1: decouple from infra (hexagonal, dependency inversion), then result verification, communication verification and contract tests. Then state machines, events and sagas L91A pure core tested by unit tests, infra covered by contract tests, business logic chained via observer L91
Responsibility-FirstYou need something that doesn't exist as a pattern, library or framework L91Object design from scratch, RDD: roles, responsibilities, collaborations, stereotypical architecture. "The most granular level we can use to think about code" L1 L91Custom abstractions: loading state, custom router, unit of work L91
Value-First"Put it all together" L91FA²STR, systems thinking, guess points, the ideal developer workflow, and design challenges broken down theoretical → physical L1 L91Consistent problem decomposition in any context L1
Bridging the Gaps"Watch someone reason through designing and implementing a system" L91Long (~2 h) live-coded front-end and back-end builds, top to bottom, with strategic decisions and technical challenges. Also building projects with others L41 L91Where to go next → Career
The game of value (why Value-First is the top)

Earlier phases treat starting a project as static and linear, like stacking big chunky building blocks. At the deepest level you see software development as a non-linear game of creating and maintaining value, and you win it with the feedback loop (many guesses, guided by principles). That's why "there's no silver bullets." L85

  • Essentials are levelled skills. Think of them like game skills you rank up. At Code-First, horizontal decoupling is about 2/10, and you only work at the "code levels" of the abstraction prism. By Value-First all the physical essentials should be solid. L82 L91
  • Where the 12 came from: observe & evaluate (survey everything) → eliminate (drop what doesn't matter; the 12 essentials were what remained) → execute. The course is that "straight line" instead of wandering from topic to topic. L85 "Topics for problems": learn a topic when a problem needs it. L91
  • Right action / quantum moments: what you do at a decision point depends on the phase you're in, meaning what you currently value. More in Mindsets. L85
  • Pattern-First code is deliberately "perfect". You won't hit the ideal at work, but you'll use parts of it. L91

Using the Course to Ship an MVP Fast L40

The workflow is invariant; the effort varies

The steps are the same for an MVP and for a feature on a mature product. Only three things change: time available, effort you're willing to invest, and quality of the guesses you've already made. L40

  1. Learn the mental models: the Metaphysics, at least the 12 essentials. They act "like landmines and the opposite of landmines", showing what to avoid and what to move toward. L40
  2. Watch the ideal developer workflow (pieced together from GOOS, Continuous Delivery, Clean Architecture, DDD and BDD). L40 → Workflow
  3. Get clarity on the theoretical guesses: problem, solution (domain boundaries; process modelling for the first one or two user stories), architecture (patterns, tools). Turn their inputs and outputs into a checklist. Use the abstraction prism as the readiness roadmap: "This is also just BDD." L40
  4. Pick a testing strategy: at least one acceptance test for customer correctness, plus a configuration of inner-loop tests for the internals. Start with either E2E or a high-value integration test. L40 → Testing
  5. Build and deploy the walking skeleton. It's messy and takes time, but it establishes the test strategy for the whole product. L40 Deploy early: the worst case is building for months and finding it can't be deployed. L82 The first job on a new project is to remove as much uncertainty as possible. L91
Unvalidated MVP = optimize for answers
  • Priority is getting solid answers to your theoretical guesses (do customers value it?). Heavy testing and polish aren't critical, but still build "on a good foundation of guesses". L40
  • With zero theoretical guesses confirmed, don't do multi-loop TDD at every guess point. Push one guess through fast, then "start playing defense" with physical-level tests. L85
  • Once you have a platform (shared infra, deployment, known services), later features can skip guess points and score faster. L85

Top recommended viewing (as of recording): "Acceptance testing a walking skeleton from UI to DB" (Best-Practice-First). Also the Frontend Architecture 2 Q&A (builders, application interface), the theoretical guess points, and the Value-First testing strategy video. L40 See Frontend and DDD & FeedBook.

Assignments, Branches & Peer Review L43 L41

Lesson format in the skills phases: a slideshow lesson → a demo → an assignment, or apply the idea to your own project using the provided next steps. L91 Order after the Code-First assignment: emergent design → stateless testing assignments → Best-Practice-First, starting with acceptance testing a feature. L82 Katas are in Kata Walkthroughs.

  • A branch per attempt lets you redo a kata several times, even on the same day, and gives reviewers one URL to comment on. L43
  • Reviewing others' work is mandatory. It mirrors PR review at work and prepares you for the collaborative Bridging the Gaps section. L41
  1. Submit your own first, then filter the community by level or theme (e.g., FizzBuzz). L41
  2. Pick the oldest unreviewed submission (sort by date). L41
  3. Open the PR, glance at Files changed, then go to the first commit and click next through each one, reading it "like a story". You're reviewing the process, not only the final diff. L41
  4. Check against the grading checklist, not your personal taste. The checklist is designed so reviewers at any skill level can use it. L41
  5. Comment inline, then mark the community post as reviewed so nobody duplicates the work. Optionally redo your own attempt with what you learned. L41

Terms used across the guide are in the Glossary. Session-by-session context is in Q&A Highlights.

Mindsets (Distilled)

The course's mindset lessons, cut down to the frameworks you can act on: 4 mindsets, 2 obstacles to flow, 2 clarity strategies, 4 motivation techniques, and 2 habits for decisions (thinking backwards, right action). Hype, anecdotes and pep talks are left out. L3L4L5L6

The 4 Key Mindsets & the 90%/10% Framing L3

“The value of 90% of my skills just dropped to zero. The leverage for the remaining 10% went up 1000x. I need to recalibrate.” — Kent Beck, on ChatGPTL3

The course uses this tweet to frame software essentialism: work out which skills dropped to zero, which gained leverage, and master the ones that matter. L3

Software essentialist — Follows the Pareto principle (80% of results from 20% of effort), is value-focused, and goes after perennial skills. A skill that wasn't perennial: being the "Webpack guru". L3

1 · Refinement

  • Ask: is it working and doing what we need? If yes, move on. You can refine later. L3
  • Stop chasing perfect, because returns diminish. Don't get attached to a design: "kill your designs and do it again." An impasse just means it's time to redesign. L3
  • “The road to success is built from bricks of feedback.” L3

2 · Clarity

  • Don't stop at "it depends". Know what it depends on: when to use a tool, when not to, and what its role is. L3
  • Clarify before you code. Think backwards: start from the end state (see below). L3

3 · Purpose

  • “Everything has a purpose”: polymorphism, encapsulation, every tool. Know each one's purpose before you use it. L3
  • Clarity builds confidence, and confidence keeps you going. L3

4 · Experience

  • What counts is how many reference experiences you have and how deep they go, not your senior/junior title. L3
  • If work doesn't give you the chance, practice on your own time (problem decomposition, the 12 essentials). Build up tools and mental models over time. L3
Cost of mastery — “Dedication, discipline, and continually returning to the path.” Mastery also means staying in the game. The tedious katas are there to give you reference experiences. L3L85
AI-era lens · Copilot

When agents write most of the code, syntax, framework trivia and typing speed move into Beck's "90%". The "10%" is:

  • Clarity: stating what "done" means
  • Decomposition: splitting work into small, verifiable steps
  • Judgment: telling good output from plausible output and throwing away bad designs

These map directly onto Clarity, Purpose and Refinement. Output is cheap to regenerate, so the leverage is in knowing what "better" means.

The 2 Obstacles to Mastery: Anxiety & Boredom L4

Mastery — Skill in a domain where you're “maneuvering in 3D”. You combine ideas creatively, the work feels effortless yet challenging, and you learn fast because you're building on a strong foundation. Example: once you master abstraction design, you can vet tomorrow's libraries and frameworks. L4

Flow (extreme focus and presence) is the shortcut to mastery. You can't switch it on. It sits between anxiety and boredom. L4

BlockerCauseSymptomsAntidote
AnxietyChallenge exceeds your skill or clarity. You have the wrong mental models, or the puzzle isn't pieced together yet. L4Overwhelm, jargon overload (dependency inversion, aggregates, domain events…). Cognitive dissonance: "foot on the gas and the brakes at the same time". You plateau. L4Clarity L4L89
BoredomNo challenge. The work feels irrelevant or like a waste of time. L4Your mind wanders, you get distracted, and you quit to start something else. L4Purpose: tie the work to something that matters to you and set goals that inspire you. L4

Cognitive-dissonance detector

If you catch yourself asking “Am I doing this right? Is this best practice? Should I be testing this?” while coding, you're out of flow. Go fix your mental models instead of pushing harder. L4

Boredom anti-pattern

Hopping between new libraries, frameworks, jobs and half-started side projects. It gets you no ROI, no growth, and eventually burnout. L4

End goal

The coach becomes superfluous. You can then mentor others, and teaching is a higher level of mastery. L4

Clarity Strategies: Mentorship or Essentialism L5

Clarity means knowing where you're going and how the pieces fit before you start executing. “It's always going to be the first step.” Without first principles you pattern-match, doubt yourself, defer to others, and relearn the basics with every new tool. L5

“If you're experiencing a lot of anxiety when you're doing your work, it's because you don't have enough clarity.”L89

Symptoms of low clarity → response

Anxiety

A feeling that it might blow up later, because you have no solid mental model. Treat it as a signal of where your skill is, not as a failure. Be coachable. L5

Overwhelm

You're trying to fit DDD, TDD, BDD and RDD into one picture. That's the signal to zoom out. L5

Analysis paralysis

Perfectionism: going down every rabbit hole. Aim for a good enough mental model, then act. L5

Clarity excludes — Getting clear on what realistically has to happen rules out thousands of other options. Khalil writes a detailed process document before starting, so that implementation “just feels like typing”. Put the what before the how. L89

Quantum moments & triple blindness

Quantum moment — A point where one decision drastically changes the outcome. Recognize it and you land on the results timeline; miss it and you land on “the timeline of no results”. L5L85

Examples from the course L5:

  • Writing the test first, or not.
  • Writing lots of code for a product nobody has validated.
  • Building a testable architecture from the beginning.
  • Deriving data and behavior from use cases instead of building up from the DB layer to the API.
  • Accepting that design is non-linear: like writing, great design comes from redesigning. Don't quit after the first attempt.

Triple blindness is “the greatest manifestation of a lack of clarity” L5. It has three layers:

  1. You're not aware that quantum moments exist.
  2. You don't know how to rise to them. For example, you're told to "start writing tests", but how, especially in React?
  3. You don't know what's possible. For example, shipping features in hours, or building about 90% of a React feature without starting React, because it's decoupled from infrastructure and the view is hooked up last.

Strategy 1 — Decide on your mentor

A person (phronimos)

Someone who is where you want to be in design, architecture or testing, and who can still tell you the next step. “Absorb the mentor spirit” (Robert Greene), and aim to surpass your mentor. L5

Reality

Khalil's own path: learning from reality itself, using the process of essentialism below. It's slower, and the course exists to shortcut it. L5

Strategy 2 — The process of essentialism

  1. Observe & Evaluate — Take in as much information as you can (books, code, blog posts, other developers' views, being corrected) until the bigger puzzle shows. Shorten this step by asking questions in the community. L5L85
  2. Eliminate — Get clear on your purpose or goal, spot the patterns, and keep only the essential forms. Khalil's years of eliminating left the 12 essentials. L5L85
  3. Execute — Commit fully to execution and learn that subset in a “straight line” instead of wandering from topic to topic. L5L85
Use it as a diagnostic — Start from a concrete goal: “What is your current goal?” Many developers “don't even know what they need to know”, so they can't form a question. The course's action item: post one question and help two other developers. Teaching sharpens your own understanding. L85L5

Endless Motivation: 4 Techniques L6

Motivation drops at the first sign of friction, because we default to the path of least resistance. Purpose is the antidote to boredom, and emotional reasons keep you on track better than logical ones. You don't need all four techniques; use them when motivation dips. L6

1 · Trail of whys

Ask “why?” again and again until you reach something with an emotional charge. Learn DDD → my codebase is a mess → I want to do a good job → … Spend 5 minutes on paper and keep the real reason front of mind. L6

2 · Correct social ties

Peer norms shape behavior. In the study cited, when a friend became obese you were 45% more likely to gain weight; for a friend-of-a-friend it was about 20%. Join a community with high expectations: ask questions, share wins and losses, help others. L6

3 · Positive/negative × short/long term

In the short term, discomfort wins (“I don't want to do it”). Write out the long-term vision and the anti-vision (the future you want to avoid) so the long-term difference outweighs short-term comfort. L6

4 · Commit to the process

Write a contract or letter to yourself, print it, and keep it where you'll see it every day. “Quality is not an act, but a habit.” L6

Thinking Backwards L75L3

Start at the end: get clear on where you want to be or what something should do, and only then do the work. Khalil calls this “pretty much the whole idea of test-driven development”. L3

  1. What do we need to have next? — Name the next result. L75
  2. Where do I want to be next? — Name the destination. L75
  3. What is the state of the universe I'll be in? — Describe the end state concretely, then let it “carve the pieces moving back” to the present. L75

In code

Write the assertion or desired outcome first, then work back to the setup. This is the same move as Arrange-Act-Assert written backwards. Working backwards with TDD “forces you to kind of have faith” (student). L75L51

In life / daily planning

Khalil writes down the desired end state every day. It counters the tendency to dilly-dally without a defined target. L75

Right Action at Quantum Moments L85

Quantum moments come up constantly during work. Right action is choosing well at those moments. L85

  1. Become aware — Learn to recognize the decision points, starting with “how do I start this project?” L85
  2. Know what to do next — What looks "right" depends on the lens you currently see reality through (code-first → best-practices-first → pattern-first → DDD-first → responsibility-first; see Course Map). L85
“Right action really, truly, is based on what you currently value.” … “Whatever you place your awareness on … is what you're going to achieve.”L85
Heuristic — If you value writing code, you'll get code. If you value creating value, your first thought at the start of a project becomes “we need to be creating value”, and that's where “the game of software design” begins. L85

Metaphysics: Mental Models & Systems

The first principles of being a developer: what software is, what it is for, who it serves, and how scalability is won or lost. Every later section (12 essentials, guess points, FA²STR, testing, DDD) is built on these models: systems thinking, the value creation system, the 3 roles, the 4 pillars, and the essence → role/goal → purpose → form chain. L7L8L9L10L11L12

Why Mental Models Matter L8

Metaphysics — “the branch of philosophy that helps us define reality and our understanding of it”. At root it is cause and effect: kick the ball, it moves. In the live sessions Khalil shortens it to “the first principles of reality”. L8L94
Mental model — a simplification of the world (a “map of meaning”), held mostly in the subconscious (~90% of the mind), that lets you interpret reality and choose future action without re-thinking everything. L8
  • Internal representations. Read “dog” or “red” and something pops up automatically. You never consciously chose it, so take ownership of how your subconscious is programmed. L8
  • You are an abstraction designer. Code creates internal representations for you and for every developer who reads it. L8
  • Missing outcomes signal a bad model. A graphic designer who only works in their own style and never sells; a coder who only has fun trying new tech and never gets hired. Something is missing from the model. L8
“A mental model is only as good as how close it maps to reality.”L8
“You're also an abstraction designer. You are someone who is creating and using mental models.”L8
Test for any mental model — (1) Does it produce beneficial outcomes? (2) Does it let you reason from where you are to where you want to be? Good models are based in reality and need first-principles clarity. L8

Khalil's two flawed models (and what replaces them)

ModelHow it thinksWhat it produced
API-first“Build this REST endpoint, that REST endpoint, connect front end and back end.”Worked for a while, then turned into expensive messes. L8
Database / data-model-firstStart from data and relationships at the code level.Code that didn't scale. L8
Value-based (the replacement)Clarity on how reality works and how software fits into it. Start from value, roles and use cases.The path to scalable code. L8L85
“Reality is not based on APIs or RESTful endpoints. Reality is much more nuanced and complex than that.”L8

Models as levels of thinking: the phases of craftship

The flawed models map to the phases of craftship: code-first → best-practice-first → pattern-first (DDD-first) → responsibility-first → value-first. Each phase is a different lens for seeing the same problem. L8L85 Code-first sees “app + DB” blocks. Responsibility-first sees “the fabric of reality itself”. Beyond that, you see reality as value-based, and “the game of software design… actually begins”. L85 See the full ladder in Course Map.

Quantum moments — moments that matter more than others, where the right action pays off. The classic one is the start of a project: code-first thinking designs from the database; a value-based model uses other techniques that lead to scalable code. What you do in that moment depends on what you currently value (Mindsets → right action). L8L85
“At the start of a project is often one of the most important parts.”L8
Reprogram with essential questions — Ask the foundational questions to dig into your subconscious “database” and reorient it: What is software? What is my role? How do I do it well? What is scalable code? The Metaphysics section is organized around them. L8L7

Systems Thinking: The Most Important Mental Model L9

“The world is a patchwork of systems.”L9
System — “a model in some environment where there's an input and there's an output.” Purpose of a system: “to achieve a goal”, which means moving from state A to state B. The system between two states can be one system or a composition of many. L9

One lens, every scale

ScaleInputModel / processOutput
Function"12:01 - 14:21" (string)military time validator: parse range → validate start → validate end → start before endtrue (boolean) L9
Applicationuser actionUI → backend → databasechanged state / response L9
Businessideas, demandleadership → marketing → sales → operations (“the thing that does the thing”) → financevalue, revenue L9L94
You, the developerexperiences + intent/goalyour actions and decisionsdesired state. The course keeps refining this model. L9
Your processproblem statementFA²STR: each step is its own input → process → outputtested design L94

State-transition examples: package not mailed → package mailed; video files acquired → videos edited and exported; unvalidated raw text → validated text. L9

Three payoffs

  1. Problem decomposition — breaking any problem into sub-systems and state transitions. Becoming “an excellent problem decomposer” is a main goal of the course. L9
  2. Debugging — if you can break a system into parts, you can isolate the part that fails. You spend less time debugging overall. L9
  3. Refinement & learning — “You can only really refine if you know what to refine.” L9
Anti-pattern: mindless debugging — “What I don't want you to be doing is refreshing the page and just doing mindless stuff.” Reason through the system's parts instead. L9
Why it's “the” mental model — The course's two foundational models are the feedback loop and abstraction, “pieced together” by systems thinking: “If you understand those things that is the entire course really.” Tools are also judged as systems: “It's less about the tool. It's more about the inputs, outputs of the system of creating value.” See 12 Essentials I. L90L85

The kata itself is covered in Kata Walkthroughs.

AI-era lens · Copilot
  • An input → output spec with a precise state A → state B makes a well-scoped, verifiable task for an agent.
  • When generated code fails, isolate the failing sub-system instead of re-prompting blindly. Re-prompting blindly is the AI version of “refreshing the page”.

Essence → Actor/Role/Goal → Purpose → Form (the Mug & the Stone) L10L94

This is the metaphysics behind every abstraction you design. “Perhaps the deepest level of abstraction you need to think theoretically” about why you do anything. DDD and BDD practitioners use it too. L10

TermMeaning
EssenceWhat a thing is: all of its properties. Mug: ceramic, has a hole, handle, rounded, has a base, printable. L94
ActorA person (e.g. Khalil) who plays many roles: brother, coach, skateboarder, musician; programmer, entrepreneur, writer. L10L94
RoleA part an actor plays. Each role has its own goal. L10
GoalWhat the actor in that role wants: the desired state B. L94
PurposeWhy the object is used. It comes from role + goal + the chosen how. “It's always up to the actor to decide what the purpose of something is.” L94
FormThe properties that are essential for that purpose. L94

Worked examples: same essence, different purposes

Mug

  • Programmer (be alert/energized) → drink coffee. The essential form is the hole. Handle and ceramic are nice but not essential, and printable doesn't matter: “this could be my hands”, unless the coffee is hot. L10L94
  • Landscaper (finish the job without tools) → scoop dirt, because it can hold matter. L10
  • Business owner (more clients) → advertise on it. Printable becomes essential. L10

Stone

  • Child (have fun) → skip it on water for ripples. L10
  • Warrior (provide for the tribe / slay the dragon) → forge weapons. L10
  • Hunter → a tool for getting food. L94
  • “Based on who is using it and what they're trying to do, the stone is going to turn into something else.” L94

Nuances

  • Many hows per goal. Energy can come from exercise, coffee or sleep. The mug's purpose only matters once you choose “drink coffee”. L94
  • The actor matters too. A young kid may need the handle for safety, but that still depends on their purpose/goal. L94
  • “There is no one singular purpose of the mug.” L10
“The purpose of anything completely depends on the goal of the role.”L10
Where features come from — Actor → role → goal → feature/use case → minimal essential properties. This is how you write the minimum amount of code: “We just saw the birth of features.” Run this critical-thinking process every time you design an abstraction. L94
“You should be writing no code unless you're very clear on who plays what role and why do they need that.”L94

The mug exercise trains you to think about the forms things have and what they combine into. Good OO designers notice when something is pluggable, serializable, and so on. “Printable” already sounds like programming (Serializable, XYZ-able), which is why OOP should start here. L10L94 More in Abstraction, OOP & RDD.

What software is (the essence of software)

  1. Purpose of computing: solve problems. Math and automation aren't strictly necessary to solve a problem. L94
  2. Essential forms: sequence, selection, iteration. Directions to a store use all three. L94
  3. A problem = being in an undesirable state A and wanting a desirable state B. L94
  4. Transition = behavior. Event = the fact that a transition happened. Real work is many small steps, and each step is both. L94
  5. Data = initial state + events. Behavior acts on state and produces version 2, 3, 4… of the data. L94
  6. Namespacing encapsulates data and behavior (an event concept, a transition, a bounded context). Its purpose is understanding: “so really, this is abstraction. This is where abstraction comes from.” Abstraction is the first of the three metaphysical essentials. L94
“We have the behavior, which is the transition. And we have the event, which is the fact that a transition happened.”L94
Feature / use case (anatomy) — data in → validation rules (how data may come in) + application rules (what may happen to it) → state changes + events out. Its only purpose is to decide whether data may change and to keep things consistent. L94
Work with the grain of reality — “The correct architecture is the event-based one.” Reality is event-based, so CRUD-shaped solutions to event-shaped problems don't fit. Event sourcing and CQRS “at the deepest level” strip away everything that isn't the essence of computing. See DDD: FeedBook for state machines and events. L94

L94 covers the essence of software. The essence of software development is saved for later: that's the value creation system below. L94

The Value Creation System & the Purpose of Software L10

What makes software valuable (user role)

  • Pain → benefit. Value is created when someone moves from pain to benefit, or remains in benefit, over time. The idea is borrowed from the business world. L10
  • Two mechanisms: time saved (given back) or time enriched. Time is humans' most valuable resource. People spend it working toward their needs (physiological, safety, love, esteem, self-actualization), so solving time-consuming tasks is valued highly. Entertainment and memes are time enriched. “This is why we buy anything.” L10
“We are either giving back time or enriching time and we are trying to move people from pain to benefit.”L10
Human state management — Multi-step human processes, each with many states, can be offloaded into software, collapsing days into minutes. L10
Before — human runs every state

Assemble the package → travel through traffic → post office closes at 4 pm (you work 9–5) → retry another day → package mailed. 3–7 days. L10

After — software manages the states

Assemble the package (~10 min) → courier pickup → “package mailed” notification (~2 min to read). Time given back. L10

Software artifact of value — a thing that is valuable because it creates human state changes over time (pain → benefit, or remain in benefit). L10
“Do not discount the power you have, my friend, as a software developer. It is some serious, magical stuff.”L10

The system that produces those artifacts

Value creation system — the developer's work end to end. Theoretical work (high level) → physical work (low level) → a software artifact of value out of the system and in users' hands. L10 Artifacts move left → right: from “they don't really exist yet and we don't even know if people want this” to “done and in somebody's hands using it”, as fast as possible. L85

Rules of the game

  • Theoretical first, then physical. Go left to right. L85
  • Score, then score faster. Getting one artifact through is “scoring a point in the soccer net”. After that, keep doing it faster “without introducing negative value, which is bugs”. L85
  • Contending elements: domain complexity, team size, and how many theoretical guesses you've gotten right before. L85
  • Every guess can be wrong. Wrong physical guesses become negative value (bugs), and tests are how you check your guesses. Upfront design is a guess too: “The more work we do here, the better our guess is probably going to be down here.” L94
  • Zero validated theoretical guesses? Don't run multi-loop TDD at every guess point. Push one guess through fast, then “start playing defense and adding tests at the physical level.” See Testing. L85L94
  • Platform strategy: once shared infrastructure exists (deployment, architecture, known services, tested code), you can skip guesses at some guess points and score faster. L85
  • Tools belong to guess points. Big-picture event storming → problem; tactical event storming → solution; impact mapping and user story mapping → theoretical guess points. Processes change, but the value creation system “will never change”. See 12 Essentials III. L85
  • The 12 essentials are the skills that move code through this system: from requests, to deployment to the user, to product metrics, back to leadership deciding what to build next. L90
Before any code — “It is not advisable to write code without clarity on at least the who, what, why, and how.” L10

There are two more roles, and what makes software hard is that several roles with different goals interact. See the next topic. L10

The 3 Roles & Their Goals: Why Software Development Is So Hard L11

Game theory — the study of how and why we make decisions among active agents trying to reach goals. Chess is a two-player game with a single goal (checkmate). Software development is a team sport, but one full of contending elements. L11
“Strategy gets introduced when you have multiple roles, multiple goals, and they're all contending to get to their goals.”L11
RoleGoal (L11)Goal as restated in the 1-on-1 (L94)
UserGet time back, or have time enriched. L11No bugs; a correct solution to the actual problem. L94
CustomerIncrease revenue or protect revenue (make money, save money). L11Fast builds that cost less. The customer and user can be the same actor. L94
DeveloperKeep users and customers in benefit at the same time, and set things up so the key developer use cases stay easy over time. Developers are paid when users and customers stay in benefit. L11Build effectively; keep the code maintainable. L94

Contending elements

These make winning hard: the status, structure and maintainability of the codebase; the market; the competition; how much time you have; the skill level of the team. L11

Assistive elements

These help you win: the 4 pillars (architecture, design, testing, strategy). L11L12

Key developer use cases

Developers work against features, the building blocks of artifacts of value (see vertical slicing in 12 Essentials II). The use cases are to discover & understand (especially in a new codebase), test, extend/change, add, and debug features. L11

Why it's hard: constraints shrink the option set — “Make $1,000 by the end of the month” can be done many ways. Add “as a landscaper” and the options narrow. A developer carries three goal sets at once, so the space of acceptable actions is small. You need “extremely effective mental models” that fit all three. L11
Scalability — “the word that best describes what it is we're trying to achieve as the apex of all three of those goals.” L11 Students' concrete goals (easy to change as features are added, many devs on one codebase, easy to navigate, fewer maintainers needed) all reduce to this: “Scalability is when one two three are winning.” L90
Negative value (moving from benefit to a bad place) — bugs, defects, regressions; missing requirements; incomplete implementations; features that take longer and longer to build (“This one hits close to home”); codebases that get harder and harder to change. The antidote is mental models “closely aligned with reality”. L11
AI-era lens · Copilot
  • Agents make code cheap but can speed up negative value (regressions, hard-to-change code). “Who, what, why, how” and the role/goal behind a feature are the context they can't invent.
  • Balancing user, customer and developer goals is a strategic trade-off that humans own. Organizing work around features gives agents testable units.

The 4 Pillars: Architecture, Design, Testing & Strategy L12

The four pillars are the assistive elements that make scalability possible. Scalability is achieved by doing all four well and lost through bad design, bad architecture, bad testing or bad strategy. L12L90

Architecture

“Will the structure support the long term goals of these three roles?” L12

Covers: architectural styles, patterns, components, tools, how to break up and organize code, frameworks and libraries, project structure, monolith vs split, shared folders. L12

Classic violation: not starting a project with testing in mind. For example, building frontend components on top of components and then testing only through them, which makes useful tests hard to write. L12 See Architecture.

Design

How easily can other developers discover and understand how to perform their key developer use cases against the codebase? L12

Tools: folder structure, signs, symbols, names, consistency, design patterns. “Design patterns themselves are mental models”: observer/Redux is an object in the middle that emits events to subscribers. L12

Symptom: you open a project (or your own old code) and can't tell what it does. Example: packaging by infrastructure (routes/, controllers/) says nothing about what the code does. L12L90

Testing

Can I define what the system does (ahead of time) and be aware whether it still does it successfully? L12

Covers: test strategies, types of tests, TDD schools (classic, inside-out, mockist, outside-in), and CI/CD that runs tests in a pipeline before production. L12

Main reason people struggle to write tests: coupling, “the enemy of testing”. L12L90 See Testing.

Strategy

How can we make the most effective use of the contending and assistive elements we currently have? L12

Elements: time, money, current codebase quality, the team, the market, the competition. Know techniques and when to use them: how much architecture, design and testing is right, which shortcuts to take now, where to invest, and what to do quick and dirty. L12

Design deep-dive: Don Norman's two gulfs

From The Design of Everyday Things: between a goal and knowing whether you reached it are two gaps. Use them to judge developer experience. L12

Practice — Build awareness of how quickly and smoothly you (and others) can discover how to perform each developer use case. Think from a developer-experience point of view. L12

Why you can't learn one pillar in isolation

  • Every topic sits in a mesh of the four pillars. Clean code is mostly design, partly architecture, somewhat testing. Stubbing/mocking is mostly testing, a bit of design, some architecture, and strategy (when to use them). The same goes for DDD, BDD, encapsulation, polymorphism, composition over inheritance, programming against an interface, and testing against a production-like environment. L12
  • “It is a fabric of topics that are related to each other.” Proper end-to-end testing is a graph of many essential subtopics. Decoupling with an event-based backend needs vertical slicing, temporal decoupling, and messaging (a massive topic). “It's a complexity explosion.” Be easy on yourself. L12
  • Essentialism: find the few things that produce most of the results and refine them. The claim relayed about top developers is that they're more productive “not by a factor of 10x or 100x or even 1000x, by 10,000x.” L12
  • Raise the level of thinking. “Information is consciousness. Consciousness is information.” Getting closer to first principles means solving problems at a deeper level instead of at “fractured points”. L12
“Mastery takes time. It is an untangling process.”L12
The 12 essentials detangle the pillars — They're broader than techniques and patterns but low enough that you know what to do next. “Perhaps even more helpfully, they help us understand what it is we should not do.” Use them like RPG stats that start low and level up. They also work as self-coaching questions: Am I respecting vertical slicing? Do I have clarity over the subject under test? Am I decoupling concerns horizontally? See 12 Essentials. L12
AI-era lens · Copilot
  • Agents produce code within one pillar easily. Weighing trade-offs across the mesh (strategy) stays a human job.
  • The gulfs apply to agents too: a structure that shows what the code does and clear test output help agents and reviewers cross both gulfs.

How the Models Fit Together L12L90

The recap chain Khalil builds up to before the 4 pillars: L12

  1. Problem decomposition — the most important skill. L12
  2. Systems thinking makes it possible: inputs, outputs, model/process, environment. L12L9
  3. Purpose of software — the goals of the 3 roles. L12L10L11
  4. Your responsibility — the key developer use cases, done so that all roles stay in benefit, including the other developers on your team who must understand and work with your code. L12
  5. Assistive elements — the 4 pillars, detangled by the 12 essentials, give a shared understanding of the problem and how to move toward solving it. L12

The course is taught the same way: each iteration makes the important things clearer and abstracts away the rest. You won't get it right the first time: “it's going to be a mess but do it again.” L90

12 Essentials I: Metaphysical — Abstraction & The Feedback Loop

The 12 essentials are practicable "thinking tools" one level below the four pillars. Two of them are metaphysical, meaning they describe how the world works: abstraction (split the what from the how and work top-down) and the feedback loop (everything is a guess, so make it, check it, refine it). The other ten derive from these two. L13 L91 L93

The 12 Essentials at a Glance L13 L93

The four pillars (architecture, testing, design, strategy) are "the only things that actually really matter", but they form a "tangled maze". The essentials are a lower level of abstraction built on the pillars that you can practise as skills and apply to real use cases. L13 L93 L82 They exist because all three roles (customer, user, developer) must win at the same time, and that constraint is what gives them their meaning. L93

Principles > tools L13

The woodworker parable: he mastered the plane and the drill but never learned which types of wood to use, so he couldn't build the table when it mattered. Tools, techniques and patterns are useful, but principles are the thinking tools you orient yourself by.

Sophia vs Phronesis L13

Sophia is the love of knowledge (philosophy). Phronesis is practical wisdom, or mastery. The essentials were distilled from studying phronimos developers, the masterful ones. The course aims at phronesis.

Skills, not a menu L93 L82

Each essential is a stat you level up, like character stats in Fallout. You can be "2 out of 10" on horizontal decoupling and still follow the workflow. You need all 12; you don't pick them per use case. The essentials have no order of their own. Ordering comes from the ideal developer workflow and FA²STR.

Why learn them early L93 L91

They prime your subconscious (the "red Audi" effect), so you notice violations while moving through the phases of craftship. Without them, the demos were "quite confusing". Plant the seeds now and refine them later. L13

“Tools, techniques, and patterns are important, yes, but principles, thinking tools upon which you can orient yourself, these things are foundational.”L13
Three categories L13
  • Metaphysical: the foundation, based on core mental models, especially systems thinking. "Basically the way the world works." They show up in every other essential. L93
  • Theoretical: everything before code. Who we're helping, how, capabilities, features, use cases, concrete examples.
  • Physical: writing the source code that implements features.

Abstraction: Taming Complexity L14

"Thought works by abstraction." The Chinese character for "man" started as a head-and-legs figure. It cuts out detail and leaves a simple image you can grasp. A washing machine's start cycle button and a TV remote's power button are public interfaces. The low-level steps behind them stay hidden and only the builders need to know them. L14

“It's a way to tame complexity, which is the default state of the universe.” … “Never forget that you yourself are abstraction designer.”L14
Definitions of abstraction
  1. The root principle of design, where design means discoverability + understanding (Norman's two gulfs) for the key developer use cases: discover, understand, add, change, debug, test, plan features. L14 "It's what from how." L82
  2. Separating the theoretical from the physical, visualized by the abstraction prism. L14
  3. Your highest-level understanding of the problem (getting from here to there) plus the concrete, discrete steps to get there, written as past-tense events, states or steps. Smaller steps sit behind them, "abstracted away from us". L91

Many names for the same split: essential vs accidental complexity, upfront vs emergent design, theoretical vs physical, what vs how, declarative vs imperative L14. Also high vs low level, contract vs concretion, abstract vs real, type vs implementation L93. It's hard to grasp because it is everywhere; it is "the fabric of how we achieve goals". The developer's job is to be a problem decomposer who uses abstraction to break problems down. L93 The "abstract vs real" axis is developed as levels of realness. L91

Use case: add a feature L14

Package by infrastructure (folders named after technical parts) tells you nothing about where a feature goes. Screaming architecture / package by feature (module, domain) lines the folders up with goals, so it's obvious where to add one. See Architecture.

Use case: change a feature L14

Deeply nested technical code is hard to trace. A Gherkin feature file (feature + scenarios) that informs an executable specification reads like a table of contents. You find the scenario to change, or add an edge case.

The Abstraction Prism: Theoretical Above, Physical Below L14 L93

The prism starts from the theoretical questions before any code (Who are we helping? What will we help them achieve? What will they be enabled to do?) and narrows down to code. Khalil returns to it whenever he decides how to structure or organize code. L14 He also built his course "topic map" on it (goals → capabilities → features → acceptance criteria → deeper). L91

  • Chapters vs sub-chapters. High-level events are the chapters (1 → 2 → … → end), "the truth of the story". Code is the sub-chapters along the path. Those events form a state machine: dirty clothes → … → washed clothes, where one event (start cycle) is a slice holding many low-level steps. L14
  • Directionality. "We always need to start from the top and go downwards." Coding from the bottom up toward the vision "always results in a mess". Khalil calls this "the major big learning". L93
  • Top-down sequence: who (roles) → why (goals) → what (features) → stories → acceptance criteria → concrete examples → validated → then code. L93
  • The highest theoretical abstraction in code is the acceptance test / feature file, with stories, acceptance criteria and a table of concrete examples. If someone can read it and know exactly what the software should do, you have the top-level abstraction. L93
  • Code-first developers live only in the code levels of the prism. They can connect a frontend to a backend but can't connect an endpoint to acceptance criteria, goals or roles. L91
Ideal codebase entry path L93

README says "go to the tests" → tests folder broken down by capability → one feature file per feature → stories → scenarios with concrete examples → then into the code.

Physical layers look alike everywhere L14 L90

React components and Express request handlers both deal with the outside world. Both are interfacers and belong to the infrastructure layer. The same stereotypical layers appear on frontend, backend and desktop: "We're doing the exact same things on the front end on the back end." Knowing this stereotypical architecture brings calm about where things belong. See Physical essentials and Architecture.

Working Top-Down: Start From the End, Think Backwards L14 L93

  1. Start from the very end: clarify the end goal. In practice, clarify your theoretical guesses upfront and embed them in the codebase as high-level tests that describe features and scenarios with concrete examples. L14
  2. Think backwards: this narrows the ways you could reach the goal. L14 (Deep dive: L75.)
  3. Write the minimum code that reaches the goal. Less code means less to maintain, which is why TDD matters. L14
  4. Theoretical first, then physical. In the physical, write tests and code together and move deeper toward the core. L14
  5. Know the purpose (the theoretical side) of every abstraction before you implement it. L14

Role → goal → features → concrete examples → acceptance tests is the 1-2-3 chain that drives all work. "Never start a project without these four words clearly understood": who, why, what, how. L82 Example: DDD Forum had weak motivation while it was "just build these endpoints". Reframed, it serves a conference organizer whose goal is to "obtain an audience of devs curious about DDD to sell tickets to". Its features become register, buy tickets, view ticket advertisement, ask questions about DDD. L82 L93

Self-check while coding L93

"What is the actual value of me doing this thing… how can I connect this to a role's goal?" If you can't answer, you're thinking forwards, which means reacting without clarity on why.

Anti-patterns
  • Perfectionism / rabbit-holing: aiming for chapter 1 → 8 but stuck in 1.1 → 1.1.1 → 1.1.2… In code, the goal is a frontend app, yet you're deep in Webpack's nuances and then its plugins. Start from the end goal and stop once the problem is solved. L14 L93
  • Code-first development: throwing tools and technologies at problems. L14 Thinking in endpoints instead of features, and skipping concrete examples to write code directly. L82
  • API-first / code-level-first design: "extremely common". Khalil recommends BDD in Action. L93

Example A: code-first vs abstraction-first

Before: HOW first. The WHAT is never written down
After: WHAT as an executable spec, then the minimum HOW

Example B: a test as a "flag post in the future"

“Writing tests is just setting a flag post in the future to explain what we are about to realize.”L93

Project into the future, then bridge the gap with code. The test declares the value you are about to deliver and tells you when you're done. L93 The concrete example below is the DDD Forum "buy tickets" scenario. Khalil narrowed "billed + emailed" down to "an order placed" because the rest should be temporally decoupled. L82

The protocol driver and the four-layer acceptance-test stack are covered in Testing. L82

AI-era lens · Copilot

AI generates the physical (the sub-chapters) cheaply. Humans still own the chapters: role, goal, features and concrete examples. A feature file plus a failing acceptance test is the most precise prompt you can give an agent, and it caps over-generation at "minimum code to reach the goal".

The Feedback Loop: Everything Is a Guess L15

Take a frontend-only registration feature. It already contains many guesses: present the form, maintain form state, validate, marshal data, make the request, show a spinner (that actually works), present errors, and navigate to onboarding on success. Each one is an acceptance criterion you need confidence in. L15

“Everything that we do in software development is one big guess.” … “We're going to make a lot more mistakes than we will successes.”L15
  • Definition: feed forward, get feedback, learn, and make the next attempt faster and better. Refine one system before moving to the next. L91
  • Never go too far without knowing whether the abstractions you just made work. That's why testing comes right after code-first. L82
  • The first guess is theoretical: "does anyone even care?" (e.g. an anime debate app). You validate it with value identification. L93 A student summary Khalil endorsed: "Clarity means less guesses." L93
  • No known alternative: you can't reach a goal without splitting it into high and low levels (abstraction) and trying, failing, learning and retrying (feedback loop). L93
  • It takes the pressure off. The course itself was built by abstraction plus feedback loop. "You're not going to get whatever it is you're trying to do right the first time around… but do it again." This connects to the mindsets kill your designs and design it twice; see Mindsets. L90

The 3 problems with guesses L15

1. Not knowing what guesses you're making

This is typical of code-first developers who don't know the abstraction prism or abstraction layers. Layers are buckets for your abstractions and for implementing guesses. Fix: abstraction prism and guess points.

2. Not knowing how to validate a guess

Many developers only black-box test through E2E tests. Fix: more targeted tests via subject/system verification and Testing.

3. Loops that aren't tight enough

Write code, save, wait to compile, eyeball it. Answers arrive late. Manual testing doesn't build confidence, and its cost grows with the code and the team.

Tests are the maintainable fix L15

Every feature is a guess, and the number of guesses only grows. The only maintainable way to keep re-validating all of them is to cover them with tests. Also: clarify before building, and check with users that you built the right thing.

AI-era lens · Copilot

AI shrinks the feed-forward step to seconds, so feedback becomes the bottleneck. Generated code is still a guess. Humans own the theoretical guesses and the verification: tests, CI and real-user signals are what turn a generated guess into verified value.

Guess Points: A Map of Where the Guesses Live L15

The guess points are the value creation system seen through systems thinking. They apply abstraction and the feedback loop to decompose problems. Each guess point is a small input → output system with its own questions, mostly answered with tests. The output of one is the input of the next. "It's just systems thinking and it's just inputs and outputs." L15

  • Theoretical guess points: problem (vision, role, goal, capabilities; its output is the input to the solution), then solution, then architecture. Each contains smaller systems that bring the abstraction closer to code. L15
  • Physical guess points (past architecture): e.g. incoming adapter, stateful domain modelling and others. Each has its own questions, answered mostly with tests. They come from heuristics, mostly the stereotypical architecture (responsibility-first phase). L15
  • Frontend too? Yes. Frontend patterns come in pattern-first, then responsibility-first, then back to guess points in value-first. L15
  • More guess points? Possibly. It's Khalil's decomposition layout. A code review process, for example, is another system with its own inputs, outputs, processes and environment. L15
  • When to use: not right away. You first climb the phases of craftship. Guess points are the main decomposition approach in value-first, where you "just do the things that have the most value at the right time". L15 L82

Walked example: slot-booking system notifying ~7 services L93

  1. Problem clarity: value identification / impact mapping (who, what, impact, capabilities).
  2. Solution clarity: domain discovery. Big-picture event storming first, then process-model one story end to end.
  3. Problem-decomposition guess point: the experience, screens, data in and out, speed needs (maybe WebSockets).
  4. Architecture guess point: tools, tests, CI tests, and whether to go event-based from day one.
  5. Walking skeleton: then move into the physical.
Psychic entropy L93

Without a consistent process, decomposing a problem feels overwhelming. Knowing which guess point you're at tells you whether you have enough clarity to move forward. The full process is in FA²STR & the ideal developer workflow.

AI-era lens · Copilot

Guess points show which questions a human must answer (problem, solution, architecture) before handing a physical guess point to an agent. Each guess point's tests then act as the acceptance gate for what the agent produced.

Debugging by Zooming Out L82

If you keep changing something and it keeps failing, stop. "You're just so too deep into the how." Example: Khalil and a collaborator editing Dockerfile lines one at a time, with a 30-second feedback cycle on each change. L82

  1. Stop the change-fail loop.
  2. Zoom out and draw it upfront.
  3. Clarify what needs to happen and which responsibilities are involved.
  4. Descend one level and act again.
“When I'm coding, I actually spend very, very little time debugging because I always make sure I start with the question, do I know what I'm doing?”L82
Pre-flight questions L82

Do I know what I'm doing? Why? Who is it for? At what level does this need to happen?

Added by Copilot Read through the two essentials: the loop failed because each guess had no clear target. Zooming out goes back up the prism (abstraction) so the next feed-forward is aimed (feedback loop).

AI-era lens · Copilot

Re-prompting an assistant through changes that keep failing is the Dockerfile loop at machine speed. Restate the what (expected behavior, responsibilities, level) before asking for another how.

Mapping Jargon onto the Essentials L91

The hierarchy runs like this. Industry topics are interlinked (e.g. builder pattern → open-closed principle → …). Above them sit the 12 essentials. Above those sit the two mental models, abstraction and the feedback loop. Every essential stems from at least one of the two. L91 "There's two mental models for this whole course: it's just the feedback loop and abstraction," tied together by systems thinking. L90

Learn the 12, then classify L91

Horizontal decoupling alone pulls in hexagonal, onion, ports and adapters, stereotypical, core vs infra, levels of abstraction, separation of concerns… "It destroys the mind." Learn the 12 essentials and map each new term onto one of them instead of chasing every term. Many terms are "the same concept said a little differently".

Deriving composition L91

Abstraction: composition is "inherently the art of abstraction", building up layers. Feedback loop: encapsulation makes it evident what you can and can't do, and that constraint makes feed-forward easier.

Deriving sagas L91

Every app can be seen as states: signing up moves you from "not existing" to "just signed up". A saga chains events and state machines, e.g. Amazon's place order kicking off further events.

"No more room for it depends" L91

Run the scenario through systems thinking: theoretical → physical → which guesses → time budget. Short on time? E2E tests on the main flows, then high-value unit tests. Stripe API behaving oddly? Add more outgoing tests. That is what it depends on.

Beyond hexagonal L91

Hexagonal covers technical isolation from infrastructure. The course adds what drives development: BDD, DDD, impact mapping, value, pain and benefit. See Architecture and RDD.

12 Essentials II: Physical

The seven physical essentials turn a clear “what” into running, verified, shipped code. Slice work by features, split each slice into layers, push time-based requirements into events, compose the parts in one place, put a boundary around what you verify, deploy a walking skeleton first, and gate everything with a deployment pipeline.
