Example mapping, Given/When/ThenSolution → crossoverConcrete examples that become acceptance testsL82
Component stereotyping, build-vs-buy, core/supporting/genericArchitectureChoose and integrate architectural componentsL23 L93
Map any question to its essentials L85

Any developer question = one metaphysical essential + one physical or theoretical essential. The metaphysical ones “permeate every single thing that we do.” Example: “How do I do transactions in use cases?” is physical (writing code) → temporal decoupling, plus abstraction design (filling responsibility gaps). For tool questions, first ask which guess point you’re at. See mapping jargon onto the essentials.

Choose tools by responsibility L85

Khalil applies this to his own course: the needed responsibility was “collect feedback”, and Kajabi comments already did that, so no extra tool was needed.

FA²STR, Guess Points & The Ideal Developer Workflow

Three tools fit together. FA²STR is the design method you run on any problem. The guess points tell you which level you are testing at. The ideal developer workflow orders the work from theoretical clarity to a deployed feature. The workflow is the same for an MVP and for a mature product; only the effort per step changes. L27 L26 L40

FA²STR

Find → Architect → Automate → Specify → Test → Refine. An abstraction over the ideal developer workflow that is easier to remember. It trains the main skill, problem decomposition. L27 ↓

Guess points / test levels

Stateless (1), stateful (2), application (3), outgoing adapter (4), system (5), incoming adapter (6). “It is just all inputs and outputs… It's feature decomposition.” L81 ↓

Ideal developer workflow

Clarify theoretical guesses → broad-stroke architecture → walking skeleton → feature work with outer-loop and inner-loop tests. Based on the GOOS double loop. L26 L87 ↓

FA²STR: The Design Method L27 L52

Definition

A six-step design method: Find, Architect, Automate, Specify, Test, Refine. It takes you from a non-trivial design challenge to action steps covering decomposition, architecture, design, implementation and testing, on any side of the stack. It integrates the four pillars (design, testing, architecture, strategy) into one method. L27

Inputs and outputs of each step

StepInputOutputMaps to
FindProblem statement, design story, rough description or vague exampleResponsibilities (doing / knowing) plus concrete examples, and the starting guess point (the system under test). At higher levels: who / role, why, capabilities, then features, stories, acceptance criteria, scenarios and examples. L52 L27Problem + solution guess points; workflow step 1 L27
ArchitectResponsibilities + examplesThe subject under test (stateless → a function or static method). At higher levels: patterns, new components, the testing strategy and a broad-stroke architecture. L52 L27Architecture guess point; workflow step 2
AutomateResponsibilities, examples, SUTA clear picture of how you will test it: a test harness/scripts that also work in the deployment pipeline. Success criteria are defined before any code (“think backwards, start at the end”). L52 L27Test infrastructure / pipeline; workflow step 3
SpecifyOne exampleA failing test specification (red). At feature level, the first one is the outer-loop acceptance test built from the acceptance criteria. L52 L27Red
TestThe failing specTest and production code using arrange-act-assert and subject verification. Pass with fake it or the obvious implementation, then commit (green). L52Green
RefinePassing codeRefactor, removing duplication only when you've seen it three times. Commit, line up the next test, loop back to Specify (refactor). L52Refactor; nth looping L27
Upfront vs emergent

Upfront = Find, Architect, Automate (theory). Emergent = Specify, Test, Refine (the physical mechanics: red-green-refactor and the three laws of TDD). They are hard to learn together, so the course drilled the emergent part first on FizzBuzz and Palindrome, then added the upfront part with the Password Validator (see Kata Walkthroughs). L52 Find + Architect + Automate is “pretty much all of the upfront design we need to do”; after that comes emergent design and feature work. L87

Why it exists

  • The main skill is problem decomposition. The ideal developer workflow has many parts and is hard to remember. FA²STR is a more useful level of abstraction to think with. L27
  • It works for unfamiliar problems. Faced with, say, Spotify-style playlist reordering on the backend or auth on the frontend, you can tell yourself: “No, I actually do have the tool to do this. I know how to walk through this properly.” L27
  • A shared vocabulary lets a team or community break problems down the same way. L27
  • Khalil uses it “in my head every single time I need to think through a design problem.” L27 He “can't find a problem” it does not work for. L85
  • Phase: it's the final tool, used in the value-first phase of craftship once the essentials are in place (see 12 Essentials). L27

Course worked example: Notion ↔ Google Calendar two-way sync L27

The feature: Notion tasks sync to Google Calendar, and new Google Calendar events sync back to Notion.

  1. Find — who: Khalil. Role: business owner. Why: it speeds him up, since he does most of his work from Notion. Capabilities: synchronizing, writing into Google, writing into Notion, updates. Then write stories of intended use, document acceptance criteria and scenarios, and pass in concrete examples.
  2. Architect — patterns, any new components, testing strategy, broad-stroke architecture. If the architecture, testing strategy and patterns already exist, this step is a checklist.
  3. Automate — decide how the feature will be tested and set up the infrastructure. “Think backwards, start at the end, and I define the success criteria.”
  4. Specify / Test / Refine — turn the acceptance criteria into an outer-loop acceptance test, then work inwards with red-green-refactor, loop after loop.
Added by Copilot Filling in the Architect and Automate steps for this example
  • Patterns / components: a SyncTasks use case, a TaskSource gateway (Notion API), a CalendarGateway (Google API), a SyncLinks store mapping task id → event id, and a scheduled trigger.
  • Testing strategy: one E2E acceptance test against a test Notion workspace and a test calendar (outer loop). Use-case tests with in-memory fakes and a calendar spy (inner loop). Contract tests over the fake and real gateways (level 4).
  • Automate: npm test in the commit phase, with E2E in the acceptance phase against staging (see Deployment & Delivery).

The code for this lives in the worked example and the ideal workflow.

“The goal here is to develop your problem decomposition skills, because this is the main skill.”L27
AI-era lens · Copilot
  • Find + Architect + Automate is the spec you hand an agent: responsibilities, a table of concrete examples, the subject under test with its signature, and a runnable test command.
  • Specify + Test are how you verify its output. Write or approve the failing test yourself, and the agent's “done” becomes a green run rather than a claim.
  • Refine stays human-led. Agents tend to abstract too early. The rule of three is a good review filter.

FA²STR at the Stateless Guess Point L52 L51 L86

The stateless guess point is the first feedback-loop level: data in, data out, maybe some processing. Problems are simple enough to design in your head. The new idea at this level is awareness that the upfront work exists, even when it happens mentally. L52 L86

Responsibilities: doing vs knowing (from Responsibility-Driven Design)

Every responsibility is either a doing (an action, e.g. a User's setName) or a knowing (knowledge implied by a rule, e.g. getName, or “knows passwords without a digit are invalid”). “All of your requirements ever are going to be things that are done or they're going to be things that are known.” L52

That's one doing with many knowings, and “this is really going to be the majority of the tests that we're writing.” L52

Rules for each upfront step at this level

  • Find the guess point from the problem statement. The statement hints at the system under test. Later assignments won't tell you where to start, so you find it by elimination and by mapping the statement to a subject under test. The same problem could be tackled at the end-to-end, application or stateful points. L52
  • Know when to go to paper. “The mind can only hold up to, I think like four pieces of information at a time.” Collaborating objects exceed that, for example autosuggestion in a text editor or assigning a skin to a weapon in CS:GO. “Relationships… implies collaborations, which implies that they're going to be more complex and there's more moving parts.” Use paper, a whiteboard or the responsibility-driven design process (see Abstraction & RDD). L52
  • Automate before code. Have “at least a picture of that… before you begin to write your code.” Sometimes it's genuinely unclear, as with cross-system integrations, web scrapers, browser automation and Chrome extensions. In the course the starter project already provides the scripts. L52
  • Build metacognition now. Practise noticing the upfront steps on easy problems, because higher guess points will demand them on paper. L52

Two techniques inside Specify: AAA backwards & programming by wishful thinking L51

Overwhelm comes from starting where you are and heading toward a vague end. Start at the end instead: write the assert, then the act, then the arrange. While doing so, pretend the API already exists (“What if it was real?”) so you feel out its design in real time. Start with the most complex example, which settles most of the design early. “Vagueness does not compile.” L51

  • Everything you write is an API for someone else: code, project organisation, test scripts. People “find ways to… circumvent” abstractions they don't enjoy using. L51
  • Don't copy utility classes such as Khalil's Result, value object or entity classes. Students who did ended up complaining about the API. Grow your own through emergent design. L51
  • At the stateless level you only get result verification. Higher guess points need state and communication verification, which is how TDD teaches OO design: “So much of design is just structuring out relationships properly.” L51
  • Use the same backwards technique to design fixtures and builders at the stateful level, “treating your code as your paintbrush.” L86
Anti-patterns
  • Jumping straight to code on problems with collaborating objects, skipping upfront design. L52
  • Writing code before knowing how it will be tested. L52
  • Refactoring before you've seen the duplication three times. L52
  • Starting at arrange and fumbling toward a vague goal, only to find at the assert that the design doesn't work. L51

Worked Example: FA²STR End to End Added by Copilot

This takes one stateless piece of the course's Notion ↔ Google Calendar sync L27 and runs all six steps on it, following the inputs/outputs from L52. The problem and code are illustrative, not from the course.

Problem statement: “When a Notion task is synced, decide whether it becomes a Google Calendar event and what that event looks like. Timed tasks become timed events (30 minutes unless the task has a duration). Date-only tasks become all-day events. Tasks without a date, and archived tasks, are not synced.”

1 · Find: responsibilities + concrete examples

Doing: decide the calendar event for a task. Starting guess point: stateless, since it's data in and data out with no stored state or I/O.

KnowingExample input (task)Expected output
Knows undated tasks are not synced{ title: 'Someday idea' }{ kind: 'skip', reason: 'no-date' }
Knows archived tasks are not synced{ title: 'Old plan', date: '2026-10-01', time: '09:00', archived: true }{ kind: 'skip', reason: 'archived' }
Knows date-only tasks become all-day events{ title: 'Pay invoices', date: '2026-10-02' }allDay: true, date: '2026-10-02'
Knows timed tasks default to 30 minutes{ title: 'Write newsletter', date: '2026-10-01', time: '09:00' }start: '2026-10-01T09:00', end: '2026-10-01T09:30'
Knows a duration is respected, even past midnight (the most complex example){ title: 'Deploy window', date: '2026-10-01', time: '23:30', durationMinutes: 90 }start: '2026-10-01T23:30', end: '2026-10-02T01:00'

2 · Architect: the subject under test

3 · Automate: know how it runs before writing logic

4–5 · Specify & Test: one example at a time

  1. Undated → skip — red, then fake it: return { kind: 'skip', reason: 'no-date' }. Commit.
  2. Archived → skip — red. The fake no longer holds, so add a guard. Commit. The two skip cases share a shape, so parameterize them.
  3. Date-only → all-day — red, then the obvious implementation. Commit.
  4. Timed, default 30 min and timed with duration past midnight — red, green, commit each.

6 · Refine: duplication seen three times

Before — green, but the result wrapper and the date maths repeat
After — each rule reads like its knowing; tests unchanged and green

This function is a level-1 construct. In the real feature you'd reach it by drilling in from the SyncTasks use case, as shown in the ideal workflow. That drill-in is the n-loops idea. More katas using the same loop are in Kata Walkthroughs.

FA²STR at Any Level: n Loops L86 L89

FA²STR is an input → output system, so the same tool works from a pure function up to an architectural problem such as designing a job queue. L86 The same system-finding works for, say, a Chrome extension: what's its incoming adapter, and what's its system-level test? L89

  • Start anywhere, then drill in. “It doesn't matter where you start. What always tends to happen. Is you need to drill in. With several. Loops.” A student, Lucas, framed it as “n number of loops” rather than an “nth layer loop.” L86
  • Shortcuts are allowed. You don't have to test at every level. Double, triple or quadruple TDD versus one E2E level and “call it a day” depends on “the score of the game we're playing.” L86
  • Stack theoretical guesses. An extendable architecture or platform lets you skip the Architect step for infrastructure, so physical guesses go faster. That's the case for strategic monoliths and well-designed platforms. L86 L85
  • Level 3 Find is the hard one. See why level 3 is hard. L89

On AI, Khalil's view is that it “crunches down and minimizes” some of the state-change and decision-making logic you'd otherwise write. The skill left is knowing the inputs and outputs you plug it into and the goalpost, and it still has to connect to the rest of the process model. L89

Guess Points as Test Levels L81 L87 L89

The physical guess points exist “to carve out your ability to write tests strategically.” L87 They come from systems thinking plus vertical slicing, so each level is an input → output system with its own subject under test. L81 The theoretical guess points (problem, solution, architecture) are mapped in 12 Essentials I.

LevelGuess pointWhat's verifiedTypical testNotes
1StatelessData transformation. Result verification only: data in, data out.Unit test on a pure function or static method; concrete examples, then parameterizedFizzBuzz, Palindrome, Password Validator; utilities and validation. L87 L52 L81
2StatefulOne state machine: invariants, valid and invalid transitions. State verification (state “loiters”, so you inquire into it).Unit tests on entities / value objects, with fixtures and builders for initial state“Problems are stateful.” Encapsulation protects how the model changes. L86 L87 L89
3ApplicationUse cases: coordination and control, indirect inputs/outputs, time, transactions. A mixture, adding communication verification, the only level where you do it.High-value unit test / use-case test with in-memory repos and handwritten spiesDeveloper boundary. ~80% of the work. Khalil's favorite guess point. L87 L89
4Outgoing adapterThat external infra (DB, APIs, clock) behaves as the contract says, so fakes stay in parity with real implementations.Contract / integration test (.ispec.ts) looping one spec over every implementation“You're testing the contract, not the implementation.” L81 L87 L89
5System (end to end)The whole system as a black box. Result verification only; other types here are “bad practice.”E2E acceptance test: Gherkin → executable spec → protocol driver → system. Happy path + 1–2 sad pathsCustomer boundary. The one acceptance test per feature. L81 L87 L89
6Incoming adapterRoutes and allowed request shapes haven't changed.API / driver testMatters less on the frontend. L81 L87
—ExecutionAfter users use it: “are we getting the KPIs we want?” (usage, sales…)Metrics, not testsCloses the value-creation feedback loop. L81

The verification mapping is “not strict”; these are the predominant types. L87 L89 also mentions a “level 7” in passing, near deployments and feature flags, without defining it. L89 Techniques for each level (spies, builders, contract tests) are in Testing, and verification types in Subject/System Verification.

“Level 3 is the developer boundary and level 5 is the customer boundary.”L89
Why level 3 matters most
  • It's “the heart, the core” of what makes your app special. It's pure code with fast tests, full control and easy edge cases, and it gives “crystal clear clarity on the way that our system is interacting with libraries, APIs, and also how it's being called.” Khalil calls it “quite literally life-changing.” L87
  • High-value unit tests on core code should give about 80% confidence in the commit phase. That needs a testing strategy and decoupling from infrastructure. L81
  • Applications force purposefulness: working from level 3 or level 5 stops you modelling an infinite world of entities. L89
Why level 3 is hard (and so rarely done)

In FA²STR's Find step at level 3 you have to find every responsibility at that level: time, repositories, inputs, saving transactions, pulling events out of aggregates, and cross-cutting concerns like auth. That's why so few people write high-value use-case tests, and why the course teaches inside-out (level 2 first) while the projects go top to bottom. L89 Testing is hard to learn more broadly because “you can't really get good at testing without getting good at object oriented design and also understanding architecture.” L87 Guess point 3 was expected to need 3–4 parts to teach. L86

AI-era lens · Copilot

Picking the level is the judgment call agents get wrong most often. Left alone they write either browser-driven E2E tests for every edge case or mock-heavy tests of private helpers. Name the level and the verification type in the prompt: “level-3 use-case test, in-memory repo, spy on the mailer.”

The Ideal Developer Workflow L26 L87 L81

Definition

A way to put the 12 essentials together to move from the theoretical to the physical through the guess points, on any side of the stack. L26 Khalil pieced it together from the experts: GOOS (Steve Freeman), Continuous Delivery, Clean Architecture, DDD and BDD. L40 It's a consistent way to work “95% of the time,” frontend or backend. L87

  1. Clarify the theoretical guesses (non-negotiable) — work through the abstraction prism: vision, role, goal, capabilities, down to concrete examples. Khalil's standard answer to problem questions on Discord is “first, we need to clarify the theoretical guesses.” L26
  2. Broad-stroke architecture — relatively high level, but clarify the patterns, architectural components and the testing strategy: how you'll verify features work and how tests plug into the deployment pipeline. L26 This step is for developers: shared clarity on patterns, tools, roles and responsibilities. L81
  3. Build, test and deploy a walking skeleton — one slice of functionality taken all the way to deployment, even if tiny. L26 (See Walking Skeleton.)
  4. Feature work with nth looping — outer-loop tests plus inner-loop tests, then fill in the remaining gaps (~20% of the work) before shipping and moving to the next feature. L26
Workflow stepFA²STRGuess points touchedOutput
1 · Clarify theoretical guessesFindProblem, solutionStories, acceptance criteria, concrete examples L27
2 · Broad-stroke architectureArchitectArchitecturePatterns, components, testing strategy L27
3 · Walking skeletonAutomateAll physical levels, thinlyTestable architecture + deployed tiny slice + pipeline L87
4 · Feature workSpecify, Test, Refine (n loops)5 → 3 → 2/1 → 4/6A shipped feature; next feature L87

FA²STR is the abstraction layer over this workflow. L27 Steps 1–3 are the upfront part and step 4 is emergent. L87 The first steps apply to new features on existing projects too: clarify the theory, know the architecture, know how features are verified, and have infrastructure to run high-value tests. L26

Outer loop vs inner loop

Outer loop · customer

Acceptance tests that turn user stories into proof that “this is what the customer wants.” L40 Written in the user's language at the system boundary (level 5). One acceptance test per feature, shared by frontend, backend, mobile and desktop teams (Dave Farley), and never rewritten per environment. Result verification only. L87 Run it as E2E or as a high-value unit/integration test. L26

Inner loop · developer

Things developers need to know about: logic that isn't a feature but could cause problems if untested, e.g. a validation object for a User or JobPosting. L26 Unit tests plus incoming and outgoing contract tests. You don't need all of them, and choosing is the “strategy” part. L40 The main inner test is the level-3 use-case test. L87

Per feature, step by step L87

  1. Failing E2E acceptance test — system boundary (level 5), in the user's language, from the user's perspective. It can mention pages or things that don't exist yet.
  2. Move in one level — write a failing use-case test at the developer boundary (level 3). About 80% of the time is spent here.
  3. Loop over every scenario — a feature is one success case and many failure cases (“five, six, seven, eight, nine”). Mention things that don't exist yet and carve them out, recursing into smaller objects and back up.
  4. The remaining ~20% — make the E2E test pass by filling in the other guess points (outgoing and incoming adapter tests), then hook up the view: components plus component tests.
  5. Connect everything — the feature is done. Deploy, then tidy up with infrastructure tests (DB, service connections: contract/driver tests). L81

Outer + inner loop pair for the sync feature

The CalendarSpy and in-memory fakes need contract tests against the real gateways (level 4) to stay honest. See Testing. L81 L87

Heuristics
  • E2E: the happy path plus one or two sad paths (check that error messages reach the screen). Then about 12–20 high-value tests with concrete examples, parameterized to add data cheaply. L81
  • Push what E2E can't see down to level 3. You can't sensibly assert “I should get an email” at E2E (automate logging into Gmail?). Verify it with an email spy at the application level. L87
  • New abstraction → new tests. “Anytime we mention a new abstraction, we're going to want to write some new tests.” L26
  • If testing a feature means starting React, React is doing the coordinating. Keep features and their specs apart from the UI, libraries and APIs. L87
  • It's an ideal. Legacy code and cut corners are real. Work toward it, and use it to measure how far off you are. L87 L26
Anti-patterns
  • Khalil's own mistake: writing all the pure application-layer code first, then trying to deploy, and hitting “all these weird CORS errors.” Deploy as early as possible. L81
  • Building for a month, then finding deployment is hard: “a very bad situation to be in.” L87
  • Mixing feature development with architecture setup, e.g. discovering DB issues mid-feature. It's “a lot cognitively.” L87
  • E2E-only or unit-only strategies: “You're always going to fail.” L87
  • Leaving internal logic untested because “it's not a feature.” L26
“It is an ideal and ideals are never perfect. But having this as something that we could use to determine and know how far off we are is incredibly powerful.”L26
AI-era lens · Copilot
  • Humans own the outer loop. Write or approve the acceptance test. It is the one spec the agent can't negotiate with.
  • Agents are good in the inner loop. Level-3 tests are fast and have no I/O, so an agent can go red → green → refactor through many scenarios quickly. Review the scenario list, not only the code.
  • The workflow gives fixed checkpoints (skeleton deployed, acceptance test red, inner tests green, acceptance green) at which you review agent output.

From Theoretical to Physical L72 L89

After the theoretical guess points (the FeedBook case study, see Theoretical Design & DDD), you already know how to organise code, you're aware of the stereotypical architecture, and you're committed to vertical slices. “When we move to the physical, we have literally all of this stuff.” L72 The crossover from what to how is the acceptance test. L81

Ideal kickoff on a real project
  1. Get the deployment pipeline working. L72
  2. Write the end-to-end test — “Make sure that end-to-end test works in a prod-like environment.” L72
  3. Jump into level-three tests — “where all the fun stuff starts.” L72

In practice, with a familiar standard architecture, Khalil plans, clarifies the inputs and outputs, process-models, then goes straight to level 3 and uses the required inputs to create the needed entities and value objects. L89

The course's learning order (inside-out)
  1. Level 2, stateful first — “Because we're still learning the physical, we're actually going to jump to level two.” L72
  2. Then level 3 — do the modules in sequence (theoretical → level 2 → level 3), because level 3 has too many responsibilities to find at once. L89
  3. Projects go top to bottom — the backend and frontend projects apply the workflow outside-in for real. L89
Starting level 3 from one feature L89

Create a use case and go through all its success and failure scenarios, letting the needed concepts emerge. Forget the word “aggregate” at first. Ask what goes in, what must come out, and what must change all at once. Don't create base classes such as AggregateRoot until you absolutely need them.

Khalil considered a faster path (skip entities, build success/failure cases, then discover you need entities) because jumping straight to a feature is more motivating, but kept the current order for now. L89

Shipping an MVP & When to Go Light L40 L85

Asked by a student (Aaron) who already had designs ready how to ship an MVP fast, Khalil's answer was to use the same workflow. “Those steps are going to be the same, regardless of if you're shipping an MVP or you're going to be developing a new feature on an existing product.” L40

What changes between an MVP and a mature product L40
  1. How much time you have.
  2. How much effort you're willing to put in.
  3. The quality of the guesses you've made.

The MVP path: theoretical → testing strategy → physical L40

  1. Step 0: learn the mental models — metaphysics and at least the 12 essentials. They work “like landmines and the opposite of landmines,” telling you what to avoid and what to move toward.
  2. Problem guess point — do you have clarity on the problem?
  3. Solution guess point — how you'll solve it and the boundaries between domains. Process-model the one or two user stories you most want to build first.
  4. Architecture guess point — decide the patterns, tools and architectural components.
  5. Testing strategy (the bridge) — outer-loop acceptance tests from user stories, plus inner-loop developer tests (unit, incoming/outgoing contract).
  6. Walking skeleton — draw the architecture, build one user story as a vertical slice from UI to DB, decide the project structure, and deploy it. Expect it to be messy and slow. It's worth it because it sets up the initial testing strategy for the whole product.
  7. Recommended MVP tests — start with either E2E tests or a high-value integration test. Either way you need an acceptance test for customer correctness and a set of tests for the internals.

When to go light

Unvalidated MVP · zero theoretical guesses

The priority is getting real answers from customers. Heavy testing and top quality aren't critical, but build “on a good foundation of guesses.” L40 Multi-loop TDD at every guess point? “Maybe not.” Push one theoretical guess through as fast as possible, then “start playing defense and adding tests at the physical level.” L85

New feature, existing product

Run the full workflow. If architecture, testing strategy and patterns already exist, the Architect step shrinks to a checklist. L27 The walking skeleton and pipeline are already there, so start at the outer-loop test. L26

Platform · stacked guesses

With shared infrastructure (deployment, architecture, known services, tested code) you can skip guesses at some guess points and score faster over time. L85 An extendable architecture lets you skip Architect for infrastructure. L86

Familiar standard architecture

Plan, clarify inputs/outputs, process-model, then drop straight into level 3 and skip setting up level-5 infrastructure first. L89 How many loops to test at “depends on the score of the game.” L86

Recommended viewing for an MVP (as of recording) L40

Course contentWhyIn this guide
Metaphysics + 12 essentialsMental models (landmines and anti-landmines)12 Essentials I · II
Ideal developer workflowThe fixed sequence of stepsabove
Theoretical guess pointsSee them as inputs and outputs; build a checklistGuess points
Abstraction videoThe abstraction prism as a roadmap to know you have everything before code. “This is also just BDD.”Abstraction prism

Frontend Architecture 2 Q&A, Value First testing strategyBuilders, application interface; test strategyTesting
Anti-patterns
  • Inventing a different process for MVPs instead of dialling effort per step. L40
  • Heavy testing and polish on an unvalidated MVP (poor allocation of effort). L40 L85
  • Skipping clarity on the guesses before building. L40
AI-era lens · Copilot

AI makes the physical side cheap, so an MVP's bottleneck moves to the quality of the theoretical guesses and to the acceptance test that defines “done.” A deployed walking skeleton gives an agent a working, tested frame to extend one slice at a time, instead of generating a whole system you then have to deploy.

Testing: Principles & Techniques

Testing is one of the four intertwined pillars, and the core skill is to “isolate exactly what it is you would like to test and forget everything else.” This section collects the concrete techniques: commit discipline, AAA backwards, naming tests as responsibilities, picking the verification type per guess point, 4-layer acceptance tests, hand-written fakes kept honest by contract tests, builders for fixtures, and choosing a strategy by ROI. L31 L12

TechniqueUse it whenSmell it fixes
Commit on greenEvery TDD cycleHistory full of broken “save points”
AAA backwards + wishful thinkingStarting any test, especially when overwhelmed10–15 minutes of arrange, then the assert doesn’t work
Responsibility specs + it.eachNaming describe/it, 3+ similar examples“sets result to true and error to null when…”
Verification per guess pointDeciding what to assertProving emails were sent from an E2E test
4-layer acceptance testsEvery feature, E2EFlaky E2E tests
Hand-written spiesVerifying side effects (indirect outputs)Inline library-mock soup
Contract testsEvery fake you write“We’re only testing our mocks”
Builders for fixturesLong state-setup in arrangeTests that are 30 lines of game.move(...)
Value-first strategyDeciding which tests to write at allOne testing dogma for every project

Why the boundary matters and the definitions of result, state and communication verification are in Subject/System Verification. Kata-level examples are in Kata Walkthroughs.

Testing Roadmap by Phase of Craftship L31

Khalil’s own testing started badly. He tested things that didn’t need testing (Sequelize models) and wrote flaky E2E tests. “Testing sucked for me.” His fix was a roadmap that follows the phases of craftship. You need “to build up a little bit in all of them [the pillars] in order to do even one of them.” L31

PhaseTesting skill to build
Code-firstBuild basic backend operations. The backend is “raw”: no front-end tools or thought-leadership noise, so you think purely about structure and tests.
Best-practice-first (1)TDD mechanics: red-green-refactor, start from examples, parameterize. Simple input-output tests (stateless).
Best-practice-first (2)Non-flaky E2E tests with four layers of abstraction. Test “the entire system as a function”. Run tests in different environments (composition).
Pattern-firstDecouple core from infrastructure (hexagonal / clean / onion, “all different ways to say the same thing”). High-value unit and integration tests, stubs, mocks, edge cases, state and communication verification, then contract tests.
Value-firstPick testing strategies: the ideal developer workflow and its variations.

Sources: L31, with the pattern-first order (result → communication → contract tests) from L91.

The test type is the boundary you draw

“All tests fundamentally are input-output tests.” The name follows from which systems you include in the boundary: L31

  • Integration test: application → outgoing infrastructure, all the way to the database and the services it uses.
  • Unit test: application + domain logic, up to but not including the database. Pure core code.
  • E2E test: the entire system treated as a function.
“You just want the highest level of confidence to have to do the least amount of work based on where you currently are.”L31

Red-Green-Refactor Commit Discipline L44

Commits exist to make your work easy to read for whoever gives you feedback. L44

Rules
  • Only commit on green. Committing on red is like pausing Mario mid-jump over the flames: “not a very safe place to be for you to unpause the game.” Green is standing on a platform. L44
  • Two reasons to commit on green, and the message must say which: new functionality, or a refactoring (“all that we’re doing here is changing the structure of the code”). The wording (refactor/design/improvements) doesn’t matter; the intent must be clear. L44
  • Exception: the Emergent Design section (the first assignments). Commit on every phase (red, green, refactor) so reviewers can check your TDD mechanics. From the stateless section onward, go back to committing on green only. L44 L56
  • Rule of three: after seeing duplication three times, “you’re probably going to want to refactor. In fact, you should.” L44
  • Flip the switch: after going green, deliberately break the code, watch it go red, then restore it. That proves the test can fail. L44
  • Make commit messages express behavior, not internals: not “return result as true and error as null on valid password”. L56
Before — red save points, messages that hide intent
After — every commit is a green platform with a declared intent

More commit reviews (“a story of commits”) are in Kata Walkthroughs. L60

Comments Only Explain “Why” L48

“Your code should always express what happens. Comments should express why you’ve chosen to do what you’re doing.”L48
  • If code can’t say what it does, that’s a code problem. “Always make that readability change first. And at a last resort, use comments.” L48
  • The last resort is almost always the why, because code has no way to express rationale. L48
  • This comes up again and again in kata reviews: “delete the comments”. L60
Before — comments narrate the “what”
After — names carry the “what”, one comment carries the “why”

Arrange-Act-Assert Backwards & Programming by Wishful Thinking L51

Overwhelm comes from not knowing how you’ll make it work. If you start where you are and head toward a vague end, there are endless paths. If you start at the end, there are few. “Vagueness does not compile.” L51

  1. Assert — write the expected output first, using the most complex example, so the hard design is settled early. L51
  2. Act — write the call that would produce it, as if it already existed. L51
  3. Arrange — set up the inputs last. L51
Programming by wishful thinking

Imagine the code already exists and write it piece by piece, as if real, even though it won’t compile yet. Judge whether you’d enjoy using the API, then implement it. It is abstraction applied: specify what, not how. It’s the same idea as “tell, don’t ask” and declarative code. L51 L81 “What if it was real? Think about that.” L51

Before — forwards: arrange first, discover the API is awkward only at the assert
After — backwards: the assert designs the API (a result plus all errors)

Khalil first wrote a single error key. After rereading the spec (“for all errors in occurrence”) he changed it to an array, before any implementation existed. L51 In the emergent-design demo he also renamed result.result to output.result because it read badly. L55

Everything is an API

Code, project layout, test scripts. “Every single time that you’re writing code… is you designing an API for someone else to use.” People will get around abstractions they don’t enjoy using. L51

Clarify before you verify

Get clear on the input/output shapes (object vs string vs array) and how each responsibility will be asserted, before you code. L58

Don’t copy utility classes

Students copied Khalil’s Result class and then complained about its API. “Don’t copy mine, just do your own”: grow a minimal one through emergent design. L51

It scales up

The same move finds state APIs (game.getCurrentPlayer(), game.getGameState()) and builder APIs. At higher guess points it forces you to understand collaborations: “so much of design is just structuring out relationships properly.” L84 L78 L51

AI-era lens · Copilot

Write the assert yourself, because it is the spec. Then let the assistant fill in the act/arrange plumbing and the implementation. An agent will happily invent an awkward API that satisfies a vague test. A hand-written assertion pins the contract and leaves you to judge whether the API is pleasant.

Naming Tests as Responsibility Specifications L56 L59

A test file has two parts. Responsibility specifications (the describe/it titles) name a doing or a knowing and stay abstract. Examples are as concrete as possible. Drive the code with concrete examples and end up with abstract responsibility specs. L59 Responsibilities come from Responsibility-Driven Design: everything a system does is either knowing or doing. L56

Before — names describe the how (keys, flags, null)
After — names state the what; the how lives in the body
Heuristics from the kata reviews
  • Lead each new responsibility with one concrete example, and refactor to it.each once you see duplication three times. L56 L57 Refactoring applies to tests too: three “Fizz” tests become one “returns Fizz for multiples of three”. L45
  • Encapsulate what varies. Hard-coded reasons in names and assertions produced “too long” tests that still said “too short”. Put the reason in the example data. L56
  • Keep each example’s input and expected output together in one object. L59
  • Parameterized tables keep a suite open-closed: a new example is just a new row. L61 They’re cheap: parameterize to add “20 more units of data”, and they run fast because they’re pure. L81
  • Don’t over-refine examples, but “never sacrifice readability”. L59

Full reviews: Kata Walkthroughs.

AI-era lens · Copilot

Responsibility specs are the part of a test a reviewer reads first, and they make good prompts. A list of “knows that… / can…” titles tells an agent what to build without prescribing how. Watch for generated names that leak internals (“returns object with errors array”), because they lock the test to one implementation.

Which Verification at Which Guess Point L53 L87 L84

Verifying the assert is one of the hardest parts of testing. It’s easy at the stateless level and gets harder as the relationships grow. “Each guess point requires different forms of subject verification.” L53 Definitions and examples of the three types are in Subject/System Verification.

Guess pointSubject under testPredominant verificationExample
1 · StatelessFunction / static methodResult onlyisPalindrome("mom") → true
2 · StatefulEntity, value object, state machineState: state “hangs out”, so you inquire into itchess game.getGameState()
3 · ApplicationUse case with injected collaboratorsMixture, adding communication: the only guess point where you do itCreateUser + email spy
4 · Outgoing adapterRepo / clock / service implementationsContract testsClock contract
5 · System (E2E)Whole system as a black boxResult only201 response, page shown

Mapping: L87 (“not a strict mapping”), L53, L84, L89. The six test levels (incoming adapter as level 6) come from L81.

Direct inputs/outputs

Passed in or returned, like the palindrome string. L81 L87

Indirect inputs

The state of injected dependencies. Seed the user repo with an existing user and the same use case must fail (“user already exists”). L87

Indirect outputs

Commands sent to dependencies: save called, cache.hasItem called, email sent. A repo can be both an indirect input and an indirect output. L87

Before — state/communication checks forced into an E2E test
After — E2E checks the result; the application-level test checks communication with spies

Being pedantic, Khalil noted that result.isSuccess() plus reaching into the success object is closer to state verification on the result. The spy call assertions are the communication verification. L87

Anti-patterns
  • State or communication verification at E2E is “bad practice”. It conflates concerns and makes tests messy. At E2E the email may just be a no-op. L87
  • An email-provider sandbox doesn’t validate delivery. At most it saves money per run. L87
  • Real network calls to external services in tests slow them down. L53
“It’s the hardest one but it’s the one that’s going to lead to the tests that are the most valuable.” (communication verification)L84

Acceptance Tests: the 4-Layer Architecture L82 L81

An acceptance test is a concrete example (Given/When/Then) put straight into the code base. It’s a shared executable specification that can drive either the frontend or the backend. L82 It’s where work crosses over from what to how. L81 E2E tests “are incredible when they are designed with the appropriate levels of abstraction”. L31

Rules
  • “Then” tense: past tense usually fits (“order placed”, “email sent”). Present tense (“I should now be logged in”) is fine for UI experience. The hard rule is to describe the system the way the user interacts with it. L82
  • How many: the happy path plus one or two sad paths (error messages show up on screen). Then about 12–20 high-value tests with concrete examples and parameterization. L81 Roughly 10–12 application-level scenarios per acceptance test. L82
  • Idempotent: tests can run “over and over” and still work. L82
  • Existing code: start with a characterization test that pins current I/O end to end (tailor’s pins), then “move in a layer”. Don’t rewrite from scratch. L81 L84
  • Reusable page objects pay off: a friend’s team using four-tier E2E went “from requirement to implement it with just mixing together a couple of page objects”. L92

Three test categories (acceptance, unit, infrastructure): Subject/System Verification. Where acceptance tests run in the pipeline: Deployment & Delivery. Where they sit in the double loop: Ideal Developer Workflow.

Test Doubles & Hand-Written Spies L73

Test double

“A test double is just anything that stands in for the real one.” Skip the spy/stub/mock taxonomy and call them fakes or test doubles. L73 L84 “In-memory repo” also sidesteps the naming debate. L87

A student used a mocking library to spy on a collaborator and felt something was off. Khalil updated the assignment to require a hand-written spy: “I think you need to learn that. And we all need to learn that.” The fake plays two roles: it implements the email service contract, and it records calls for assertions. L73

Before — library-mock soup, inline and duplicated per test file
After — a hand-written fake that implements the contract and records calls
Rules
  • Give the real collaborator an interface so the fake can implement it. L73
  • Put hand-written spies in their own files, not inline in tests (inline leads to duplication). Hand-written fakes are preferred because growing the contract forces you to implement it. Library mocks are fine only if they “yell at you” when the contract grows. L87
  • Library mocks are for trivial stubs whose behavior doesn’t matter (“this thing needs a logger… here, just take this”). Stateful dependencies are indirect inputs, so use fakes covered by contract tests. L81
  • Wait for the rule of three before extracting a generic spy contract. L73
  • Use controllable fakes to set up “the state of the world” for each edge case: user exists, banned, email taken, username taken. L87

Contract Tests Keep Fakes Honest (and the Clock role) L81 L87 L89

A common complaint about high-value tests is “we’re not testing anything, just what we put into the tests.” That feeling comes from missing contracts: the fake and the production implementation have no test parity. L81 Without contracts, mocks create “two divergent code paths”. L91 The fix is not “stop mocking”. It’s one contract test run against every implementation of the role. L87

Worked example: decoupling from time L89

new Date() and Math.random() are infrastructure because they touch the system clock and the random generator. “It’s not about where it comes from, it’s about what it touches.” L84 Time is an application concern (level 3), not a domain (level 2) concern. State machines protect their data and change when told to. Knowing when to tell them belongs to the application, and time can live in its own context folder. L89

Before — hidden dependency on the system clock
After — a Clock role with a real and a fake actor

The repository version of the same idea (userRepo.ispec.ts looping over InMemoryUserRepo and the production repo) is in Subject/System Verification. L81 It’s expensive because it hits the real backend, but it keeps fake and real in parity. L87

When the fake is hard to write L81
  • Complex filters/aggregations: find the concrete use cases you actually need, and pull heavy filtering into its own abstraction (e.g. “search”) tested on its own.
  • Don’t build a do-everything fake filter. Extend the in-memory implementation until the contracts are covered.
  • If the DB does the heavy lifting, test the contract and “let the external tool do the external tooling”. “Raise the level of abstraction of what it is you’re looking at to test.”
“It’s okay to mock… but just make sure you mock correctly… You want to create parity between what’s real and fake.”L89
“What you want is your production code and your test code to be the exact same.”L91
AI-era lens · Copilot

AI-generated mocks can lie. They return whatever makes the test green, and nothing checks them against production. Ask for a hand-written fake plus a contract spec looped over fake and real, so a hallucinated fake fails the moment it diverges.

Fixtures = Initial State, Encapsulated with Builders L78

Fixture

“What is a fixture really? … It means the initial state.” If arrange/act lines only get the system into a state, they are setup, so move them into a builder. L78

Khalil’s example is chess: detect a checkmate (Scholar’s mate, Fool’s mate). It sits at the stateful guess point because it depends on a sequence of state changes. The assertions were carved out by wishful thinking: getGameState() is end and the reason type is checkmate. Ideally the test would “describe the state of the universe” at game end. L78

Before — the test is mostly moves
After — a named initial state; the test shows only intent
Rules
  • Name well-known states in team or domain vocabulary (“Scholar’s mate”, “the most brutal game ever”). Moves could even live in a file. L78
  • Design the builder API by wishful thinking. Treat code as a paintbrush: “we’ll figure out how to make it happen later.” L78
  • Turn in-memory repos into builders (e.g. seed N random users) so tests stay domain-driven and readable. Store plain objects, with a mapper if needed, to keep parity with the real store. L87
  • Real-database strategies need builders even more, because setup is complex. L64

Stateful modelling and invariants: Theoretical Design & DDD.

Value-First Testing Strategies L64 L92

Prompted by a post on “TDD-induced design damage”, Khalil objects to prescribing “one testing strategy 1000% in every scenario”. Learn every way to test, then choose by ROI: time, cost and the quality you need. “There is no perfect testing strategy. It’s going to be entirely context dependent.” L64

OptionBenefitsDrawbacksChoose when
A · App-level + real DBTests the DB for real, no mocksComplex setup (builders). Slow at hundreds of edge cases. Alone, it leaves the request → use case translation unverifiedSqueezing “just a bit more” confidence tactically. Add incoming tests.
B · Controller → real DBAs A, plus covers validation and extraction of requestsAs A; “can get very expensive”“A really nice middle ground”, e.g. if you don’t want E2E. Khalil likes it a lot.
C · Use cases + fake DB, with IDW E2EHundreds of fast concrete examples; result verificationInfrastructure interactions need communication verification (spies), which is more complexKhalil’s default: “combine those two together, we’re in really good shape.”

All rows: L64. “This tiny little connection [controller → use case] has messed me up plenty of times.” Before adopting the ideal developer workflow, Khalil wrote only high-value unit tests, and then “nothing’s really working properly”. L64

Two valid strategies L92

Strategy 1

E2E (whole thing, touches the DB) + carve inward with high-value unit tests (no DB). For most task-based UI apps, E2E is the best way to begin and gives the greatest certainty. L92

Strategy 2

Incoming (contract) tests + high-value integration tests. Works for any app with an interface. More relevant with many clients (REST + GraphQL). L92 L64

Choosing

“It’s just your level of confidence in your code base.” Logic-heavy apps: many application/domain examples. Simple apps: check that major components (Stripe, etc.) work together. Mixing is fine: “You don’t have to have a perfect parity.” L92

This verifies everything before the app call: routing, extraction, validation. It minimizes the uncertainty of Express, “a whole… framework”. A high-value integration test uses the same entry point with the real app, all the way to the DB. L92 For the application interface itself, see Composition.

“E2E tests, they suck, right?… But there’s very little that’s going to be as good as E2E tests.”L92

“We Don’t Have Time to Test” L91

A student’s managers said there was no time for tests. Khalil’s answer was about strategy and roles, not craftsmanship. L91

It’s a strategy decision

“I don’t have time” is a limiting belief. It’s really a value choice: fast / good / cheap, pick two. Shipping without tests trades quality for time. L91

Capability ≠ choice

“There’s a difference between not being able to do something and not doing something.” All-manual testing scores 1 on subject/system verification, and that is acceptable sometimes. L91

Know your role

“Customers [are] supposed to make business decisions and developers make development decisions.” Your professional responsibility is to tell stakeholders the consequences, ideally ahead of time. L91 Automated testing is an investment, and paying a firm for manual testing is valid if the customer knows the alternatives. L92

Practice off the clock

Tire-change analogy: the customer cares about the outcome and wouldn’t want experiments. Practice new techniques on your own time and bring proven skills to work. L91

  1. Stop the bleeding — first ask: “do the features that need to work right now work?” Wrap the whole thing in E2E tests (tailor’s pins) before any pattern-first surgery. L92
  2. Short on time — E2E tests on the main things, then high-value unit tests if there’s time. L91 With zero customers, “maybe I’ll just chuck some end-to-end tests”. L64
  3. Weird third-party API (e.g. Stripe) — add more outgoing tests there. That’s what “it depends” depends on. L91
  4. Switch to test-first — when the potential negative value outweighs the cost of building a little slower. L84
  5. Roll it in — apply the approach on the next feature, or on an existing feature in a new branch, and make it part of your infrastructure. L91
Don’t
  • Test only for craftsmanship’s sake. Do what keeps customers and users in benefit. L91
  • Experiment with unfamiliar techniques on paid client work. L91

Mindset side of this (“know your role”): Mindsets. Career angle: Learning Path & Career.

Each kata below is written up the same way: the problem, the test sequence the course used, what the reviews caught, and the code before and after that feedback. Code narrated in a lesson is marked Reconstructed. Illustrations of the feedback are marked Added by Copilot. The last topic collects the recurring feedback into one review checklist.

How to Do Kata Assignments L43 L44 L52

  1. One branch per attempt — use the pattern <project>-<date>-<iteration>. You can redo the kata several times, even on the same day, and each attempt has a single URL to share for feedback. L43
  2. Use the grading checklist as your spec — Khalil copies it straight into the test file to start. L45 L42
  3. Map the problem to input → output before coding. A stateless guess point is “data in, data out.” L46
  4. Loop red → green → refactor, one example per loop, committing at the points shown in the diagram. L44 L49
  5. Open a pull request so reviewers can comment inline. Reviews read the end result first, then walk back through the commits. L46 L47
SectionCommit whenMessageSource
Emergent design (FizzBuzz, Palindrome)On every phase shift: red, green, refactor. This lets reviewers check your mechanics.red: returns Fizz for 3 / green: … / refactor: …L44 L45 L46
Stateless guess point onward (Password Validator …)Green only (new functionality) and after a refactor. Never on red. Committing on red is “pausing Mario mid-jump over the flames.”Say which kind: new: … vs refactor: …L44 L55 L56
Rules of the stateless guess point (as enforced in the reviews)
  • Data in, data out. The SUT is a function or a static method on a stateless class. Don’t instantiate it. L52 L54 L56
  • Red for the right reason. A missing function or import is a compile failure. Export a stub and import it first, so the test fails on logic. L45 L49
  • Simplest transformation to green. Fake it until you see duplication three times. Obvious implementation is allowed when you’re confident. L45 L47 L60
  • Rule of three. Ignore duplication in red and green. Refactor it only on the third occurrence, and never add examples during a refactor. L45 L52
  • One example at a time. Several examples at once force more complex transformations and give unclear failures. L49 L55 L62
  • Refactor XOR transformation. A step does one or the other. L49
  • Refactor the tests too, not just production code. L45
“You only want to commit on red when you're in red for the right reason.”L49
AI-era lens · Copilot

Agents default to the obvious implementation and batch several tests together. Ask for one failing test, then “the smallest fake-it change that makes only this test pass,” and commit before the next prompt. Your commit history then shows the red → green → refactor path, and each AI diff stays small enough to review.

First Milestone: “Just Make It Work” Backend API L42 L86

Problem: build three user use cases for DDD Forum as a RESTful API. The grading checklist asks for (1) three routes: POST /users/new, edit user, get user by email, (2) a relational or NoSQL DB, (3) an optional ORM (TypeORM / Prisma), (4) manual verification with Postman or curl. Khalil used Express + TypeScript + Postgres + Prisma, and ChatGPT wrote most of the code from the pasted checklist. L42

  1. Prompt — “generate the code needed to build an MVC RESTful API with Express.js, Prisma, TypeScript, and Postgres, with the following API endpoints…”, with the grading checklist pasted in. L42
  2. Paste & fix — install @types/express, move the misplaced prisma/ folder, delete the generated app.ts, delete the redundant models/user.ts (the Prisma client already provides the types), fix a string→number id error. L42
  3. Fight the environment — Postgres via Homebrew, a “failed to create user” error surfaced with try/catch, a DATABASE_URL mismatch fixed with createdb, then npx prisma db push. L42
  4. Verify by hand — curl create → edit (John → Jonathan) → get by email. L42
Why it’s messy (on purpose)
  • Fat functions wired straight to Express. Basic functions act as “pretty much the entire service layer,” connected directly to controllers. HTTP, validation and Prisma calls all live in one handler. L42
  • Blind copy-paste (“pretty brainless on my part”) led to wrong folders, a duplicated model and type errors. L42
  • DB installed on the machine, not in a container. Docker and idempotency are deferred to Best Practice First. L42
  • No automated tests. Verification is manual curl, and a lot of time goes into debugging. L42

Where this code goes later: splitting the fat handler into a use case behind a repository contract is covered in Horizontal Decoupling. The katas below practise the other half first: the smallest, stateless unit, test-driven.

Context from the “First Milestone Review” Q&A

Despite its title, the session reviewed no milestone code. It pointed students to FA²STR at the stateless guess point and explained that FA²STR is an input → output tool usable at any level of abstraction. Wherever a problem starts (stateless, stateful, application, E2E), you “drill in with several loops,” which Lucas summed up as n loops rather than a fixed nth layer. L86

“Writing code is not the hard part. It is all of the other aspects of writing code, the design, testing, architecture, and strategy parts.”L42

FizzBuzz L45 L46 L47

Problem: a function that takes a number from 1 to 100 and returns a string: "Fizz" for multiples of 3, "Buzz" for multiples of 5, "FizzBuzz" for both, otherwise the number as a string. L44 L45 L46 Trains: red-green-refactor, fake it vs obvious implementation, rule of three, commit per phase. L45

Demo test sequence (commit on every phase) L45

#PhaseTest / changeWhy
1red“returns Fizz for 3”. Create export function fizzBuzz and import it first.Fail on logic, not on a compile error
2greenreturn "Fizz"Fake it, the simplest transformation
3–4red → green“returns Buzz for 5” → if (num === 3) return "Fizz"; return "Buzz";Refactor check: nothing ×3 yet
5–6red → green“returns FizzBuzz for 15” → if (num === 15) return "FizzBuzz";Test duplication noticed and ignored (wrong phase)
7–8red → green“returns Fizz for 9” → if (num === 9) return "Fizz";Still faking
9refactornum === … seen three times → isMultipleOfThree = num % 3 === 0. 15 then returned “Fizz”, so the 15 check moved above it.Rule of three. Accept the simplest fix.
10refactor (tests)Added “returns Fizz for 6” while green, then merged 3/6/9 into it.each “returns Fizz for multiples of three”. Did not add 12.Name the higher-level behavior. No new examples in a refactor.
11—Stopped. Buzz multiples, “both”, and the rest of the checklist were left to students.

Review feedback → fixes

Before — wrong system shape: nothing goes in, a sequence comes out (a generator) L46
After — stateless system: one number in, one string out

The same submission had everything in one commit (“FizzBuzz returns the string”, “generate sequence”, “FizzBuzz logic”) and was not a PR. The fix: commit on each phase shift and open a PR. L46

Before — else if chain: every branch adds a code path L47
After — early-return one-line ifs: same behavior, flat paths
Before — abstract names and several expects per it: when one fails, the reason isn’t clear L47
After — abstract behavior in describe, a concrete example in each it: one it, one expect
  • Commit messages say what happens: “handle when the input is not divisible by three and five” → “when given 43, returns '43'”. L47
  • Throw assertions must wrap the call: expect(() => fizzBuzz(102)).toThrow(). L47
  • Extending the assignment (e.g. non-number inputs) is fine if tests express it, after the required behavior is done. L47
  • Obvious implementation from the first test is fine on a problem this simple. Harder katas will need fake it. L47
“One it, one expect. No more. One it, one expect. And that's the rule.”L47

Palindrome L49 L50

Problem: detect palindrome words (mom and wow are palindromes, bill is not) and phrases (“Was it a rat I saw?”, “Never odd or even”), plus the grading-checklist examples. L49 Trains: the micro-mechanics of red-green-refactor, which matter much more at higher guess points (outgoing adapters, E2E). L49

Before — red for the wrong reason, two tests at once, a transformation mixed with a refactor L49
After — each commit is one phase, one example, one kind of change
Before — double negative: hard to parse
After — positive, concrete “knows that …” names

Review #2 L50: the final tests read well (describe + it.each for palindromes, including books, movies and places; non-palindromes; non-strings that throw). The mechanics were off. The student started with a fake implementation before any red. The second commit was too big (“normalize to lowercase, reverse it, compare it” plus all the examples). Commit messages had no phase labels, and there was an unnecessary comment. Verdict: redo the kata with strict red/green/refactor commits. The student also asked whether the solution was a pure function:

Before — “functional, but not a pure function” by Khalil’s definition: const introduces state
After — pure by his framing: no declarations, just a pipeline of functions

Added by Copilot This is Khalil’s stricter definition. Many FP references treat local immutable bindings as compatible with purity. The review’s practical point stands either way: no side effects means an input/output system.

Commit-size trade-off

“How much complexity can you tolerate?” One example per commit is slower but simpler. Many at once is faster but more complex. Default to one, because FA²STR at the next guess points will require it. Put the “throws when not a string” feature in its own commit. L50

Comments

“That comment is unnecessary. So get rid of that.” Code says what. Comments are a last resort, used only for why. L50 L48

Password Validator L54 L55 L56 L57

Problem: a function or stateless class that validates passwords. They must be 5–15 characters, contain at least one digit, and contain at least one uppercase letter. It returns an object with a boolean result and an errors key listing every error that occurred. L54 Trains: FA²STR (upfront + emergent), AAA backwards, program by wishful thinking. L56

Upfront design: Find → Architect → Automate L54 L52

Find

Read the problem. Write success and failure examples for each criterion in a “find” file. Classify the requirements: one doing (validate password) and many knowings (5–15 is valid, no digit is invalid, …). The knowings become most of the tests. Sketch the output for an input that breaks every rule ("s"). L54 L52

Architect

Get clear on the system under test: string in, object out, through a stateless class with a static method or a plain function. At the stateless level this step is “extremely simple.” L54

Automate

Set up the test infrastructure. Here that’s just Jest. All of this can happen “in a millisecond” in your head. Writing it down makes the metacognition visible. L54

Emergent design: Specify → Test → Refine (commit on green only) L55

  1. Valid password — written backwards (assert → act → arrange). result.result read badly, so the variable became output. Fake it: return { result: true, errors: [] }. Commit.
  2. Invalid length — expect exactly one error. errors became its own array, with an “is between 5 and 15” check that pushes InvalidLength. Commit.
  3. Another length example — passes immediately. Commit.
  4. Refine — length examples go into an it.each table (input, expected result, expected errors) nested under a describe naming the behavior. Commit.
  5. Digit feature — the success example passes immediately. The failure example drives hasDigits. A copy-pasted test still expected a truthy result and was fixed. The next example passes. The feature is refined into it.each the same way.
  6. Detect multiple errors — a feature only implied by the statement (“read between the lines”). The expected errors were deliberately listed in a different order from the push order. toStrictEqual failed, and the fix was per-error toContain.
  7. Stopped before the uppercase feature (“pretty much just typing”).
Levels of abstraction in a test file

Specification (feature/responsibility name) → concrete examples → test code → production code. “You always have a higher level of policy that's describing what is happening.” L55

Review feedback → fixes

Before — instantiating a stateless class; the test name describes how (keys, flags, null) L56
After — static call; the name states a responsibility (“can … / knows that …”), the how stays in the body
Before — hard-coded reason copied across tests: the “too long” tests still said “too short” L56
After — encapsulate what varies: password + reason in one row, substituted into the name and the assertion
Before — order-dependent assertion couples the test to push order in production L55
After — assert containment: “I don't really care about the order”

Review #2 (Tim) L57 was mostly praise. It used a plain function (the closest to essential complexity), a fake-it first commit, tiny transformations and toContain (“a very good API”). It also strictly typed the response, which turns the return shape into a role:

Breadth triangulation

One concrete example per responsibility, then move to the next feature. Tim did this. Adding the uppercase test forced him to update older inputs so they kept passing. L57

Depth triangulation

One feature, with more and more examples to strengthen its abstraction. Both styles are valid. L57

Next step for Tim

Near-duplicate standalone tests → it.each rows of input + expected errors, then many more combinations. Name multi-error tests precisely: “missing digit and missing uppercase letter.” L57

“You want to decouple the how from the what. That's huge. Because the how could change. But you still want the what to stay exactly the same.”L56

Stats Calculator L58 L59

Problem: process a sequence of integers and report statistics on them (e.g. minimum and maximum). The what is fixed. The how (return an object, a string or an array) has many valid answers, and “that is a key distinction.” L58

Clarify before you verify (new Find-step principle)
  1. List the responsibilities from the description.
  2. List concrete examples.
  3. Decide the output data structure (object / string / array) and strictly type it.
  4. Decide how you’ll verify each responsibility.

The reviewed student did this in the first commit: calculateStats(numbers) returns a typed stats shape. The commits then showed baby steps. L58

Before — firstInput / secondInput / thirdInput hide which edge case each covers; the tests repeat L58
After — named example sets + it.each: the intent is readable, and each example lives in one place
Before — inputs and expectations in separate structures; the spec names the return shape (how) L59
After — one object per example + responsibility specifications (a doing or a knowing)
Responsibility specification vs examples

A test spec has two parts. Responsibility specifications name a doing or a knowing (“it can calculate the minimum value”) and stay abstract. Examples are as concrete as possible. Drive with concrete examples, and end up with abstract responsibility specs. L59

Refinement budget

“You could spend so much time refactoring these examples.” Refine until the tests are readable, then stop, but never trade away readability. Parameterizing is now a grading-checklist refinement. L59 L58

“Names are not something to be wasted. Names actually do a lot.”L58

Military Time Validator L60 L61

Problem: given a string that may be a valid or invalid military time range (e.g. "01:12 - 14:32", format inferred), write a function or stateless class that detects which. Trains: picking the simplest transformation with the Transformation Priority Premise, here and in the Boolean Calculator. L60

Transformation Priority Premise (simplest first) L60

  1. nil — return nothing. Fake it can start here so the first test fails for the right reason.
  2. constant — return a hard-coded value.
  3. combine constants — e.g. add two constants.
  4. scalars / arguments — use the input.
  5. single statement — one functional expression calling functions or “service providers” such as min/max.
  6. conditional + return — multiple statements.
  7. more conditionals, more statements — variables and mutation sit here, at the costly end.
Using TPP
  • Use it at FA²STR’s Test step (keep the obvious implementation at the simplest option every time) and at the Refine step. L60
  • “If you feel like you need to add a variable or you think you need to do some mutations, question your transformation.” L60
  • For reference, a condition-map abstraction on test one sits around “level seven or eight.” L63

Review #1 (Loki): functional decomposition, commit by commit L60

“Some of the most readable commits in a story of commits” Khalil had seen. The problem was decomposed down to the tiniest responsibility and composed upward:

Before — one function doing everything: a mutable flag and nested branches (high on the TPP list)
After — tiny responsibilities composed upward; helpers encapsulated by not exporting them
Before — “revise index file for clarification” added comments that restate the names L60
After — delete them: the names already say what. “Do we really need comments? I wouldn't say we do.”

Review #2 (Kareel): class-based, “an exemplary demonstration” L61

Commit story: fake a basic valid example → a falsy example (hour 25) forces parsing → refactor “group test by validity” → hour bounds with isHourValid → minute checks → refactor merging the helpers into one isTimeValid + parseTimeRange → a finite-number check → start must be before end (several examples had to change). L61

Before — a copied test per example: each new case duplicates structure (closed to extension) L60
After — responsibility spec → parameterized examples: “super open closed”, so a new case is just a new row
Levels of abstraction, highest → lowest
  1. You explaining the problem out loud to someone.
  2. The specifications.
  3. The test code.
  4. The first level of production code: the function or static method that kicks off the SUT, reading as the algorithm’s steps.
  5. Encapsulated lower-level helpers, seen only when you “descend a layer deeper.”

“That sort of gradient like movement from theoretical to physical.” L61

Functional vs OOP encapsulation: functional code co-locates state and behavior in one file and hides helpers by not exporting them. OOP encapsulates them together in a class. L60 Kareel’s class had to be instantiated. A static method would also work, which is “not a huge deal.” L61

AI-era lens · Copilot

TPP gives you a shared vocabulary for keeping AI diffs small. Try “make this test pass using the highest-priority transformation on the TPP list: constant before conditional, no new variables.” If the diff introduces a let, a loop or a lookup map for one new example, reject it and ask again one rung lower.

Boolean Calculator (Design It Twice) L62 L63

Problem: evaluate a boolean expression given as a string, such as "TRUE", "FALSE", NOT, "TRUE AND FALSE", and later parentheses. It has “one other aspect” that makes it harder than Military Time. Khalil flagged it as a kata that may need upfront design. L62 L63 L60 L54

Johan: emergent, swim lanes L62

“One of the best ones I've seen so far.” Tests are grouped into describe swim lanes (incorrect input, TRUE/FALSE, NOT, AND), which is categorical thinking, so it’s obvious where the next test goes and you can triangulate within a lane. Transformations are simple. Trouble starts at AND: two tests in one loop, deeply nested describes, and vague words (“parts”, “one/two/three”).

Shannon: upfront, one big guess L63

All tests pass, but the first commit already had describe.each table infrastructure plus a “condition map”, a stack, tokens and operands. That’s an upfront design decision (FA²STR’s Architect), “five, six, seven different guesses all at the same time.” The design lives in the author’s head, not in commits a reviewer can follow.

Johan’s sequence L62

  1. Invalid input → throw — obvious implementation, “a great first defensive coding commit.” Rename the context to “when input is not correct.”
  2. TRUE → return true — the simplest thing, even with foresight. “Lead with the guess.”
  3. FALSE — evaluate the condition inline instead of adding an if.
  4. NOT — “input includes NOT”. Similar code appeared twice, so no refactor yet (rule of three).
  5. AND — two tests at once (flagged). Split on AND and require every token to be true. A refactor introduced transformValuesToExpression, and words like values and expressions began to appear.
  6. TRUE AND NOT TRUE — checkNegation works, but the test name was hard to read.
Before — conditions encoded as nested describes: high “psychic entropy” for the reader L62
After — lead with the concrete example. “It's always going to be easier to just use an example.”
Before — an if adds a statement and a branch (lower on the TPP list)
After — evaluate the condition inline: one expression, the simpler transformation
Before — test one arrives with table infrastructure and a condition map: TPP “level seven or eight” L63
After — “take one example, write it as English, make that your it statement”; production starts at return true
Design it twice

Once you have a working upfront solution, redo it and arrive at the same place emergently, one guess at a time (from A Philosophy of Software Design). “Allow the tool to be doing the heavy lifting, which is to make the small guesses and lead with that.” For stateless problems, start with plain it tests and refactor toward describe.each/it.each later. L63

Name the concepts (ubiquitous language)

“What is a part really?” A part, a token, a value, an expression? Name the concepts instead of numbering them, and refactor test names for meaning too. Pushing complexity into deeper layers is fine: “That complexity needs to go somewhere and it's essential.” L62

Both reviews end positively. Shannon’s code “looks really elegant”, and nested statements get refined in the later stateful sections, not here. It’s a spectrum: if you’re confident and short on time, the whole thing can be an obvious implementation. L63

“All of what is happening here is happening within your brain. It's not happening within the code to be read as a story.”L63

The feedback that came up again and again across the reviews, in one place. Run it over your own PR, or anyone else’s, before asking for review.
