AI-era lens · Copilot

This table works as a review rubric for AI-generated tests and code. Agents often trip rows 3, 5, 6, 8, 10 and 18: one-shot implementations, batched tests, mixed refactors, multi-assert tests with “returns an object with…” names, and “what” comments. Paste the table into your review prompt or PR template, and send back any diff that fails a row with that row as the instruction.

Theoretical Design & DDD: The FeedBook Case Study

One running example goes all the way from the problem to tested code. FeedBook lets authors run feedback cycles on a book in progress with pre-readers. The path: problem guess point (impact map, glossary, subdomains) → solution guess point (bounded contexts, context map, event storming, views, state machines) → architecture guess point (modular monolith, event bus) → stateful domain modelling guess point (the PreReaderInvite entity). L65 L88

StepGuess pointOutput artifactLessons
Understand the problemProblemImpact map (actor → role → goal → features), concrete examples, glossaryL66
Find subdomainsProblemRaw, ungrouped list of problem categoriesL66
Group by languageSolutionBounded contextsL67 L68
Classify & mapSolutionCore/supporting/generic, build vs buy, context map, foldersL68
Event storm a scenarioSolutionEvents → commands → actors → aggregates → boundariesL69
Add views & dataSolutionScreens, input/output per command–event, relationshipsL70
Decide the shapeArchitectureModules, deployable units, event busL71
Model stateSolution → statefulState machines with invariantsL74 L76
Size the boundariesStateful / applicationSmall aggregates, references by IDL88 L89
ImplementStateful domain modellingTested entity + value objects + GuardL77

Roadmap: The Theoretical Guess Points L65 L88

Design = abstraction

“If nothing else, the most important thing to understand is abstraction. It's the thinking before doing.” What vs how, declarative vs imperative, theoretical vs physical, upfront vs emergent are all the same idea. It follows that theoretical guesses come before physical ones. Why model a domain before you know the problem, its solution and the architecture that will implement it? L65

  • Start from the problem and the people, not the code. Crunch domain knowledge with your boss or the domain experts. L65
  • Carry three things into the solution space: the problem, concrete examples of what you’re building, and concrete examples of why. Several techniques get you there: BDD’s feature injection, impact mapping, user story mapping, and Khalil’s role-goal “mishmash”. L65
  • Drive everything through a concrete scenario: “Person is at state A, person wants to be at state B, and here's their experience.” Event storming without one leaves your brain “like mush”. L65
  • Framing changes the work. “Build tic-tac-toe” vs “web-based multiplayer tic-tac-toe” adds concurrency, client and server domains, rooms and network issues. On a McDonald’s order terminal it changes again. L65
  • Order, via the value creation system: problem → solution space (domains; core/supporting/generic) → architecture (build vs buy, tools per subdomain) → physical guess points via the ideal developer workflow. “You never want to be making physical guesses unless you have your theoretical guesses sorted.” L88
  • The hard part is the what. “What makes programming really hard is not the programming part.” Anxiety at work signals a lack of clarity. L89

Assignment sequence

  1. Find the subdomains — FeedBook first, then the other assignments. L65
  2. Consolidate into bounded contexts L65
  3. Process-model (event storm) a concrete scenario. L65
  4. Classify core, supporting and generic. Khalil later suggests classifying before process modelling. L65 L69
  5. Implement the domain model at the stateful guess point with value objects, entities and identifiers. L65
“You can't really do the stateful part unless you made your theoretical guesses first.”L65

The FeedBook Problem: Impact Map, Concrete Examples & Glossary L65 L66

FeedBook: an author invites a group of readers to review a book, then creates a feedback cycle that runs at a particular time. Readers leave reactions (hearts, thumbs up) and feedback per chapter. The author drills in to see where people react, comment and “fall off” in the book. L65

Problem guess point outputs
  1. Know the problem.
  2. A few concrete examples (the most valuable ones).
  3. Domain knowledge.
  4. Clarity on subdomains.

Stay on the what and why. The how belongs to the solution guess point. L66

Impact map (Khalil’s variant: actor → role → goal → capabilities)

Impact mapping puts the impact front and centre, which protects you from building things that “just don't matter”. Khalil finds the standard diagram “a little bit backwards” and starts from role and goal, because goals are easier to drive for real people. L66

ActorRoleGoal / notes
Entrepreneur (Khalil)AuthorA final version of the book, written with high quality (desirable, effective, …)
SolidBook readersNew pre-readersInvited to give feedback
SolidBook OGsExisting pre-readersHave already read the book

Source: L66.

  • It isn’t the only solution. Collecting buyers’ emails and emailing back and forth works, but it isn’t a fun experience. A platform gives back or enriches time. L66
  • Each feature → a concrete example or design story (e.g. Khalil uploading the book). L66
  • What a concrete example needs: the starting state, the ending state, what the person does, and what they should see. “If we're getting really fancy”, add what they experience and how they feel about it. GWT or user-story format both work. L68
  • Khalil skipped the concrete example here and had to write it at the solution guess point. L69 See event storming.

Domain knowledge & glossary

What it is

Facts about the conceptual (“metaphysical”) reality you’re creating. It is “locked in the domain experts' heads”, so extract it and get it on the page. For the assignments, Khalil plays the domain expert. Ask him “what happens if…”. L66

Questions to ask

“What is true of this metaphysical reality you're creating? What is not quite true? How do these things interact? What belongs where?” And what must happen before what? L66

Why write it down

You’re building a conceptual model, “not a real one yet”. If a consultancy parts ways with the client halfway through, the knowledge survives in documents. Start with facts like “a feedback cycle is…”, “a feedback cycle has…”. L66

Open questions are normal

“What are the results of feedback cycles going to be?” Khalil had no answer yet. Wireframes or talking to real authors would help. L66

“We want to know what it is we're building. We want to know why we're building it. But we don't really care about how we're going to build it just yet.”L66

Finding Subdomains L66

Subdomain

Whatever category of the problem comes straight to mind. “They're parts of the problem that could be solved. They don't really have a solid grouping to them.” They can be big or tiny. The domain is the big problem: “literally everything involved in me operating this business.” L66

  1. Brain-dump — “Just get as much as you can out of your brain. What are the major categories?” Don’t worry about size or grouping. L66
  2. Stop when exhausted — you’re done when you can’t think of more categories needed to solve the problem. L66
  3. Group later — turning subdomains into bounded contexts belongs to the solution space. L66
Subdomain (as named)Why it showed up
Notion integration · Book / text parsingUpload the book from a Notion link, then parse it
Pre-readers / pre-reading · Feedback cyclesThe core activity
InvitationsInviting pre-readers
Users & identity · Sign-up / registration“For sure”
Scheduler / scheduled jobsFeedback cycles run on a schedule
Payments · Credit card managementAuthors could pay for it
Pre-reading sessions · Browser sessionsHow long a reader stays on a page, when they leave
EmailsInvitations
Book feedback · Emoji managementFeedback left via emojis
VersioningNew book versions
Project sourceChat suggestion, not elaborated

The raw brainstorm from L66. It shows “this is actually a very complex problem to solve.”

Core

What makes your business unique. You must build it. L66 “The unique new stuff that matters that you can't get anywhere. You can only get here.” L68

Supporting

Not tied to the problem you’re currently solving, but strategic, so you build it rather than buy it (e.g. reporting). L66 You also end up building one when no off-the-shelf tool plugs in. L68 You “have to build anyway but don't really want to”. L71

Generic

Something you can pay an external service to do (email, auth). L66 Don’t build email or auth yourself. But if you’re building a Google Calendar, scheduling is core, so keep control of it. L65

Anti-pattern

Treating neat, granular splits like “delivery, shop” as subdomains. Khalil would call those bounded contexts. Real subdomains are rarely that neat, and the line is “incredibly subjective”. L66

Bounded Contexts, Cohesion & “Be Aristotle” L67 L68

Bounded context

A major domain formed by combining subdomains that use the same language. L67 Khalil’s extension: “placing a boundary around the context of language that is allowed to be used within a sphere of the domain of that problem or knowledge space.” A chat definition he liked: subdomains are what your app needs, and bounded contexts categorize them. L68

  • Skip subdomains? Fine if you’re experienced. Khalil usually goes straight to bounded contexts. L67
  • “Act like you're Aristotle”: for each item, ask “is this actually part of that topic?”, then combine and name. Example: book feedback + emoji management share language → Feedback. L67
  • It’s all language. “This is all language. So it's language and it's crunching language.” That’s why it’s hard, and hardest for people who struggle with English or creative thinking. L68
  • Add rather than take away while grouping (e.g. add “Google integration” next to Notion). New language emerges. In Feedback, reactions, comments on lines and comments on whole chapters appeared, with the verbs posting a comment and posting a reaction. L68

Coupling & cohesion at every level

Grouping subdomains is “coupling and cohesion at the problem level. We're doing coupling and cohesion everywhere.” Khalil files coupling, cohesion, RDD and category theory under one umbrella he calls abstraction design: “what belongs together. What doesn't belong together?” L67

Cohesion

How well things belong together. Given JobScheduler and BurgerCreator, lettuce goes with BurgerCreator. L67

Coupling

Referring to something you aren’t related to. “It's just really about a relatedness and it's about tightness to what it relates to.” Khalil admits his example isn’t the best. L67

SRP at two levels

Problem level: “single bounded context, with clear responsibilities.” Class level: a class whose responsibilities are cohesive. L68

“You're placing a boundary around the context of language that is allowed to be used within a sphere of the domain.”L68

Consolidating Into Bounded Contexts: Build/Buy, Context Map & Folders L68

  1. Clone the domain board and drag the subdomain stickies into clusters. L68
  2. Group by shared language and name each cluster. If two things are similar but your domain is really about one of them, keep them apart (feedback cycles ≠ scheduling). L68
  3. Classify each context as core, supporting or generic. L68
  4. Decide build / buy / must-build. This is “how you find and fill these responsibility gaps and how you determine what you want to be an external service and what you want to build yourself and how you vet libraries and frameworks.” L68
  5. Draw the context map: “What relies on what?” L68
Subdomain(s)ReasoningBounded context
Payments + credit card managementSimilar enoughBilling

Browser + pre-reading sessionsA thing of its own; involves the browserSessions
Pre-reading dataTracking reader interactionAnalytics
Book feedback + emoji managementSame languageFeedback
VersioningThe book is what’s versionedBooks
Notion integration + book parsingParse the book from a source; parsing split outImporting + Text parsing
Pre-reading, invitations, feedback cycles, pre-readers, authorsConverge on the actual productFeedBook (core)
Emails · Users & identity · Notion APIOff the shelf / externalEmails · Users · Notion

Consolidation moves from L68. Some placements (authors in FeedBook) are Khalil thinking aloud: “that's probably going to go in here as well.”

FeedBookCoreBuild: our codebase (“you can only get here”)

Classification from L68.

Always one core context

“You always want to have one bounded context that represents your actual domain.” For FeedBook it’s named FeedBook. Choose tools only after listing needs. For example, to pick a frontend framework, start at the problem guess point (do you need SSR?), then find tools that fill the gaps. “Architecture is not technology.” L68

  • Links between contexts are events. When a feedback cycle is scheduled or created, Scheduling listens, creates a Job, and the Job state machine starts. L68
  • The context map is the foundation for understanding state machines, sagas and temporal decoupling. L68
  • Don’t force the dependency rule between contexts. Sometimes it’s unavoidable. Example: Stripe sends a credit-card-expired webhook and you adjust the account. DDD calls these relationships customer–supplier and upstream/downstream. “Sometimes you don't really have a choice.” Inside a context the rule still holds: a value object or entity doesn’t rely directly on a repository. L68
  • “It's just a network of systems talking to each other.” Companies work the same way. L68

Folder structure falls out of the contexts

Before — package by infrastructure: “just know you're screwed”
After — package by domain: one folder per bounded context
  • Team adoption: get buy-in before changing a team’s conventions. TS-Arch can enforce rules as tests, e.g. value objects and entities may not import Express controllers or DB models. Persuade with first principles, expert precedent and questions. L68
  • Tech-first conventions (e.g. Angular’s) serve you early on. Once a project has many capabilities, structure the code closest to “the essence of the hard problem”. L68
  • Design it twice. Seeing an upfront design in a new light yields different solutions. L68

Event Storming (Process Modelling) the Concrete Example L69

“The first thing we need is a story, concrete example.” The feature is “create and invite pre-readers to and manage feedback cycles”. The scenario goes a bit beyond one feature so it’s interesting enough to model. L69

The procedure

  1. Concrete example — GWT (or a user story) with a clear beginning and end. L69
  2. Domain events — past tense, unordered at first (“just get these events… out of our head”), then ordered. Consolidate language as you go (“Invite sent” / “Invite accepted” → “Pre-reader invite …”). L69
  3. Commands — the same phrase in the imperative. “Pre-reader invite created” → “Create pre-reader invite”. “All we really do is we just write it in the imperative.” L69
  4. Actors — a person or role (Author, Pre-reader), or the System for automatic follow-ups, “because this is event based”. L69
  5. Aggregates — “the data that we're doing work against.” L69
  6. Bounded contexts — they were found upfront, so “all we have to do is just place the boundaries around these properly.” L69
  7. Critique — hunt for same-context event chains and fix them with state machines. L69

First model (with the smell)

#CommandActorAggregateDomain eventContext
1Create pre-reader invitesAuthorPre-reader invitePre-reader invite createdFeedBook
2Send emailSystemEmailEmail sentEmail
3Accept pre-reader invitePre-readerPre-reader invitePre-reader invite acceptedFeedBook
4aCreate pre-reader accountSystemPre-reader accountPre-reader account createdFeedBook: same context, same process
4bSend email (to author)SystemEmailEmail sentEmail

Source: L69. The invite being sent and the email being sent were split after a question from chat.

The smell: same-context events changing the same concept

An accepted invite triggers “create pre-reader account” within the same process and context. “Whenever I see this relationship here, I don't really love this.” The rule of thumb: “When you have domain events occurring within the same domain… to change the same concept, you want to be very wary of that.” “You might be missing a potential state change, or you just might've modeled your state changes a little bit wrong.” Events that cross contexts are fine, because another context listens and time passes. L69

Redesign with a state machine

Ask how a pre-reader can come to exist in the platform. The answer: “You can't really be created without being invited.” So a pre-reader is created in the Invited state and moves to Accepted, and the separate create-account step disappears. The domain rule goes on the board as a note: “In order to create a pre-reader, they start out invited.” L69

Invite new pre-reader(s)AuthorPre-readerPre-reader invitedInvited (initial)

Send emailSystemEmailEmail sent—
  • Criticize names hard. “It's worthwhile spending time really criticizing this language here”, because it becomes the code. Khalil considered “Accept invite” but kept “Accept pre-reader invite” to stay specific for now. L69
  • User ≠ Pre-reader. User lives in the generic Users context. Pre-reader lives in FeedBook. L69
  • Order: classify core/supporting/generic first and process-model last. The process model is “probably the most key part”. It gives clarity on the data, behavior, relationships and process that the domain model must codify. L69
  • Two forms (“non-negotiable”): big-picture event storming, to understand an existing project, and process modelling of one feature, for new work. L88
  • Events may branch across contexts, e.g. OrderPlaced → billing + email. Don’t branch into two paths in the same namespace. L89
  • Look for required inputs and outputs rather than trying to name “aggregates”. Khalil avoids the word because there are so many ways to model it. L89
AI-era lens · Copilot

Grouping by language, placing boundaries and spotting a same-context event chain are human judgment calls. An agent will generate an extra PreReaderAccount entity and a synchronous “accept then create” just as happily. Hand it the GWT scenario and the redesigned event table as the spec, and review its output against the smell rule.

Refining the Process Model with Views & State Changes L70

When Khalil started coding, details were missing. That’s emergent design: recalibrate. “It's very easy to miss details if we don't actually have a concrete example of what it is we're trying to build.” A story is still abstract, and wireframes or screens make it real. L70

  1. Add views — attach screens to the event storm: invite form → Gmail inbox → accept page → register page → dashboard. L70
  2. Tally input and output data — for every command–event pair. L70
  3. Identify the types of state to model. L70
  4. Identify state machines and transitions — “It will dictate what moves to change and in what sequence. And it's going to dictate the state machine.” L70
  5. Implement the domain model. L70
What the views surfaced

How does an invited pre-reader log in again? Username? First and last name? An auto-generated password, or one asked for right away? “These are all things that will get missed if you don't do the problem space correctly.” Take these questions back to the domain experts or a designer. The chosen answer: after Accept, go to a Register screen, then the Dashboard. Question even polished, pre-made stories and screens. L70

Tally from L70. Required inputs like authorId and preReaderInviteId are application rules: needed to operate, but not domain invariants.

One state change per step, per context, linked by events

“Design out state changes that are happening one step at a time within one subdomain or one context at a time.” Doing 3–4 state changes at once needs a transaction around them all, which is hard. Linking steps by events means “your system could fail any of these steps and you could bring it back up and you know that your system is going to be in a consistent state”. The course calls this idempotency. L70 See the terminology note. Order matters: “You can't create a pre-reader account until you have a user account for them.” L70

“Even if someone else has done this work… do question and do continue to question that things might be missing.”L70

Architecture Guess Point: Modular Monolith & Event Bus L71

This is the last theoretical step. “Once we get to this architect step, we've done the majority of the hard work.” The modules are already known from the bounded contexts. L71

Questions Khalil asks

  • External systems, components, modules and deployable units (modular monolith vs microservices). L71
  • Components such as Redis, which can play many roles: caching, Pub/Sub, key-value storage, and queuing/scheduling with BullMQ. These come up again at the outgoing adapter guess point. L71
  • How do we organize our code? Classification decides it: core = build, generic = import a library, supporting = build reluctantly. L71
  • Non-functional requirements. The three-step RDD process can find the right architectural components (mentioned only). L71

Modular monolith ≠ single process

“Modular monolith does not mean modular process. This is just how you organize your code.” At bootstrap you choose which modules share a process. For FeedBook: billing is external, the core runs together, and sessions/scheduling likely run in a separate process. “Just usually a better place to start than microservices.” L71

Event bus

A required component that lets modules talk: everyone registers events and subscribes. Start with everything in one process. Students suggested SOA without a bus, or WebSockets. The course goes event-driven. “At the end of the day, we just need coordinators.” L71

Encapsulation: FP vs OOP

Encapsulation means data and related behavior together, with the data protected. FP does it by co-location. OOP does it with a private constructor, a static factory, and restricted getters/setters. “The technique is encapsulation, but the way you implement it is a little bit different.” L71

Next, moving to the physical: the ideal workflow is deployment pipeline → E2E test in a production-like environment → level-3 tests. For learning, the course jumps to level two, the stateful guess point, to “encapsulate the hell out of the object correctly” with value objects, entities, domain events, Result and Guard. L71 More in Architecture & Code Structure.

State Machines, Invariants, Transitions & Events L74 L76 L86

Stateless FA²STR work (feedback loop level one) only transforms data: “mom” in, a result out. “In the real world, we're always dealing with statefulness. Problems are stateful.” You solve them by introducing state, which then has to change correctly, at the right time, and never at the wrong time. L74 L86

State

A position the system can be in. Being at a state is itself data. L74

Transition

A move from one state to the next. It “feels functional because it is functional”, so the paradigm doesn’t matter. L74 L86

Event

Created on every transition: data saying “we just moved to this state”. States and events are two sides of the same coin. L74

Invariant

“Invariance equals a rule, which really equals business logic.” It blocks invalid transitions. L74 Also: which states your concepts may be in, e.g. a washing machine can’t be “off” with settings selected. L89

Encapsulation’s purpose

“To protect the way the model changes.” “You don't want to be able to put the system in an invalid state.” L74 L86

Washing clothes by hand, built from the end

Start at the goal (clothes clean) and work backwards: clean ← dry ← washed ← washing materials assembled ← clothes gathered. “You see what happens when you start from the end? I'm telling you. It's the technique.” L74 Thinking backwards gets its own lesson. L75

This sketch throws. By the implementation demo, expected domain failures are returned as typed errors instead (below). L77 Real-world invalid states include blowing into a Nintendo cartridge, restarting the router, and an Uber Eats order placed by accident during a phone call. L74

FeedBook: tally the state, then model each piece

Piece of stateManaged byNote
Pre-reader inviteUs (FeedBook)Invited → Accepted via accept
EmailExternal (generic)Created “all over the place”
UserUsers contextNeeded before a pre-reader can exist
Pre-readerUs (FeedBook)Little change. Its complexity is in valid creation.

Sequence of creation: author (created long before) → pre-reader invite → user → pre-reader. “A pre-reader can only really come to be if an author is there first, then a pre-reader invite is there, and then a user exists.” A domain model must encapsulate data, rules, processes and relationships. Use a state machine first to get clear on how each thing can change over time. L76

  • Few transitions → focus rigor on creation. Pass in all the correct pieces and “make sure that they can't be created without those things.” The pre-reader also gets a demo rule: edit the display name, which defaults to a combination of first and last name. The exact format was fuzzy in narration. L76
  • Richer example: a washing machine goes Off → Idle (waiting for cycle selection) → Sensing. Off → Sensing is invalid. L76
  • Information systems are state machines. One machine emits an event that creates or triggers another. Follow the inputs, outputs and flow of data. L89
  • Keep time out. A state machine holds and protects data and changes correctly when told to. Knowing when to tell it is an application concern. L89 The domain model must be pure: no new Date(), Math.random() or setTimeout. Inject a clock. L88
  • Fixtures = initial state. Encapsulate complex starting states with a builder instead of acting them out line by line. L86 L78
“Every single time we do a transition, we get something called an event created.”L74
AI-era lens · Copilot

Agents generate public setters freely. Invariants encoded inside the domain object (a guarded acceptInvite(), no public status setter) mean AI-generated callers can’t push the system into an invalid state, whatever they do. The state diagram doubles as a checklist: one test per arrow and one per forbidden arrow.

Aggregates: Minimum Data, Transaction Boundaries L88 L89

Minimum data for a command

“An aggregate is the minimum amount of information required for you to perform a command.” It’s the absolute minimum needed to execute the command and evaluate its rules, and the result is saved into an event. It isn’t necessarily the input data. L88

Transaction / consistency boundary

“It's a transaction boundary”: the essential data that changes together in one transaction. Aggregates are application-level (feedback loop level 3). Entities and value objects are level 2. “More of a philosophical thing”, and maybe not a real code construct. L89

Not a DTO

A DTO is “data in a certain shape” with no behavior, e.g. the input that invokes a command. A student’s definition, “objects that enforce invariants”, got “fair enough”. L89

Keep them small

  • Per-command aggregates. createUser needs an email and password (email unique, password valid). editUser needs id, names and email, but not the password. A new rule (edit only if verified) turns Email into a value object with a status. Otherwise the User aggregate grows with every command until a simple edit loads “9,000 other things”. L88
  • Rule of three: command-specific aggregates may later refactor into a common abstract User. L88 “I don't even like to give things concrete base classes until I absolutely need them”, so skip an early AggregateRoot. L89
  • Reference by ID. Loading an Author with 30 feedback cycles for every request is bad and may crash things. L89
  • Lists: design for the worst case. Moving a playlist track from position 3 to 50 shouldn’t update every item in between. Use previous/next pointers, and update the rest later (eventual consistency). L89
  • Boundary test: walk the state-change code line by line. If the system could die midway and restart half-done, the boundary is wrong. L89
  • Two state machines → a domain service, e.g. syncing a tasks list with a calendar into a sync plan (adds, updates, removes) that the application layer applies. L88 L89
  • Three ways to model them: an OO Order class, per-command data slices, or pure functional inputs → outputs. Khalil won’t give “solid statements” on which is right. L89
Aggregate per command
Reorder in one small transaction

Can’t find the boundary? You’re doing too much in one command

Transaction script: makePurchase

One call gets cart items, checks inventory, bills the card, updates inventory and sends an email. A crash between billing and the inventory update leaves an invalid state. Khalil did this on the solidbook website and suffered, including serverless cold starts that cut requests off. The fix is temporal decoupling: each subdomain’s state machine reacts to events. Model the success scenario, then the failures (billing fails → email, wait, cancel after 3 days, release inventory). L88
