Implementing the PreReaderInvite Domain Object L77

Goal: move “from state machine to domain model.” Domain objects are “really simple state machines at the class level, but these are the decision-making objects that happen in most information systems.” L77

  1. Find — responsibilities (data, behavior, processes, rules). The state machines already did most of this. L77
  2. Architect — map doings and knowings onto DDD tactical patterns: entities, value objects, domain events (domain services aren’t needed here). L77
  3. Automate — Jest is enough. GWT/feature files can come later. L77
  4. TDD each transition — work backwards: input → act → assert → make it exist. Drop inward to value objects and Guard (level 1), then come back out to the entity (level 2). L77 L88

Entity vs value object

Compared by value → value object (PreReaderEmail, and IDs too: “a little bit of a tricky one”). Compared by identity → entity (PreReaderInvite). L77

Input vs state

PreReaderInviteInput is raw strings. PreReaderInviteState holds value objects plus a status. Converting input into state is where validation happens. L77

Props pattern

All state lives on one props object instead of separate fields. It’s easier to maintain and makes immutability easy. L77

Only non-initial input

Status is set to Invited internally, so create takes just 3 inputs: invite ID, author ID, pre-reader email. L77

1 · Test layout: one describe per transition

Failure tests are named by reason: “fails to create when value missing”. “Missing value” beats “missing property”. Placeholder IDs like '123' aren’t valid UUIDs and caused confusing ValidationErrors, so keep a known-valid SAMPLE_UUID. Remember to unwrap with getId().getValue(). L77

2 · Errors are returned, not thrown

Before — classful Result: “way too confusing, especially if you're just starting out”
After — plain union return types: “this is how you say or”

“This could have just been so much simpler… It just gets way too complex using the result.” Model result types strictly. Avoid optional fields that are really variant-specific. L77

3 · Value objects own validation

AuthorId and PreReaderEmail follow the same pattern. The UUID check ended up copied three times. “When you see things three times, it's a good chance to refactor.” The refactor was deferred, but Khalil noted where it belongs. Prefer a validation package, since regex “can be pretty expensive”. L77

4 · Guard from programming by wishful thinking

The return type evolved: boolean → result → { success, data?: { keysMissing } } → firstKeyMissing → discriminated union → hasErrors()/getFirstError(). “This is telling it instead of asking. Tell don't ask. This is much nicer of an API.” Guard is a level-one construct, and the entity is level two. L77

5 · The entity: private constructor + static create

A class plays two roles: a service provider (static create) and a blueprint (constructor, private props, instance methods). The private constructor stops consumers from building invalid objects with new. “If this feels like a lot of typing, it is a lot of typing. But this is what is required in order to encapsulate and protect the ways state can change in your app.” L77

6 · Next transition: acceptInvite

Before — anemic model: public setters, thrown errors, rules somewhere else
After — encapsulated entity: the invariant lives in the transition
Rules from the demo
  • Structure tests by transition, with success and failure cases for each. L77
  • In create, check presence, then validity, then construct. Return early with the first error. L77
  • Put validation in value objects. The entity composes them. L77
  • “Never just want to be creating stuff and not testing it.” Every new abstraction (Result, Guard, each value object) gets a test. A failing placeholder spec is an acceptable reminder. L77
  • Failure output should say which property failed. L77
  • “Naming is a process as well”: InvalidProperty → ValidationError, keysMissing → firstKeyMissing, validateUUID → validateIdentifier. L77
  • “Takes just sitting in like a little bit awkwardness for it to get cleaner.” L77
Mistakes called out (several self-admitted)
  • Public constructors that bypass validation. Throwing for expected domain failures. Validation inside the entity. L77
  • Over-engineering early with a full Result class. L77
  • Silencing a type error once (“It's not the best”). Barely writing value-object tests. Skimping on commits. Khalil admits all three and says not to copy them. L77
AI-era lens · Copilot

Ask an agent for “a PreReaderInvite model” and you’ll typically get the Before column. Specify the shape instead: private constructor, static create returning Entity | DomainError, value objects owning validation, one describe per transition. Then point the agent’s tests at the invariants: accepted → accepted errors, exactly one InviteAccepted.

Continue with fixtures and builders in Testing and object design in Abstraction Levels, OOP & RDD.

Abstraction Levels, OOP & Responsibility-Driven Design

Pick the construct that matches a concept’s intended level of abstraction: interface → abstract class → class → object. Abstract only when more than one actor can play the role. Below patterns sit responsibilities (doings and knowings). You group them into roles using six object stereotypes and wire up collaborations last. That is Responsibility-Driven Design, “the deepest level of design” Khalil teaches. L79 L23 L94

TopicQuestion it answersKey heuristic
Levels of realnessInterface, abstract class, class or object?Start concrete. Interface for infra seams and >1 actor. Abstract class only after the rule of three.
Roles, actors & contractsDo I need this interface?George Clooney test
How much OOPDo I need to study OOP first?No. Same steps/events abstraction, as scripts or as an object network.
Getting better at designWhat is “good design”?Discoverability + understanding. Metacognition + empathy.
Responsibility-Driven DesignHow do I design something no library gives me?Responsibilities → roles → collaborations
Object stereotypesWhat kind of object owns this responsibility?Six stereotypes. Control center = coordinator + controller.
“Category theory” for designWhere does this responsibility go?Categorize as hard as possible. Lean into the dominant role.
Worked example: zoomWhat does RDD look like on a real feature?Concrete example → responsibilities → stereotypes
Critique & next stepsWhat happens after the upfront design?Controllers don’t subscribe. Make small guesses. Then write the use-case test.

Levels of Realness: Interfaces, Abstract Classes, Classes, Objects L79 L84

A student built a TrafficLight class and then extracted an interface from it as its “public API”. Khalil used that to explain a spectrum of realness, running from “not real at all” (interfaces) to “completely real” (concretions). Many developers struggle with when to use interfaces, abstract classes and concretions, and with what a contract is. L79 Khalil calls levels of realness “a really key concept”. He dislikes OOP taught as “here’s a class that does this” and wants each tool traced back to a purpose, which here is writing scalable code. L91

Interface / type

“A pure abstract conceptual idea of what it is that something should be.” It describes a role, like a job description that exists before anyone fills the job. A TS type sits at the same level. L79

Abstract class

Both concept and real. It has some implementation (e.g. a standardized getById) plus abstract members you must implement. Best example: the React Component, where you implement render. L79 L84

Class

Real, but it needs new. It’s a blueprint, so it is slightly less real than a plain object. L79

Plain object

Real right away. TrafficLightProps as a type describing a plain object is fine. It’s a typing shorthand that avoids getter/setter boilerplate. L79

Rules
  • Only make something abstract when multiple different actors can play that role. Otherwise default to a concretion. L79
  • Choose the construct by the concept’s intended level of abstraction, not by habit. L79
  • When you do need a contract, start with the most abstract thing, an interface or type. Move to an abstract class only when the rule of three shows a real need to share implementation. L84
  • Use contracts at infrastructure seams (repositories, and a Clock around new Date()). That is what lets you decouple from infrastructure at the upper guess points. L79 L84
Anti-patterns
  • Extracting an interface for something only one actor will ever play, such as the traffic light. L79
  • Treating interface extraction as a “public API” declaration with no role behind it. L79
  • Reaching for abstract classes first instead of interfaces. L84
“Abstraction is pretty much the root principle of design.”L79

Roles vs Actors, Contracts & the George Clooney Test L79 L84

RDD vocabulary
  • Role: a job to be played. It stays abstract until an actor plays it.
  • Actor: the real thing that plays one or many roles.
  • Responsibility: what a role must do, e.g. “make house out of bricks”.
  • Collaboration: the interactions between roles (who talks to whom).
  • Contract: an actor playing a role. implements creates it (“we’re going to play this role now”), there can be several, and extends can create one too.

L79

The Broadway play

In Three Little Pigs the roles are the big bad wolf and pigs 1–3. Scenes are collaborations, and “make house out of bricks” is a responsibility. All of it stays abstract until actors play it, and any actor could play any role, even Tina Fey as the big bad wolf. The roles side is declarative (“what should happen”). The actors side is the implementation (“what actually happens”). L79

Now write a George Clooney cameo into the play, as himself. Only George Clooney can play that role, so it needs no abstraction. Khalil’s verdict on the student’s traffic light interface: “You George Clooney’d it.” L79

George Clooney test

Ask: “Who else is going to play this role?” If the answer is only this one concretion, no contract is needed. With one implementation, contract and concretion “are one and the same.” When a second actor appears (a traffic light on Mars, or a model train traffic light whose lights stay on longer), triangulate the contract. The essentials go into the contract and the details stay in the concretions. L79

Before — premature interface: two names, one actor, zero benefit
After — concrete until a second actor shows up

Where a contract earns its keep: the repository role

A use case can be pure core code if it depends on contracts instead of the DB/ORM. In the adapter layer, the UserRepo interface is the adapter: a role. FirebaseUserRepo and SequelizeUserRepo are actors that play it. The use case only cares that someone plays the role. Unit tests pass in an in-memory test double instead. L84

A career milestone

Knowing how to deal with contracts: “When I realized how to do this and I got really good at it everything changed.” Pair it with YAGNI and the rule of three. Both fight the urge to add things you “feel you’re going to need”. L84

“I can’t get more abstract than a contract and it can’t get more real than an actor.”L79
AI-era lens · Copilot

Coding agents love to add IFoo + FooImpl pairs, factories and abstract bases “for flexibility”. Run the George Clooney test in review: if no second actor exists or is planned, inline it. Keep contracts where real seams are (repos, clock, payment, mail), because that’s where agents can generate test doubles and swappable adapters safely.

How Much OOP Do You Need? L36

Very little up front. The highest level of abstraction is the high-level steps and events, and implementing them means carrying out their subroutines. The paradigm is an implementation choice under that same abstraction: L36

Functional

“Scripts talking to other scripts.” L36

Object-oriented

“A network of objects that talk to each other that do work.” Objects hold references to other objects and collaborate. L36

Why Khalil prefers objects

Expressiveness, control, and good support for encapsulation and information hiding. The course uses objects from Best Practice First onward and explains them as they come up. L36

Learning syntax

Don’t front-load OOP study. A crash course is “probably not necessary.” Ask an AI assistant “what is this?” and “why did we do this?” when you need to. L36

“The highest level of abstraction is just the high level steps and events.”L36

Getting Better at Design L30

Design = discoverability + understanding

Discoverability is how easily you find what you’re looking for, which is features (the key developer use cases). Understanding is being able to add, change and test them once you find them. Good design means you can do this, and it makes it easier for others. Every developer designs interfaces: “Your code is the interface for someone else to do their work.” L30

  1. Structure by the abstraction prism — organize the project the way requirements come to exist, get tested and get implemented (capabilities → features). It’s the most intuitive way to find things. L30
  2. Develop metacognition — understand why you understand things. Internal awareness builds external awareness at the same time. L30
  3. Establish the patterns — use patterns everyone understands conceptually, and agree on the set at project start. Patterns are mental models with stereotypical responsibilities: a Redux store is an event listener/handler/coordinator type of thing, and React components present the view. L30
  4. Study the stages of action — the seven stages of action from Don Norman’s The Design of Everyday Things. L30
Empathy check while coding

Will someone else understand what this is, how to use it and why I’m using it, and can they do their task with it? L30

Anti-patterns
  • “Loosey goosey” code whose purpose can’t be understood as one cohesive thing or tied to a known pattern. L30
  • Mixing stereotypical responsibilities, e.g. React components doing more than presenting the view. L30
“Getting better at design is really a practice of metacognition and developing awareness.”L30

Responsibility-Driven Design (RDD) L23 L38 L91 L94

Definition

RDD sees software as a set of responsibilities (doings and knowings). They are grouped into roles, the roles collaborate, and objects or functions (whatever the “syntactic sugar” is) fill and play those roles. It answers where things belong, how to organize concerns, how big objects should be and how many instance variables they should have. L23

A responsibility is the smallest building block: “something that we do or something that we know.” L94

  1. List responsibilities — every doing and knowing the feature needs, starting from a concrete example. Don’t worry about order or wording yet. L91 L94
  2. Assign them to roles — identify what the roles are, using object stereotypes and each object’s dominant role. L91 L94
  3. Define collaborations — how the roles work together. “I like to do that, that last part of collaboration last.” L94
  4. Find tools — look for existing libraries that implement those roles, e.g. a message queue for scheduling. L91

Why go this deep: phases of craftship

Code-first

“React + Firebase, hook it all up, done.” The pieces are big, technology-focused blocks with little design. It gets you a job. L94

Pattern-first

The building blocks are services, entities, repos, aggregates and factories. They’re more granular, but you get stuck choosing which blocks to use and how to fit them together. L94 L23

First principles (Responsibility First)

DDD, clean architecture and the rest are “just different lenses on the first principles.” RDD is the way in, and it’s where you design things no pattern, library or framework gives you. Examples: a loading state, a custom router, a unit of work. L94 L91

Four abilities of strategic design

Khalil says every developer needs to be able to: L23

  1. Stereotype components: see which responsibilities any library/framework/tool helps implement.
  2. Develop components: build them yourself when needed. This is where RDD comes in.
  3. Integrate components: fill “object design gaps” / “responsibility gaps” between systems that don’t talk to each other.
  4. Prioritize components: build first the contexts and modules that lead to the most business value.

Designing your own abstractions

Abstraction design, meaning building custom abstractions, is “probably the hardest part of software design in general” but “also the most important.” “If you understand the doings and knowings, you could design anything.” Work outside-in: first the conceptual flow (“presenter loads posts” → “show loading” → “presenter has loaded posts”), then the abstraction. L91

Before any code

“You should be writing no code unless you’re very clear on who plays what role and why do they need that.” Role → goal → feature → only the essential properties. That’s how you write the minimal amount of code. L94 For the metaphysics behind it (essence, purpose, form), see Metaphysics.

Where it’s taught: mainly in the Responsibility First phase, which covers the three-step process, bespoke frontend/backend abstractions, object stereotypes, and stereotypical architecture mapped to frontend and backend patterns. It’s practised again in Value First and in the guess point assignments. L38

“This is the deepest level of design I can teach you. Once you learn it, you learn how to really design anything.”L23
AI-era lens · Copilot

AI makes code-first building fast, but it doesn’t decide where the doings and knowings belong. Assigning responsibilities to roles is the design work you keep. Hand the agent a responsibility list with stereotype labels instead of “build zoom”, and it has a spec to follow and you have a map to review against.

The Six Object Stereotypes L94 L95 L38

“Six stereotypical objects that pretty much encompass every single object we will ever make.” Every object is at least one of them. L94 They answer “what types of objects should we use?”, since OO architecture is “one object talking to the next, talking to the next.” L95 Once you see how the stereotypes connect to frontend and backend patterns, “matrix just explodes.” L38 The terms come from Rebecca Wirfs-Brock’s Object Design. L94

StereotypeResponsibility (course)Frontend exampleBackend example
Information holderKnows. Just holds data, and it’s where the information belongs. L94 L95MouseEvent (type, angle). Camera (origin, zoom factor), observable e.g. with MobX. L95A request DTO or an event payload Added by Copilot
StructurerHolds essential data and the rules for how it may or may not change. “Pretty much your aggregate.” L94Camera with rules on how far it may move. L94A post aggregate that a comment is added to. L94
Service providerMostly stateless behavior and math, utility-class-like. L95CanvasService computing the new canvas state. L95A price calculator or password hasher Added by Copilot
CoordinatorLets objects subscribe to events and notifies subscribers (observer). “Maybe 10 lines of code.” L94Application observer. Redux-like store. L94 L30 Page switching. L94Express router, web server, event listeners. L94
ControllerMakes decisions and tells other objects to do work. It usually doesn’t perform the state change itself. L94 Executes use cases, ≈ DDD application service. L95ZoomController. A page can be a controller. L94 L95CreateUser use case. L84 Post-comment controller. L94
InterfacerCrosses over to infrastructure and the outside world: network, file system, human peripherals, third-party APIs. “Like a bridge.” L94Canvas, WindowAPI, CanvasAPI. L94 L95Express network handling, repositories, Stripe/mail APIs. L94 L95

Added by Copilot In Wirfs-Brock’s original catalogue, a structurer is defined as an object that maintains relationships between other objects. Khalil’s working definition (“pretty much your aggregate”) is close: an aggregate holds its parts together and guards the rules about them.

Control center = coordinator + controller

“The key place where all of the main decision making logic happens.” It can be centralized or delegated, and part of it can come from a framework (Express does some routing). Apps usually have several coordinators and controllers, not one of each. L94 Coordinating means getting requests and routing them. Controlling means saying “do this, do this.” L95

React as your control center

Write everything inside React and React is the control center, so you have none of your own and must test through React’s hidden behavior. Push React out to the infrastructure layer and take back ownership of the control center. Then “you can actually test out 90% of the core use cases without ever even starting react.” L94 More in Frontend Architecture.

One object, many stereotypes

“It’s very rare that an object plays exactly one stereotypical role.” Take a canvas service that’s an interfacer. Add caching and it becomes a structurer too. That’s normal, so don’t agonize over it. L95

“Category Theory” for Design: Cohesion & the Dominant Role L94 L95

When a design feels overwhelming, the building blocks are usually too big and too vague. The student’s “camera service” was “a container for everything related to this type of behavior.” The fix is to descend granularly enough: get all the puzzle pieces (responsibilities) on the table, organize them into categories, then work out how the categories collaborate. L94 Choosing which stereotype a set of responsibilities belongs to is abstraction design plus categorical thinking, which is coupling and cohesion. L95

“We want to lean into the dominant role because this is the category theory here. We’re trying to categorize as hard as possible.”L94
Placement heuristics
  • Find each object’s dominant role. If it plays two roles, consider splitting it into two objects. L94
  • Name responsibilities generally: “allows objects to subscribe to events / notifies subscribers”, not “subscribing to the mouse scrolled event”. L94
  • “Anytime I hear state change or updating something to me, that tells me controller”, or a controller talking to an interfacer/stateful object. L94
  • Controllers delegate the actual change. The controller gets the post, creates the comment and adds it to the post, and the repo (interfacer) saves it. L94
  • Anything that touches peripherals, network, file system or third-party APIs is an interfacer. Rules about how something may change go in information holders or a structurer. L94
  • Keep IO out of the application layer. IO belongs in interfacing ports/adapters. That’s why dependency inversion and the dependency rule exist, and why being pedantic here pays off in testability. L95
  • Watch for objects that take on more responsibilities than they need, and break them out. L95
Calling everything a service

Everyone does it, especially in the application and domain layers. Services don’t break down far enough to follow the rules that apply in any architecture (“the laws of software design”), and they lead to references passed around everywhere, like a canvas object spread across many classes. L94 Code you can’t tie to known patterns is hard for others to pick apart. L30

There’s often no single right answer. A controller can be one use case, or it can hold many use cases as methods:

“There is no statically right answer to this... a fun game of coupling and cohesion.”L95

Worked Example: Role-Mapping the Canvas Zoom Use Case L94 L95

A student was building a canvas drawing app (Excalidraw/Figma-like). Canvas manipulation is the app’s core value. Blocky, pattern-first or “find a library” approaches get you partway, then break as more use cases arrive. L95 The design ran through FA²STR: a concrete example first, then the guess point (most likely application level, because the feature involves coordination and control), then RDD. L94

Concrete example

“Currently zoomed out and want to read [small] text. So I zoom in.” Vagueness does not compile. L94

Step 1 — Responsibilities brainstormed (unordered)

  • Detect mouse scroll. Pass the event somewhere it can be acted on. Trigger the event.
  • Subscribe to the mouse-scrolled event. Know when the work is done.
  • Do the zooming work. Adjust the camera’s view of the canvas.

The order was off and that was fine, because the point was to get everything written down. Responsibilities got reworded and generalized as roles were assigned, and new objects (e.g. the mouse event) showed up along the way. L94

Step 2 — Role mapping

ObjectStereotypeDoings / knowingsSrc
Canvas / WindowAPI (wheel listener)InterfacerListens to wheel, switches on event type, pushes a MouseScrollEvent to the observer. Bridge to human peripherals.L94 L95
MouseScrollEventInformation holderKnows the type and angle / delta-Y.L94 L95
Application observerCoordinator (control center)Allows objects to subscribe and notifies subscribers. Does most of the work.L94 L95
ZoomControllerController ≈ application serviceExecutes zoom in / zoom out. The feature ends at updating the zoom factor, then it emits ZoomUpdated.L95
CameraInformation holder (L95) / structurer ≈ aggregate (L94)Knows origin coordinates and zoom factor (default 1, in memory). Holds the rules on how far it may move.L94 L95
“Camera repo”Stateful updater (interfacer)Performs the camera update for the controller. Shows the repo idea outside a DB.L94
CanvasServiceService providerStateless math that computes the new canvas state.L94 L95
CanvasAPIInterfacer + controllerApplies the new projection to the real canvas.L95

Step 3 — Collaborations

Why split it? The god service vs stereotyped objects

Before — one “CameraService”: IO, rules, math, state and rendering fused; untestable without a real canvas
After — one dominant role per object; the use case runs in memory with no DOM
AI-era lens · Copilot

Ask an agent to “add zoom” and you’ll usually get the before column. Give it the role map (interfacer, coordinator, controller, structurer, service provider) and one dominant role per object, and the output becomes reviewable piece by piece. Stereotype labels also let you spot a misplaced responsibility at a glance, e.g. “this information holder is doing IO”.

Reviewing the Upfront Design: Critique & Next Steps L95 L94

Khalil confirmed most of the student’s decisions. The interfacer for window events, the coordinator as control center, the camera as information holder (“excellent decision”, mirroring DDD/hexagonal), the stateless canvas service, and designing with no infrastructure/backend yet were all good calls. He flagged one issue. L95

Before — the API/controller subscribes to events itself
After — an intermediary subscription links events to use cases

“Controllers, use cases, they don’t normally subscribe to things. They’re normally just called upon.” The subscription object keeps “9,000 different non-declarative objects” from depending on the observer. Khalil admits his own DDDForum AfterCommentPosted subscription is “not the best way.” L95

Review lessons
  • Vertical slice vs temporal decoupling. A change inside one use case/transaction (e.g. how the camera changes) is a vertical slice. Updating the canvas projection after ZoomUpdated is a separate feature, which is temporal decoupling. L95
  • Name use cases with the most command-like responsibility, e.g. “update canvas projection”. L95
  • “Lead with the guess, but make small guesses at a time.” Sending delta-Y to a backend brings a new set of responsibilities (reconciliation, network events, offline storage), so postpone it. L95
  • Extract concepts later. Zoom-factor concepts may become their own value objects through object calisthenics. L95
  • Frontend concerns are real responsibilities. View data and model data (knowings), plus updating view data, getting model data and triggering a re-render (doings), must go on objects. Put state on the objects (delegated, backend-like) or in one application data model (centralized, Redux-like). Both have trade-offs. L94
  • “The real reason we have the complexity we have is because of state management”: where data belongs, who operates on it, and which namespace that goes in. L95

Next: from upfront to emergent design

  1. Relax on certainty — upfront design is a theoretical, good-enough guess. It only becomes real (physical) in test form. L95 L94
  2. Write the first test at the application guess point — take the dominant zoom use case, make it readable (Gherkin-style), and ignore backend persistence, subscriptions and outside coordination for now. L95
  3. Let the design emerge — red-green-refactor produces the real design. L94
  4. Match rigor to product stage — build fast until the theoretical guesses are validated, then go defensive. “There’s no right tests always.” L94
  5. Clarity → elimination → execution — “Now you need to weed out what you don’t need. And then you can just go and build.” L94

Upcoming “straight line” curriculum: state machines → object calisthenics → object stereotypes → use-case testing → common collaborations on the use case → stubbing & mocking. L95 Test levels and guess points are covered in FA²STR & Workflow and Testing.

“If I hadn’t stuck to the responsibility-driven mindset, I would have gotten lost.” (student)L95

Architecture & Code Structure

An architect makes the smart decisions at the start of a project. Most of those decisions come from knowing one stereotypical architecture (read/write paths, events, layers, the dependency rule) and from picking tools by responsibility and non-functional need. Code is structured feature-first: modules/ for the customer, shared/ for the developer, tests mirroring features. A modular monolith wired by an event bus is the default starting point. L32 L92 L71

Layer mechanics (dependency inversion, repositories, fakes, the clock contract) live in Horizontal Decoupling. The composition root lives in Composition. This section covers the architecture-level view and code structure.

What an Architect Does & the Stereotypical Architecture L32 L88

Architect

“What is an architect really? It's about making the decisions at the start of a project that are going to be really smart to make.” The skill comes from experience plus education. Education means knowing the foundational styles and patterns, summarised as the stereotypical architecture, plus a working knowledge of platforms and tools. L32

The laws of the stereotypical architecture

The same architecture shows up on frontend, backend and desktop. Hexagonal, onion, ports & adapters and even event-driven are all “one stereotypical architecture.” L32 L88

1 · CQS: read path + write path

“There has to be a read path and a write path.” Commands change the system; queries read it. L32 Khalil files CQS under vertical slicing. L91

2 · Event-based

“We could scale features horizontally because we could just temporally decouple features.” See Temporal Decoupling. L32

3 · Layers of concerns

Horizontal decoupling. Put responsibilities in the correct abstractions, assign those abstractions to layers, and let abstractions talk only to the appropriate ones. Layers: domain → application → adapter → infrastructure. L32 L88

4 · Dependency rule

“An abstraction inside of the application layer is not necessarily supposed to know about directly an infrastructure concern. That's called the dependency rule.” L32

Domain layer concerns (4): data, rules, relationships between data, processes. The domain model is “anything tasked with representing your data, your rules, your processes and your relationships.” L88 L84 Khalil pictures it as “building this little world and just connecting to it using infrastructure.” L88

“Once you're aware of the stereotypical architecture and the layers and the concerns within those layers, you can't unsee it.”L88

Once you know it, you always know when a concern is missing and where to encapsulate it. L88 Many devs struggle to piece an architecture together because they don't know what the stereotypical concerns do or where they belong. Khalil's example: where does React Query go? L93

Picking tools: it all comes down to responsibilities

A large part of architecture is “choosing the best tool for the non-functional task that you need to accomplish.” You can only choose from tools you know, so keep learning platforms (static sites, SSG, serverless, Docker, Kubernetes, an event bus, MongoDB). For each one, learn both its functional and its non-functional reasons. L32

Responsibility / NFRCandidate tool or approachSource
Very fast data retrievalKey-value storage (alternatives: document, relational)L32
Caching, Pub/Sub, key-valueRedis. One component can play many roles.L71
Queuing and schedulingRedis + BullMQL71
SEO for user-generated contentServer-side rendering / pre-renderingL92
Security: never send protected pages to anonymous usersServer-side renderingL92
Real-time play for users worldwideWebSockets question: “really hardcore systems design stuff”L92
  1. Theoretical before physical — problem → solution space (core / supporting / generic subdomains) → architecture (build vs buy, tools per subdomain) → physical guess points. “You never want to be making physical guesses unless you have your theoretical guesses sorted.” L88
  2. List functional requirements and NFRs — the NFR (how the system does a slice) is “where the real complexity lies.” L92
  3. Run the three-step RDD process — list responsibilities → assign them to roles → define collaborations. L91 L71
  4. Find tools that implement those roles, then validate with concrete examples. There's “no more room for it depends”: systems thinking tells you what it depends on. L91 L92

Strategic design selects the platform, components, tools and external services before the walking skeleton goes out. L32 See also Strategic Design.

How to become a better architect (Khalil's path) L32
  1. Climb the phases of craftship and note the styles, patterns and tools you meet: 3/4-tier, hexagonal, event-based.
  2. Learn the stereotypical architecture.
  3. Learn object design (responsibility-first) to glue the pieces together.
  4. Use guess points and systems thinking to decompose problems and route them into the right systems.
  5. Try new tools on your own time (Docker, Kubernetes, an event bus, MongoDB). Learn what each is and why it helps non-functionally, then plug things together.
AI-era lens · Copilot

Code generation is cheap. Reworking a platform or storage choice is not. The architect's early, hard-to-reverse calls stay human. Responsibility-based selection (“which role does this tool play, for which NFR?”) is also a crisp way to review an AI-suggested stack.

One Architecture, Many Names & How It Evolves L37 L91 L84

Layered, onion, clean, hexagonal, ports and adapters, “the Rick Morty,” “9000 different names.” “Layered is actually a little bit different but it's the same thing.” L84 L37 Horizontal decoupling alone pulls in hexagonal, onion, ports and adapters, stereotypical, core vs infra, levels of abstraction and separation of concerns. “It destroys the mind.” L91

Jargon → essentials

Learn the 12 essentials first, then file every new term under one of them instead of chasing each term. Example: CQS is about read paths and write paths, so it goes under vertical slicing. The industry has many names for the same concept (“Dan Abramov just said it a little differently”). L91 See Mapping Jargon onto the Essentials.

Hexagonal architecture covers technical isolation from infrastructure. The course adds what drives development: BDD, DDD, impact mapping, value, pain and benefit. L91

Evolution through the phases of craftship

PhaseArchitectureWhat triggers the change
Code FirstView → controller → DB (MVC, JSON out)Just make it work. L82
Best Practice FirstSlim controllers + service layer = 3/4-tier. The first cut of a layered architecture.Decouple from the database so you can integration test it. Fat controllers do “way too many things.” L37 L82 L91
Pattern FirstAdd an adapter layer; core decoupled from infrastructure = hexagonal / cleanWriting high-value unit tests needs a pure application + domain core behind contracts. “Most of the work” happens here. L37 L82 L91
Responsibility FirstEvent-based architecture on top; object design for custom abstractionsChain features in time, and handle needs no pattern covers. L37 L32

“That's when it becomes the hexagonal or the clean architecture is when there's a decoupling from core code to infrastructure code.” L37 Classify code as core or infrastructure by what it touches, not where it comes from. See Horizontal Decoupling. L84

Why layers exist at all: places to test

“Everything we're doing is a guess.” Layers (domain, application…) are “giving you different places at which you can write tests that are going to have different impacts.” Application-layer tests exercise core functionality without starting React, a database or a web server, which is “incredibly valuable.” L28

Ratio: roughly 1 E2E test : ~10 high-value unit tests. The unit tests give ~80% of the confidence and take ~80% of the work. L28 See also ~10–12 application-level scenarios per acceptance test. L82

Anti-pattern: patterns without the why

Khalil learned DDD before he knew how to write tests, and calls it a mistake. Don't “chuck yourself into it and just start using patterns and then get stuck on the patterns because you don't even really know why you're using the patterns.” L28

Structuring a Codebase: Features First L35 L29 L92 L93

Judge structure through the abstraction prism, which Khalil calls “the key thing here.” Structure exists to serve the key developer use cases: discover features, work on them, test, extend and remove them. L35 Khalil revised his earlier pages/components advice. Organise by feature, the level where all three roles collaborate: “I think this is where stuff should begin becoming code… from this level of the feature.” L92

North star 1 · Key developer use cases

Discover, understand, test, add, change, execute and remove features. L29 L35

North star 2 · Customers decide

Drive code outside-in from the customer boundary, starting with E2E tests. Building a component library or tiny functions first is “fundamentally flawed.” L92

North star 3 · Discoverability & understanding

Open the codebase and see “in a second or two” how to do the use case. This is the hardest part. L92

Before — package by infrastructure: features invisible, cohesion accidental

“I hate packaged by infrastructure.” L88 Two folders for one concept (fake and testing utils) is a cohesion smell. Merge them. L84

After — modules for the customer, shared for the developer, tests mirror features

“Use cases define features, which define modules, which define sub-modules.” Khalil: “that's precisely it.” L92 src/modules/<capability>/<feature>, mirrored in tests/ with acceptance tests per feature. L29

modules/: for the customer

Essential complexity: code related to the problem itself. “It's almost like this modules folder is for the customer. And this folder is like for the developer.” L92

shared/ (shared/core/): for the developer

Accidental complexity and cross-cutting concerns, “what is required”: use-case and entity base classes, a RESTful API driver. L92 In FeedBook: core utilities plus shared domain descriptions. L71

Two kinds of slice

(1) The module: capability or bounded context, the thick cut. (2) The operation: an API call, a thin input→output cut. Features/workflows sit in between. Cohesion decides how thick to cut. L93

Rules
  • For every new abstraction ask: essential (modules/) or accidental (shared/)? L92
  • Keep siblings at the same level of cohesion. Test candidate names: is posts/ a peer of users/, or is forum/ the module and posting the feature? L92
  • “If you can't see your features from the folder structure alone, there's a good chance maintainability is under pressure.” L93
  • Folders ≠ layers. Layers are theoretical and don't need to map to folders. L84 The folder tree follows features/modules/slices. The network of objects inside a module follows the stereotypical architecture. L92
  • Rely on knowledge in the world: src/ and tests/ need no explanation. Call out uncommon folders like packages/ in the README. L92

The README test: 1–2 seconds to a developer use case

  1. README — has a table of contents such as “how to add a feature,” “how to test features,” and says “go to the tests.” L92 L93
  2. Tests by capability — the tests folder is broken down by capability. L93
  3. A feature file per feature — stories → acceptance criteria / scenarios with concrete examples. L93
  4. Then into code — the matching src/modules/… folder. L93
“It's about language. And it's about cohesion and it's about design and it's not precise… It requires constant scrutiny and philosophizing.”L92

This is covered in the Best Practice First phase. Drive structure decisions through the theoretical and the physical, not through anxiety. L35 L91

Understanding Large Codebases via Features L29 L92

A developer's one main task is to keep delivering user and customer benefit, and “the work that you need to do is entirely on features.” So “if we were to maneuver into the code base, you are looking for features.” Hunting features is the 80/20 of understanding a codebase. L29

Feature

“Features are not just specific operations, API calls. Features are user stories or more general.” In the prism: who → why → what (capabilities) are theoretical; features are the “how.” Modules map to capabilities. L29

Feature tracing: when there are no acceptance tests

  1. Find the common features — ask people, read tickets, ask which features are most used, use the frontend app. L29
  2. Trace each one into the code — “try to trace to find out how that feature is realized in the code base.” L29
  3. Infer the original mental model — the tracing shows how the original developers thought. L29
  4. Make features explicit — add a layer of tests that represent features specifically. L29 In a messy codebase, “stop the bleeding” first with E2E tests that wrap the whole thing (the tailor's pins), before any pattern-first refactor. L92
Live demo: “add create post” to DDD Forum L92

Walking in as a newcomer: the README “is not helping.” Path taken: packages/ → backend/ → tests/ (test-first) → acceptance/ (“what is that?”) → users/. Should posts/ go next to users/? Maybe forum/ is the module and posting the feature. “It's philosophizing every, every step of the way through.” The process: walk every developer use case from the README and make each one clearer.

When interfaces make navigation painful: use feature folders, cohesive naming, and consistent layer rules so use cases predictably reference interfaces. See Vertical Slicing. L84

AI-era lens · Copilot

Folder structure is now a navigation aid for agents as well as humans. An agent dropped into a modules/<capability>/<feature> tree with a README “how to add a feature” reaches the right file in one or two hops, and the mirrored feature tests tell it when it's done. Asking an agent to “trace feature X from the UI to the DB” is a fast way to run step 2 above.

Code Placement Quiz L93 L92

Every line creates a new abstraction and needs a home. A student noted that DDD gives roughly 10–15 named buckets, and that once memorised, you know where code goes. Khalil: “That's fundamentally the task here.” L93 Each line gets two answers: which module or feature (folder, essential vs accidental) and which layer (concern). L92

Student answer, confirmed: the application service / use case (application layer, high-level persistence logic), not a controller. L93

#Where it belongsWhy
1Incoming adapter: controller (infrastructure) in the feature folderExtracting and validating the request is exactly what incoming tests verify, before the app is called. L92
2Application layer: the use case“If the user already exists, return an error” is an application concern because it needs the repository. L88
3Domain: an Email value objectValidation is a level-1 input→output question. Keep data and behavior together; don't stash it in a random function in another file. L88
4Infrastructure: the concrete repositoryAn actor playing the UserRepo role. It touches the DB, so it's infrastructure. L84
5Not in the domain: inject a Clocknew Date() touches the system clock, which is infrastructure. The domain must be pure. L84 L88
6shared/core/A use-case base class is accidental complexity, “for the developer.” L92
7An event handler in the module that cares, triggered by JobPostedAppended awaited side effects are temporal coupling: if one fails, the rest never run. L93
8shared/, as an API driverA RESTful API driver is accidental complexity. L92

Tie-breaker for infrastructure vs core: “It's not about where it comes from, it's about what it touches.” L84

Modules as Mini-Applications: The Application Interface L92 L88

A student suggested that each module could be its own application with well-defined interface points. Khalil connected this to the application interface pattern: express the whole app as one API that says “everything that your app can do.” The app implements it (pure), and delivery mechanisms such as a web server use it. L92 L88 It applies the composition essential: “one big object” composing all the use cases. L88

  • Payoff for tests: incoming-adapter tests replace the app with a fake. They check only that endpoints call the correct use case with the correct parameters. L88 L92 Code in Value-First Test Strategies.
  • Payoff for design: without it, “you end up building your app within your framework” (a student's point, which Khalil endorsed). L88
  • Is jobs a feature, a module or a bounded context? Student: “It's both a module and the feature.” Khalil: “It's tricky stuff.” L92

Wiring the real app together happens in the composition root.

Modular Monolith vs Microservices L84 L71

A tech lead planned to rewrite an MVP as microservices with two backend devs. Khalil's framing: that is a theoretical architecture guess made before the problem is understood, and it “has exploded into more guesses for you to make”: observability and telemetry across deployable units, messaging infrastructure, deployment. L84

Justify potential negative value

Every architectural complication must be “solidly justified” against the negative value it can introduce. You may not even be aware of the guesses you're forcing on yourself. L84

Fewer components → fewer guesses

“The least amount of components you have to manage means the least amount of guesses you have to make.” That's why serverless is popular: you get to focus on the guesses you want to make. L84

Extensibility from first principles

Maintainability and extensibility come from vertical slicing plus horizontal decoupling, not from deployment topology. Reading: Vaughn Vernon's Strategic Monoliths and Microservices. L84

Modular monolith ≠ single process

“Modular monolith does not mean modular process. This is just how you organize your code.” Several modules live in one project, and at bootstrap you choose which ones share a process. “Usually a better place to start than microservices.” L71

How to organise it

  • Subdomain classification drives folders: core = build it; generic = import a library; supporting = build it anyway, reluctantly. By the architecture step “we've done the majority of the hard work.” L71 Details in the FeedBook architecture guess point.
  • External services are collaborators: wrap the minimum integration code (Stripe, PayPal, mail) in a service. L84 Don't build generic subdomains such as auth or your own SMTP server. L88
  • Event bus as the backbone: everyone registers and subscribes to events. Deploying everything in one process is the easiest start. Students proposed SOA without a bus, or WebSockets; the course goes event-driven. “At the end of the day, we just need coordinators.” L71
  • Microservices in the course: not covered in depth. The course covers the foundations: temporal decoupling, vertical slicing, horizontal decoupling, deployment. L84
Anti-pattern: the makePurchase transaction script L88

Get cart items → check inventory → bill the card → update inventory → send email, all in one call. A crash between billing and the inventory update leaves an invalid state. Khalil did this on the solidbook site and suffered, with serverless cold starts cutting requests. Instead, model subdomains (e-commerce, orders, billing, emails, inventory), each its own state machine, talking via events.

AI-era lens · Copilot

An agent can scaffold ten microservices in an afternoon, but the operational guesses (observability, messaging, deploys, partial failure) don't shrink with it. Default to a modular monolith with explicit module boundaries and event contracts. Split processes only when an NFR justifies the extra guesses.

Monorepo: Frontend, Backend, Shared L35 L82 L81 L28

In Best Practice First the project is a monolith inside a monorepo: frontend and backend in one project, sharing code. L35 The layout is frontend/, backend/, shared/. shared/ holds the acceptance tests (a shared executable spec) and later the shared models and DTOs, which are covered in Pattern First. L82 Kirill's exploration kept it minimal: a shared package via NPM workspaces for DTOs and even domain objects. L81 Refactoring to a monorepo lets you share DTOs and value objects between frontend and backend. L28

  • Each side gets its own MVC. Extract service/application/domain layers on both sides, and use controllers and presenters on non-trivial frontends. What gets shared is the acceptance tests, and later models and DTOs. L82
  • In DDD Forum's frontend, UserRepo does the work, “synonymous to a use case” on the backend: it takes the registration form, creates a DTO, sends it, and caches the result. L81
  • Hosting setups vary (Next.js/SSR, a backend-served frontend, Netlify + Heroku). That decision belongs to the architecture guess point. L82 Monolith vs monorepo is part of the walking skeleton. L93 Frontend specifics: Frontend Architecture.

Getting Better at Backend L39

“The way to get better at backend is to have a problem in your life or have some area where you want to get back time.” Build backend code there, and “make a commitment to actually seeing that through and seeing it actually now give you back time.” Making it public “is going to propel you.” The course final project (solo or with a community member) is the intended place to do this. L39

PhaseBackend work
Code FirstJust build it. ChatGPT can produce it, “but we need to take it a little bit further.” L39
Best Practice FirstAcceptance-test the backend, use a production-like environment with Docker, use a lot of patterns. L39
Responsibility FirstThink in responsibilities, roles and collaborations; design, then code “guided by objects.” L39
Rules
  • Pick projects with the question “What areas do I seem to spend a lot of time that I don't want to spend in my time in?” L39
  • Measure success by whether the project actually gives you time back. L39
  • Expect a fair amount of theoretical work up front. Use the abstraction prism to know what to do when. L39
  • Don't stop at looking up how to build something with ChatGPT. Code First alone isn't enough. L39

Career-level learning paths and books: Learning Path, Books & Career.

Frontend Architecture

The frontend uses the same stereotypically testable architecture as the backend, under different names. Take the control center back from React. Split the app into a read side (gateway → cache → observer → presenter → view model → component) and a write side (component → controller → domain object → repository → gateway). Test the pure middle without starting React. L33 L87 L90 L92

Same Architecture, Different Terms L33 L83 L87

“The architecture you do on the front end that you do on the back end, you do on desktop, pretty much anywhere. It is exactly the same.”L87
“It's all the same stereotypical architecture.”L83
  • Frontend and backend are “the same thing because [architectures] are stereotypical.” Learn the backend patterns first (Pattern First), build with them a few times, then look at the frontend patterns and kinds of state. It will “look a lot like the back-end.” L33
  • Only the terminology changes. Master the architecture on one side and “you've effectively mastered it everywhere.” Khalil planned to build it 4–5 times (backend, frontend, desktop, Chrome extension) to show it's “the same stuff over and over.” L87
  • Framework patterns map onto agnostic patterns. Redux store and single-file components came from the technology. Their responsibilities map onto stack-agnostic patterns: DTOs, controllers, presenters, global state (fundamentally an observer), gateway, view model, data model. All of these derive from the six RDD object stereotypes. L90
  • The frontend has real domains. React Router has its own domain layer (domain/app/adapter/infra) that you install rather than build. “Your app is just a bunch of… domains connected to each other.” L88
Frontend termBackend counterpart / stereotypeResponsibility
Component (React)Incoming adapter“Just the view.” Renders a view model and forwards user intent. L90 L92
ControllerUse case / application service (command handlers)Receives commands from components. “Effectively the exact same thing as a backend use case.” L87 L90
PresenterRoughly a repository for read modelsBuilds view models and hosts selectors. “The presenter's whole job is to build the view models.” L87 L90
Observer (global state)CoordinatorLets objects subscribe and notifies them on change. “This really is what Redux is doing.” L90 L94
Cache (API client store)DatabaseThe frontend “database”, i.e. global/app state. “GraphQL is like MySQL for front end.” L87
Gateway / API clientOutgoing adapter (interfacer)Sends requests to the backend (axios, HTTP). L90
Domain object (e.g. RegistrationForm)Entity / value objectsValidates and decides whether a command may proceed. L90
DTO / data modelDTOWire shape, often handled by GraphQL or just cached. The data model “is actually the DTO”, and it isn't the view model. L87 L90

Mapping any tool onto the stereotype L87

  1. Read the docs for doings and knowings: what does the tool actually do and know?
  2. List its responsibilities.
  3. Map each to an object stereotype and a layer.
  4. Decide where it goes and what stays out. Worked example, Redux: store/reducer = cache/gateway (infrastructure), subscribe = reactivity, dispatch = updating the store, selectors = reactive queries that keep view models in sync. Verdict: Redux has “nothing to do with features.”

The same move vets React Query or Apollo Client. They handle fetching, caching and hooks. At responsibility-first you check whether a tool covers the responsibilities you need and compose the missing ones yourself. L90

React Must Not Run the Show: Own the Control Center L87 L94

Control center

The coordinator + controller objects: “the key place where all of the main decision making logic happens.” It can be centralized or delegated, and there can be several of each (a page may be a controller, page switching may be a coordinator). L94

The coordination test

“If you want to test your features, if you need to start react, then react is doing the coordination.” A view library “becomes a framework when you let [it] do the coordinating and controlling.” You're “in really good shape” if you can go from requirement to coded feature without touching or mentioning React. L87

  • Payoff: “You can actually test out 90% of the core use cases without ever even starting react.” Add React “way later” and build the frontend “as if you're writing backend code.” L94
  • How the UI hooks up: components get state from the presenter and tell the controller what to do. That boundary lets you swap React for another view library. L87
  • Wrap framework rules you can't avoid. Hooks force a particular structure, so either design things yourself or wrap “the ugly bits and pieces” behind your own abstractions. L33 Khalil would extract a routing service rather than use the router hook: “hooks are just the worst… Don't tell me I need to name things with use in front of it.” L81
  • Strategy decides how far to go. An entrepreneur shipping fast can write everything in React, then turn defensive once value is validated. L94 For small/medium frontends, start with E2E tests and carve out layers only when internal complexity justifies it. “I cannot prescribe to you a single approach.” L90
Before: the component fetches, maps, validates and patches the cache, so React is the control center
After: the component only reads a view model and forwards intent
AI-era lens · Copilot

Ask an assistant for “a React todo list with an API” and you usually get the Before shape: useEffect fetching, inline validation, a custom hook that coordinates everything. Name the roles in the prompt (“presenter builds a view model, controller calls a domain object, component only renders”) and the generated logic ends up in plain objects that a fast test can check.

Read Side: Gateway → Cache → Observer → Presenter → View Model → Component L90

  1. Gateway / API client (infra): sends the request (axios, HTTP adapter). L90
  2. Cache (infra): stores fetched data. This is global/app state, persisted across screens. L90
  3. Observer / coordinator: listens to the cache and notifies subscribers on change. “Global state… fundamentally it is an observer.” L90
  4. Presenter: subscribes to changes and rebuilds view models. Its API is something like presenter.load(). It is also an interfacer, getting data ready for the view. Selectors live here. L87 L90
  5. View model: the shape the component actually renders from. Components “shouldn't take on the job of preparing data to be seen. They should just get the data to be seen.” L87
  6. Component, below the squiggly boundary (code we don't own). It binds to the presenter via useEffect (or MobX etc.) to re-render: “That's how you connect your pure code to React.” L90
Read-side rules
  • Components must not know about the cache/store (dependency rule). L87
  • Don't put selectors in component files. Selecting belongs in the presenter. L87
  • Reads go straight to the data store and return the simplest shape. Don't load domain objects and reshape them (“mapper hell”). Domain objects are for writes only. L87
  • Get reactivity working in the walking skeleton. L87

Write Side: Component → Controller → Domain Object → Repository → Gateway L90

  1. Component: holds ephemeral form state and calls the controller on submit (e.g. the registration page calls controller.register(...)). L90
  2. Controller: a cluster of use cases / command handlers, like a backend application service. It can be split per use case (CreateUserController, EditUserController, DeleteTodoController). L90
  3. Domain object: the decision maker. “Anytime you intend to perform a state changing command… it must typically pass through a domain object to determine if we should continue with the request or not.” L90
  4. Repository: receives valid domain objects and calls the gateway. Repo and gateway may be the same thing. L90 In DDDForum the frontend UserRepo builds the DTO, sends it, then saves to the cache. L81
  5. Gateway → backend. The cache updates and “everything flows back down reactively.” L87

The write path is about throughput: controllers and domain objects decide what gets through. Knowing where each piece belongs encapsulates a lot of frontend complexity. It scales to designs like pipes and filters (FL Studio-style effect chains). L90 Separate read and write code paths so data flows one way. L87

Share value objects

Is it OK to share models between frontend and backend? Yes. Value objects and their validation can come from a shared package, so validation isn't duplicated. Frontend-only domain objects like RegistrationForm still exist. L90 A monorepo with NPM workspaces can share DTOs and even domain objects. L81

Frontend domain logic is real

Khalil used to say DDD doesn't belong on the frontend. Now: logic-heavy apps need proper domain models, e.g. a digital audio workstation, a drag-and-drop call-flow editor, or plugin/pedal-board compatibility. Front-loading logic also speeds up feedback because there's no network round trip. L87 L88

Name use cases by intent

“Submit form” is “not a great name.” Prefer “register user”, “edit user”. L90

State Management: Kinds of State & Where Each Lives L87 L90 L94

“It's either it's global and it gets translated into domain and view or it's component state.”L87
Kind of stateLives inLifetime / notes
API cache (the frontend “database”)API client: axios store, GraphQL client cache, Redux store/reducerInfrastructure. Filled by the gateway, updated after writes. L87 L90
Global / app stateCache + observer (subscriptions)Persists across screens. “Fundamentally it is an observer.” L90
Domain modelsDomain objects (write side)Rules and validation. Derived from global state when commands need them. L87 L90
View modelsPresenterRebuilt on every cache change. Components subscribe and get their initial state from them. L87 L90
Component stateThe component (useState)Ephemeral: forms, toggles. Gone when you leave the screen. Don't hoist toggle state into global state. L87 L90

Centralized

One application data model (Redux-like global state) that everything subscribes to. L94

Delegated

Data and behavior live on the related objects (aggregates etc.) and you watch specific objects for changes, like the backend. Khalil built a chess app this way and has seldom worked on centralized ones. L94

Choose knowingly

Both have trade-offs, so decide per app. There's “probably a best of both worlds in the middle.” View data, model data, updating view data and triggering a re-render are real responsibilities that need owners. L94

  • No Redux or Context required. DDDForum's global state is a small hand-written store using the plain observer pattern, designed by programming by wishful thinking. L81
  • Use-case tests don't know Redux exists. Test cache hydration separately as an outgoing adapter test. “Keep them separate.” L87
  • State management is part of the pattern catalog, with the types of state being global, domain objects, view models and component. L92

Folder Structure & Choosing an Architecture from NFRs L92

Organize by feature, not by pages/components

Khalil retracted his earlier pages-and-components advice as “miss[ing] the mark.” Features are the abstraction-prism level where all three roles collaborate, and “this is where stuff should begin becoming code.” Pages still exist, one level below. The chain is use cases → features → modules → sub-modules (“that's precisely it”). L92

  • Outside-in, never inside-out. Building a reusable component library or composing little functions first is “a fundamentally flawed approach.” Start at the customer boundary with an E2E test. L92
  • Three north stars: key developer use cases, customers decide, and discoverability (1–2 seconds from the README to doing the use case). L92
  • modules/ vs shared/: “this modules folder is for the customer. And this [shared] folder is like for the developer.” Essential complexity goes in modules, accidental complexity (drivers, base classes) goes in shared/core. L92
  • Tree outside, network inside. The folder tree follows features/modules/slices. Inside a module, objects follow the stereotypical architecture: component → controller → … L92
  • Avoid packaging by infrastructure (top-level routes/, controllers/). L90

Choosing a frontend architecture: the architecture guess point L92

  1. List functional and non-functional requirements. “The non-functional part, it's how the system does that. And that's where the real complexity lies.”
  2. Decompose responsibilities with RDD (CRC-card style), assign them to roles, and design collaborations.
  3. Pick the architectural tools that implement those roles.
  4. Validate with concrete examples, then choose. “It depends” is honest, and knowing which NFRs to look for points you in the right direction.
NFRQuestionLever
Speed / bundle sizeHow fast is the first load?Don't ship a 200 MB build. Users drop off at around 3 seconds. L92
SEOWill user-generated content drive traffic? Ask the customer.Pre-rendering: server-render the first request, then client-side. L92
SecurityWhat must unauthenticated users never receive?SSR: for solidbook, don't even send the page. L92
Availability, real-time…How does the system do the slice worldwide?Web sockets, where responsibilities live (the multiplayer “start/join game” example). L92

The main driver is moving responsibilities between client and server: how much security and how much rendering sits on each side. Full treatment comes after responsibility-first. L92

Frontend Testing Strategy L87 L92

1 · System / E2E

Do my API calls work, can I reach the backend, do they translate into the right frontend interactions? Result verification only. L87 L90

2 · Whole app

Presenter + controller as “a regular JavaScript object”: no React, no real API. L87 L90

3 · Application logic

High-value unit tests on the pure middle. Does creating a to-do add one to be presented? Does creating a user show validation errors? L90

Components & adapters

Components are mostly stateless (level-1-style tests). Stateful ones resemble state machines (level 2). Cache hydration is an outgoing adapter test. Incoming-adapter tests matter less on the frontend. L87

One acceptance test per feature, shared by every platform

“You only ever have one acceptance test. You don't switch the test for different environments.” Frontend, backend, mobile and desktop teams take the same spec and each validates it in its own way. For example, the frontend may only check a “check your email” page, while email sending is verified at the application level with a spy. L87

Picking a strategy L92

  • Strategy A: E2E + carve inward with high-value unit tests. Strategy B: incoming (contract) tests + high-value integration tests. Judge them by confidence, not dogma. Mixing is fine. L92
  • For task-based UI apps, start with a few E2E tests: “there's very little that's going to be as good as E2E tests.” In a messy codebase, stop the bleeding first (the tailor pins before cutting). L92
  • Fakes need contract tests. Run one spec against every implementation (fake and real) so the fake stays in parity. L87
  • Structure for more than E2E. Few people structure frontend code so tests “can go further than just doing end-to-end tests.” L33
  • Page objects. A friend's four-tier E2E setup with reusable page objects made new features “plug and play.” L92
AI-era lens · Copilot

When presenters and controllers are plain objects, an agent can run the whole feature suite in milliseconds after every edit, with no browser and no backend. That short loop is what makes AI-generated frontend changes safe to accept. A shared contract test also catches the common agent failure of a fake gateway drifting away from the real API.

Frontend Anti-Patterns L87 L90

Called out in the course
  • Queries directly inside components (Apollo-era advice). L90
  • Components that fetch, display and decide how to structure information: “just too much is happening in one place.” L90
  • Using the state-management library for literally everything. L90
  • Selectors or cache access in component files, which breaks the dependency rule. L87
  • Hooks doing coordination: hooks leaking into controllers “mangle your code” and make controllers hard to test. Khalil calls his own DDDForum v2 controller messy because he was “forced to use react hooks.” L81 L90
  • Letting React be the control center, so you have none of your own and must test through React's hidden behavior. L87 L94
  • Massive coupling. “Coupling… is the enemy of testing.” Insert a contract between clumps so each can be tested alone. L90
  • Loading domain objects for reads and mapping them into view shapes (“mapper hell”). L87
  • Hoisting toggle state into global state. L87
  • Duplicating validation on frontend and backend instead of sharing value objects. L90
  • Organizing by pages/components or building a component library first (inside-out). L92
  • Only E2E tests because the code isn't structured for anything else. L33
  • Over-architecting small/medium apps without strategic justification. L90
“Once you understand this and you understand it very deeply now you understand front end architecture forever.”L90

Related: Testing (contract tests, verification types), ideal developer workflow (outside-in, walking skeleton), physical essentials (horizontal decoupling, composition).

Learning Path, Books & Career

How the course says to learn: climb the phases of craftship in order, learn “topics for problems”, and read a small shelf of books that each feed one essential. It also covers how to stand out as a developer and how to work inside a team. That means knowing your role, being honest about trade-offs, and giving estimates rather than dates. L28L34L80L91

Learning DDD as a Code-First Developer: Don't Jump In Yet L28

DDD's toolkit (impact mapping, event storming, process modelling) is held together by systems thinking: problem → solution → architecture → deployment → system → functions. A code-first mind can't “compute” that chain yet. The way in is to climb the phases of craftship, not to read DDD books first. L28

  1. Code-first — Build the API/app any way you can. Expect manual curl testing, “endpoints instead of features”, and a DB on your own machine. L28L82
  2. Best-practice-first — Start from an acceptance test. Add E2E on the backend, then the front end, then deploy. Refactor to a monorepo so front and back end can share DTOs and value objects. This is where you get the “tiny hints” of DDD. L28
  3. Pattern-first — Learn the patterns in order to carve out a domain layer. Backend: value objects, entities, use cases. Front end: presenters, domain models, controllers, view models. L28
  4. (DDD-first →) Responsibility-first — Talk to domain experts before writing code. Then move on to object design and roles/responsibilities. Stopping at DDD-first is “good progress, but we need to move past that”. L85
  5. Value-first — Guess points, FA²STR and the ideal developer workflow. These only make sense once you've climbed the earlier phases. L28L82

Why this order

  • Layers (domain, application…) exist mainly to give you different places to write tests. Learn testing first, or the layers won't make sense. L28
  • Application-layer tests run without React, a DB or a web server. They're “incredibly valuable”. L28
  • Ratio heuristic: about 1 E2E test to 10 high-value unit tests. L28

How learning actually sticks

  • Chunking: your bandwidth is limited, so you need experiences. Redo assignments using a new approach each time. L28
  • You need reference experiences from the tedious katas before abstract ideas have anything to attach to. L85
  • Rewiring from an old paradigm is “freaking painful”. Set milestones and checkpoints so you don't get stuck “in the void”. L85

“Topics for problems”

  • Learn a topic when a problem needs it. Don't spend “five months on domain-driven design” or on railway-oriented programming in isolation. L91
  • Learn the 12 essentials first, then file new jargon under them. CQS goes under vertical slicing, for example. L91
  • A DDD practice project with no real value only teaches you the patterns. You skip the part where you crunch the domain model. L93
Khalil's own mistake — “I learned DDD before I even knew how to write tests.” If you jump into patterns without knowing why they exist, you get stuck on the patterns. L28
Mastery process (how the 12 essentials were found) — First Observe & evaluate: study the phronimos (practitioners who did it well) and experiment until you reach their conclusions yourself. Then Eliminate what doesn't matter. Then Execute the rest as a “straight line”. L84L85

Deep dive: FeedBook DDD case study · Course map & phases.

“How to Get Better at X” Roadmaps L29L30L31L32L39

The FAQ answers share one pattern: go through the phases of craftship in order, anchor everything to the abstraction prism, and practice on real problems. Only the learning advice is summarised here. Each card links to the section with the details.

Design L30

  • Design = discoverability + understanding. Can you and others find, add, change and test features? L30
  • Structure projects by the abstraction prism (capabilities → features). L30
  • Use patterns everyone already understands, and agree the pattern set as a team at the start. L30
  • Practice metacognition + empathy: why do I understand this, and would someone else? Study Norman's seven stages of action. L30

→ Abstraction, OOP & RDD

Testing L31

  • Learn on the backend first. It's “raw”, with no front-end tooling noise. L31
  • Order: TDD mechanics (examples, parameterisation) → non-flaky E2E with 4 layers of abstraction → decouple core from infra → high-value unit/integration tests and the 3 verification types → choose test strategies. L31
  • Core skill: move responsibilities so you can “isolate exactly what it is you would like to test and forget everything else”. L31
  • Aim for the highest confidence for the least work, given where you are now. L31

→ Testing: Principles & Techniques

Architecture L32

  • An architect makes the smart decisions at the start of a project. That takes experience plus education. L32
  • Learn the stereotypical architecture: CQS read/write paths, event-based design, layers of concerns, the dependency rule. L32
  • Try tools on your own time (Docker, Kubernetes, event bus, MongoDB). Know their non-functional reason for existing. L32
  • “It all comes down to responsibilities”: choose the best tool for the non-functional task. L32

→ Architecture & Code Structure

Backend L39

  • Pick a problem in your life where you want time back. Build the backend for it and see it through until it actually saves you time. L39
  • Make it public. That “is going to propel you”. The course final project (solo or with a community member) is the place to do this. L39
  • Progression: just build it → acceptance tests + a Docker production-like environment + patterns → roles/responsibilities/collaborations “guided by objects”. L39
  • Do the theoretical work up front, using the abstraction prism. L39

→ Physical essentials

Large codebases L29

  • Your work is “entirely on features”, so go into the codebase looking for features. That's the 80/20. L29
  • No acceptance tests? Find the common features by asking people, reading tickets and using the front end. Then trace how each one is realised in code. L29
  • The trace shows you how the original developers thought. L29
  • Target structure: src/modules/<capability>/<feature>, mirrored in tests/ with acceptance tests. L29

→ Architecture & Code Structure

Any new field, fast L82

  • Everything is a system: inputs, outputs, environments, processes. L82
  • Isolate inputs and outputs. Start with the role and the goal. L82
  • Go as deep as you can, down to something foundational (money, value). Then climb back up, connecting the pieces. L82

→ Metaphysics & Systems

Self-assessment — Treat the essentials as game-style stats you level up. At code-first, horizontal decoupling might be about 2/10, and nobody expects 10/10 during best-practice-first. By value-first, all the physical essentials should be solid. L82L91L93
AI-era lens · Copilot

The course already notes that ChatGPT can do code-first (“we need to take it a little bit further”). L39 AI speeds up phase 1, not the climb. Every roadmap above ends with a judgment skill: where a responsibility belongs, what to isolate in a test, which tool fits a non-functional need, how to trace a feature. Put your practice hours into those.
