Philosophy shelf L82

  • Aristotle's Metaphysics (first principles, cause and effect) and Nicomachean Ethics. L82
  • Sartre's existentialism (“first you exist and then you decide your essence”), which Khalil maps to RDD roles and responsibilities. L82
  • Ayn Rand's objectivism on value (flagged as controversial) and Camus, The Fall. Summaries are fine, since the originals are “flowery” and huge. L82

Reading order hints

  • On the DDD path, read Object Design afterwards to get past patterns. L34
  • Hexagonal-architecture material is fine as a supplement. It covers isolating infrastructure but not what drives development (BDD, value). L91
  • A thick book is not a mentorship plan. Seniors who hand juniors “thick books” and say “be better” are named as an anti-pattern. L91

Differentiating Yourself as a Developer L80

“Gone are the days of just farming content with putting in little effort.”L80
Value differential — The shift in what's valuable caused by tools like ChatGPT. Generic how-to content and basic front-end work got cheaper, so authentic human experience got more valuable. L80
  1. List problems — Problems you want to solve in your life or at work. L80
  2. List curiosities — For example, building AI apps or a product that makes money. L80
  3. Pick a non-trivial goal — One you're genuinely motivated by. It's a journey. L80
  4. Chart the path, then teach it — Show what you did and what you saw (the “hero's journey”). L80
Low value nowHigh value now
“How to build a to-do list in React”“Here are the to-do libraries I tried for my project, this one won, and here's why” L80
Hunting for a “unique coding angle”Solving problems you have and sharing them. “It becomes unique when it's intertwined with your experience of life.” L80
Coding for coding's sakeCode as a medium to give back or enrich time. “Solving problems is always valuable.” L80
A persona that's only about codeA personal brand that blends your life domains (Rohan: mental health, logistics, crypto, overcoming poverty) L80

Write, build, sell

Attributed to Naval. Coding is build. Selling is selling who you are, and you do it through writing. L80

Company alignment

Writing about what you care about signals your values, so aligned companies can find you. A mental-health writer ends up at Headspace, for example. “You're going to find the people that you need to find if you put yourself out there.” L80

Value-first career question

At value-first, the question changes from “how do I do things” to “what do I want to do”: which companies, which problems, what personal vision. It's the era of the solopreneur. L93L80

AI-era lens · Copilot

This is Kent Beck's 90/10 applied to careers L3. Generic tutorials and boilerplate are the 90% that dropped to zero. Your judgment calls (the trade-offs you made, the paths you tried and dropped, why X beat Y on a real project) are the 10% that gained leverage. Writing them down is proof of judgment that generated content can't fake.

Working in Teams: Know Your Role, Trade-offs, Plans & Estimates L91L86

Know your role L91

  • “Customers [are] supposed to make business decisions and developers make development decisions.” L91
  • You have a professional responsibility to tell stakeholders the consequences of the current way of working, ideally ahead of time. L91
  • If missing tests start to hurt your ability to keep users and customers “in benefit”, say so explicitly. L91

“No time to test” L91

  • Fast / good / cheap: shipping without tests trades quality for time. That's a strategy choice, so name it as one. L91
  • “I don't have time” is a limiting belief. It's really a value decision. L91
  • Short on time? Write E2E tests for the main paths, then add high-value unit tests if there's time left. That's what “it depends” depends on. L91
  • “There's a difference between not being able to do something and not doing something.” Don't test only for craftsmanship's sake. L91

Practice on your own time L91

  • Tire-change analogy: the customer wants the outcome, not your experiments. Use proven skills on paid work and try new techniques on your own time. L91
  • Roll course material into work on the next feature, or on an existing feature in a new branch. Then make it part of your infrastructure. L91
  • Try unfamiliar tools outside work too. L32

Planning is a lie L86

  • “You have plans. You don't have a plan.” Be ready to throw out an approach when reality or users push back. L86
  • Give estimates, not dates. Everything is a guess. Keep personal deadlines from turning into other people's expectations. L86
  • Estimation is a strategy game: look at your current pieces, their state, and where you are. There's no blanket formula. L86
  • Ship a walking skeleton / tracer bullet early. You learn how fast you work and your estimates get better. L86

Don't evangelise L86

  • Don't try to get the team to buy into every named technique. Many practitioners already use event storming or impact mapping without naming them. L86
  • Being value-first is about you making better decisions. L86
  • Swap some meetings for async video (Loom), with a grain of salt: “can you give back time and enrich time with meetings?” L86

Growing shop, no clear process L86

  • Learn thinking backwards and impact mapping first. L86
  • Build your decision-making: what to focus on, when things get done, how to estimate. L86
  • Stack theoretical guesses (architecture, platform, process) so that physical work speeds up over time. L86

Career Milestones & Confidence L84

Prerequisites check Course — Before starting: you can build an Express API that talks to a DB, deploy it (e.g. to Heroku), and you know types vs interfaces in TS. You should also know the OOP basics: abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism. L84L85
