Mar 14, 2023: FDD (Figma-Driven Design) L84

First day of the early-adopter cohort. Khalil draws architecture and writes TypeScript straight onto a Figma canvas. “FDD” is a joke, not a method. The session opens with a tech lead about to rewrite an MVP as microservices with two backend devs.

Top insights

  • An architecture choice is a theoretical guess that multiplies physical guesses (observability across deployables, messaging infra). It must be “solidly justified” against potential negative value. Fewer components → fewer guesses, which is why serverless is popular. L84
  • Extensibility comes from first principles, not microservices: vertical slicing + horizontal decoupling. A modular monolith (Vaughn Vernon, Strategic Monoliths) can give you the same. L84
  • Core vs infrastructure code: classify code by what it touches (DB, file system, network, system clock, random generator), not where it comes from. new Date() and Math.random() are infra, so wrap them behind a clock contract. L84
  • Everything in the Express controller = anemic domain model. With no layers you can only black-box test, and E2E only allows result verification. Edge cases like “deactivated, rejoins → welcome back” become nearly impossible to reach. L84
  • Three verification types: result (palindrome), state (checkers, found via wishful thinking getCurrentPlayer()), communication (use case ↔ injected contracts). Communication is “the hardest one” but gives the most valuable tests. L84
  • The repository is the adapter. An interface is a role; FirebaseUserRepo and SequelizeUserRepo are actors that play it. CreateUser depends only on the role. L84
  • Abstract → concrete spectrum: start with an interface. Move to an abstract class only after the rule of three, and pair it with YAGNI. “This game is really just fighting your own self.” L84
  • Gherkin as training wheels for application-level-3 use-case tests, where setting up “the state of the world” is complex. L84
  • External services (Stripe, PayPal, mail) get the minimum integration code wrapped in a service. A capability you buy “becomes pretty much that bounded context”. L84
  • Essentialism’s steps (explore/evaluate the phronimos → eliminate → execute) are how Khalil distilled the 12 essentials. L84

Best Q&A exchanges

Q: Is microservices a good decision for a team of two backend devs? It’s a theoretical architecture guess that forces many physical guesses you may not be aware of. Justify it against negative value first. Vertical slicing and horizontal decoupling in a modular monolith give the same maintainability and extensibility. L84
Q: Is it fair to say infra code = packages you install? “Not completely fair.” An npm library that only returns a string is core. Express is infra because it opens a port and touches the network. L84
Q: Navigating interfaces is painful because I can’t ctrl-click to implementations. Three-part fix: slice features into feature folders, use cohesive naming and folders, and follow the layered rules so you always know use cases reference interfaces. L84
Q: Is a user an aggregate? “Depends.” Talk about the data and behavior each feature needs instead. That exposes what an aggregate is and isn’t. L84
“It’s not about where it comes from it’s about what it touches.”L84
“The repository is the adapter... it is a role to be played.”L84
“My goal here is for everyone to become their own coach to make myself redundant.”L84

Where this is covered: Horizontal Decoupling · Subject/System Verification · Verification per Guess Point · Contract Tests & FakeClock · Strategic Design · Modular Monolith vs Microservices · Roles & Actors

Mar 31, 2023: Mastery Foundations L85

A preview of the Mastery Foundations section, which sits between the “stay in the game” mindset material and the physical guess points. It’s mindset-heavy (“It’s extremely abstract”), followed by course logistics.

Top insights

  • Right action: work is full of quantum moments, decisions that send you down different paths. What you do in them depends on what you currently value. L85
  • Phases of craftship: code-first → best-practices-first → pattern-first → DDD-first → responsibility-first → value. At the deepest level, software development is a game of value won with the feedback loop. It’s non-linear, so there are “no silver bullets”. L85
  • Mastery process: observe & evaluate → eliminate → execute. Khalil’s elimination produced the 12 essentials, taught as a “straight line” instead of wandering topic to topic. L85
  • Value creation system, left → right: theoretical guess points (problem, solution, architecture) come before physical ones. Scoring = shipping value; negative value = bugs. L85
  • Zero validated theoretical guesses? Don’t run multi-loop TDD at every guess point. Push one guess through fast, then “start playing defense” with tests at the physical level. L85
  • Platform strategy: shared infrastructure (known deploy, architecture, tested services) lets later features skip guess points and score faster. L85
  • Tools belong to guess points: big-picture event storming → problem; tactical event storming → solution; impact mapping and user story mapping → theoretical guess points. L85
  • Any question = one metaphysical essential + one physical/theoretical essential. “How do I do transactions in use cases?” = abstraction design + temporal decoupling. L85
  • Small guesses applied to the course: MVP in text first (video feedback loops are too long), with opt-in access to rough “prod” content. L85

Best Q&A exchanges

Q (Rohan): I’m confused. What should I do now? Ask a goal-based question: “What is your current goal?” Developers often don’t know what they need to know. The course is the straight-line path that came out of observe → eliminate → execute. L85
Q: Should we TDD at every guess point? Not with zero theoretical guesses validated. Push one artifact through fast and add tests afterwards. With a platform in place you can skip some guess points altogether. L85
Q: Where do event storming, user story mapping and impact mapping fit? In the theoretical guess points. Knowing which guess point each tool serves is a “massive simplification”. L85
Q: What’s the best way of letting go of old paradigms? It’s painful (Luigi went from code-first to using RDD in interviews). Structure it with milestones and checkpoints so you don’t get stuck “in the void”. L85
“Right action really, truly, is based on what you currently value.”L85
“It’s less about the tool. It’s more about the inputs, outputs of the system of creating value.”L85
“The problem that a lot of developers have is they don’t even know what they need to know.”L85

Where this is covered: Right Action · Phases of Craftship · Value Creation System · Tools Belong to Guess Points · Mapping Jargon onto the Essentials · When to Go Light

Apr 22, 2023: First Milestone Review & Intro to the Stateful Guess Point L86

The TDD content had just moved from the book into the platform. Despite the title, no milestone code is reviewed. The session covers FA²STR at any level, how to organize code, and a long introduction to state machines, invariants and fixtures.

Top insights

  • FA²STR is an input → output tool usable at any level of abstraction, from a pure function up to a job queue. For simple problems it happens in your head. L86
  • “n loops”, not an nth-layer loop: start at any level, run FA²STR, emergent design surfaces new constructs, and you drill in again. You can shortcut levels depending on “the score of the game”. L86
  • Stack theoretical guesses (architecture, platform, process) so physical guesses go faster. That’s the case for strategic monoliths and good platforms. L86
  • Organize code from developer use cases (find/add/remove/change/extend/understand a feature, run its test) rather than folder conventions. The README should show them within ~10 seconds (Don Norman’s discoverability; Cockburn’s use cases). L86
  • Problems are stateful. The hand-washing-clothes state machine is built backwards from the end state. Invariant = rule = business logic; it blocks invalid transitions like “gathered clothes → clothes clean”. L86
  • States and events are two sides of one coin, and the purpose of encapsulation is “to protect the way the model changes”. L86
  • Fixture = initial state. Don’t act out 20 chess moves per test. Use GameBuilder.fromCommonGameState(GameStates.theMostBrutalGameEver). L86
  • “Planning is a lie”: you have plans, not a plan. Give estimates, not dates. Don’t push the team to adopt named techniques; value-first is about you deciding better. L86
  • Tracer bullets / walking skeleton show how fast you actually work, which makes estimates better. L86

Best Q&A exchanges

Q: Is there a particular way to organize code? Start from the developer role’s goal and the actors and impacts (impact mapping), then list developer use cases. Make them discoverable: the README first, then module folders that reveal features. L86
Q: What is a fixture? The initial state. The line-by-line chess checkmate test was refactored live into a builder with named, team-known game states. L86
Q: How do I fit FA²STR into team planning and meetings? “Planning is a lie… You have plans.” Many practitioners use these techniques without naming them, so don’t evangelize. Use them to make better decisions yourself. L86
“It doesn’t matter where you start… you need to drill in with several loops.”L86
“What is the purpose of encapsulation? To protect the way the model changes.”L86

Where this is covered: FA²STR at Any Level: n Loops · FA²STR at the Stateless Guess Point · State Machines & Invariants · Fixtures with Builders · Thinking Backwards

May 5, 2023: The Most Valuable Ideas, Frontend Architecture & the Ideal Developer Workflow L87

Khalil front-loads the “game-changing” ideas so students don’t wait for them: the stereotypically testable architecture and the ideal developer workflow from GOOS. Much of the Q&A applies them to the frontend.

Top insights

  • There is one stereotypically testable architecture on frontend, backend and desktop; only the terminology changes. Place any tool (Next.js, Nest.js, Redux, NgRx) by asking which responsibility it handles. Find problem points by measuring the gap to it. Source: Object Design (Wirfs-Brock). L87
  • The guess points exist to let you write tests strategically: stateless (1), stateful (2), application (3, “quite literally life-changing”), outgoing adapter (4), system/E2E (5), with incoming adapters mentioned alongside as “four and six”. L87
  • Ideal developer workflow (GOOS double loop): once per project, Find/Architect/Automate and deploy a walking skeleton. Per feature, write a failing E2E acceptance test → a failing level-3 use-case test (~80% of time) → the remaining ~20% on adapters, E2E pass and UI hookup. L87
  • If you need to start React to test your features, React is doing the coordination. A library becomes a framework when it coordinates and controls. A plain Presenter (read) and Controller (write) let you test the whole app without React or the API. L87
  • One acceptance test per feature, shared by frontend, backend, mobile and desktop (Dave Farley). Each team validates it its own way. L87
  • Verification per guess point: stateless → result; stateful → state; application → adds communication (the only place for it); E2E → result only. State or communication checks at E2E are “bad practice”. L87
  • Frontend state flow: API-client cache → global state → domain + view models → component initial state → local component state. Interactions go through the controller. L87
  • Redux mapped to the stereotype: store/reducer = cache/gateway, selectors = reactive queries that belong in the presenter (never in component files). Use-case tests never mention Redux. L87
  • Domain objects are for writes only. Queries go straight to the store and return the simplest shape, which avoids “mapper hell”. L87
  • The answer to “stop mocking”: handwritten spies and in-memory repos (turned into builders), kept in sync with the real ones by contract tests. L87

Best Q&A exchanges

Q (Tim): Does the first deployed slice have to be the first feature? No. That’s the walking skeleton (via tracer bullets). It can be as small as getting data from the DB onto the screen. The point is to surface infra problems before feature work. L87
Q (Daryl): How do I handle “then I get an email” at E2E when frontend and backend deploy separately? There’s still one acceptance test. E2E does result verification only (e.g. a 201), and email can be a no-op there. Verify the email at the application level with an email spy. A provider sandbox only saves cost; it doesn’t prove delivery. L87
Q: How do controller tests work with Redux/NgRx? Read the docs for its doings and knowings and map them to stereotypes. Selectors live in the presenter. Test cache hydration separately as an outgoing adapter test. “Keep them separate.” L87
Q: Does DDD belong on the frontend? Yes for logic-heavy apps (a DAW, a drag-and-drop call-flow editor, a pedal-board chain). Daryl added that it also speeds up feedback because there’s no network round trip. L87
“If you want to test your features, if you need to start react, then react is doing the coordination.”L87
“You only ever have one acceptance test. You don’t switch the test for different environments.”L87

Where this is covered: The Ideal Developer Workflow · Guess Points as Test Levels · Verification per Guess Point · Hand-Written Spies · Contract Tests · Walking Skeleton · React Must Not Run the Show · Frontend State Management

Front-Loading the Value for Early Adopters (short intro) L83

A short, undated intro video recorded a few days after the May 5 Q&A. It points to that ~2-hour recording and its written key takeaways. The recording itself has no Q&A.

Top insights

  • V1’s goal was to brain-dump the main, most valuable ideas into the early-adopter version. L83
  • Two reasons to front-load: students get results as fast as possible, and Khalil can see how the course is used, a feedback loop on the course itself. L83
  • Watching the full Q&A is optional. Read the key takeaways; the important clips get cut into standalone videos in the fast track and the relevant sections. L83
  • Frontend teaser: the frontend uses the same object stereotypes and architecture as the backend. L83
“My goal for V1 of this course is to pretty much just brain dump all of the main, most valuable ideas of the course into here.”L83
“It’s all the same stereotypical architecture.”L83

Where this is covered: How the Structure Evolved · Ship an MVP Fast

May 25, 2023 (Office Hours): Decoupling From Infra & the Stateful Domain Modelling Guess Point L88

The first “office hours”, where Khalil teaches live to get the tightest feedback loop. It starts from a student’s naive Express createUser (“a lot of missed concerns”, “no domain model”) and ends on aggregates and keeping the domain pure. The stateful guess point is renamed the Stateful Domain Modeling Guess Point.

Top insights

  • Two problems with a naive backend: (1) E2E tests don’t scale, because DB fixtures are complex and slow and the granularity is wrong; (2) the controller, app logic and business logic are fused. L88
  • Fix 1, dependency inversion: core code uses a persistence contract; the real DB and an in-memory fake both “play the role”. The same goes for a fake PaymentService instead of Stripe. L88
  • Fix 2, the application interface: all use cases composed into one pure object that the web server uses (the composition essential). L88
  • Incoming adapter tests only check that endpoints call the right use cases with the right parameters. They catch the “works in tests, fails when deployed” class of bug (e.g. CORS). L88
  • Avoid the word “integration” (“means so many different things”) and avoid packaging by infrastructure. L88
  • Nth looping (renamed from double looping): Student entity (L2) → FirstName/LastName value objects → level-1 validation. Level 2 uses state verification plus domain events to prove objects change for the right reason. L88
  • Aggregate = the minimum data needed to perform a command. Command-specific shapes (UserForEditUser) → rule of three → an abstract User. Can’t find the boundary? You’re doing too much in one command → temporal decoupling. L88
  • Transaction-script danger: a makePurchase that crashes between billing and the inventory update leaves an invalid state. Khalil hit this on the solidbook site, made worse by serverless cold starts. L88
  • Order of work: never make physical guesses before the theoretical ones are sorted. Problem → solution space (core/supporting/generic) → architecture (build vs buy) → physical. L88
  • The domain must be pure: no new Date(), Math.random() or setTimeout, so inject a clock. Frontends are connected domains too; React Router has its own domain layer. L88

Best Q&A exchanges

Q (Talib): Is my test structure right (acceptance tests on business logic, double-loop TDD)? Mostly. Fix the two problems with fakes plus an application interface. Then follow the ideal developer workflow: one production-like E2E, most tests at level 3, ~20% infra tests. L88
Q: Can the web server depend on use cases directly? Use incoming adapter tests with an application interface so the tests don’t have to configure every real use case. Daniel added: without it “you end up building your app within your framework”, and Khalil agreed. L88
Q: How do I design aggregates / aggregate roots? Include only the data a command needs to execute and check its rules (edit user doesn’t need the password). Event storming comes first, and it’s “non-negotiable”. L88
“An aggregate is the minimum amount of information required for you to perform a command.”L88
“You never want to be making physical guesses unless you have your theoretical guesses sorted.”L88
“The domain model needs to be super pure. It’s not allowed to know about system time.”L88

Where this is covered: Horizontal Decoupling · Composition · Aggregates · Event Storming · Temporal Decoupling · Ideal Developer Workflow

Jun 7, 2023 (Office Hours): Theoretical Guess Points, Aggregates, State Machines L89

Held after the theoretical content (problem, solution and architecture spaces) shipped. The theme: the hard part is the what. Most of the session is about aggregates as transaction boundaries and decoupling from time.

Top insights

  • The hard part of programming is determining the “what”, which is about language. Anxiety at work signals a lack of clarity. Write the process down first and execution “feels like typing”. L89
  • Information systems are state machines: one emits an event that triggers the next. Keep to one state change at a time within a context. L89
  • Events may branch across contexts (OrderPlaced → billing + email) but never into two paths in the same namespace. L89
  • Aggregate = transaction/consistency boundary, a level-3 (application) concept; entities and value objects are level 2. Test: if the system dies halfway through, is it inconsistent? L89
  • Relationships go by identifier. A playlist reorder uses a linked list (previous/next IDs), so one small transaction does the move and the rest is eventually consistent. L89
  • Applications force purposefulness: work from level 3 (developer boundary) or level 5 (customer boundary), or you’ll model dogs → owners → houses → cities forever. L89
  • Time is an application concern. Use a Clock role with SystemClock and FakeClock, kept in parity by a level-4 contract test that loops over both. L89
  • Why level 3 is hard: FA²STR’s find step must surface every responsibility there (time, repos, transactions, events, auth). That’s why the course teaches inside-out. L89
  • On AI: it “crunches down” decision-making logic, but you still need the inputs, outputs and goalpost it plugs into. L89
  • Laurent on slicing: a slice is a slice of value, not a technical slice. Technical enablers are chores. Ship behind feature flags and migrate incrementally (nullable column → required). L89

Best Q&A exchanges

Q (Lucas): Is finding the aggregate per event always a good approach? It’s the best way to find the required input. Khalil avoids the word “aggregate” while event storming and looks at inputs and outputs instead. After the process model, drop straight into level 3. L89
Q: Is an aggregate the same as a DTO? No. A DTO is data in a shape with no behavior. An aggregate is the data that must change together in one transaction. L89
Q: How do I handle time in the traffic-light / Pomodoro assignments? Time belongs to the application: a Clock role, a fake that fast-forwards an hour instantly, and a contract test against the real clock. L89
Q: What is a feature/slice? Laurent: the smallest shippable, usable result that solves part of the problem. Use user story mapping for value slices and event storming for developers. L89
“Information systems are just state machines.”L89
“It’s okay to mock... but just make sure you mock correctly... You want to create parity between what’s real and fake.”L89
“If you don’t have clarity on what matters, everything’s gonna seem like a threat.”L89

Where this is covered: Aggregates · State Machines & Invariants · Contract Tests & FakeClock · Clarity Strategies · Temporal Decoupling

Jul 4, 2023: From Code-First to Best-Practice First L82

The course is restructured around the phases of craftship, and Khalil previews what best-practice-first will fix in code-first projects.

Top insights

  • Phases of craftship are the course spine. Guess points, FA²STR and the ideal workflow only make sense once you’ve climbed them. L82
  • Why the course is built incrementally: Khalil first wrote “thousands and thousands of pages of theory” up front. Now he adds foundational theory only when it’s needed. L82
  • Code-first problems: manual testing with curl, thinking in endpoints instead of features, and a DB installed on the local machine. L82
  • Debugging loop: if you keep changing something and it keeps failing (Dockerfile edits on a 30-second cycle), stop, zoom out, draw it, clarify responsibilities, then descend. L82
  • Role → goal → features → concrete examples → acceptance tests. DDD Forum reframed: a conference organizer wants an audience of DDD-curious developers to sell tickets to. L82
  • Acceptance test = shared executable spec for frontend and backend. Four layers: example → runner → test code → protocol driver (a page object on the frontend) → system. L82
  • Three test categories: acceptance (“does it do what the customer wants?”), unit (~80%), infrastructure (start/stop DB, web server). L82
  • Minimal pipeline (after Dave Farley): commit phase → release candidate → acceptance phase in a production-like environment → infra tests → deploy. L82
  • Architecture progression: view-controller-DB → service layer (four-tier, slim controllers) → pure application/domain core. Add a composition root and Docker for the dev DB. L82
  • Monorepo with frontend/, backend/, shared/ (acceptance tests, later DTOs). Each non-trivial frontend gets its own MVC with presenters. L82

Best Q&A exchanges

Q: One acceptance test for the whole app, or separate ones for frontend and backend? Write it so it can run on either side, as a shared executable specification. Run it against the backend, or end to end through a page-object protocol driver. L82
Q: Should “Then” be past tense, like an event? Usually (“order should have been placed”, “email sent”). Present tense is fine for UI experience (“I should now be logged in”). The hard rule is to describe the system the way the user interacts with it. L82
Q: Our team of three has strong product ownership. Which artifacts should we use? Role-goal (≈ impact mapping, feature injection), process modeling, user story mapping and example mapping. Documents are a side effect of shared understanding and go stale. Read BDD in Action or Specification by Example. L82
“You’re just so too deep into the how. What you need to do is stop, zoom out, draw it up front.”L82
“Never start a project without these four words clearly understood.”L82

Where this is covered: Debugging by Zooming Out · Role → Goal → Features → Examples → Tests · 4-Layer Acceptance Tests · Deployment & Delivery · Phases of Craftship · Monorepo · Recommended Books

Jul 27, 2023: The Walking Skeleton, Pipeline & Contract Tests L81

More restructuring: the DDD Forum build assignments become optional, and students apply the 4-layer E2E setup to their own work instead. The session ends with the definitive answer to “we’re only testing our mocks”.

Top insights

  • Developers do two things: improve existing features and add new ones. To improve, write a characterization test around the black box, then move in a layer and distill (Evans). Don’t rewrite from scratch. L81
  • New flow: code-first → testing basics → best practices (E2E backend with Docker → E2E frontend → walking skeleton → deploy → minimal pipeline → improve the design) → pattern-first. L81
  • Walking skeleton = tracer bullet. Khalil’s own mistake was writing all the pure core first, then hitting “all these weird CORS errors” on deploy. L81
  • Execution guess point: after users use the code, check the KPIs. That closes the loop back to the start of the value creation system. L81
  • Pipeline: commit phase (lint, build, unit tests giving ~80% confidence, package) → acceptance phase (staging + E2E) → production. Put tests in CI, not only in Husky hooks. L81
  • Six test levels via systems thinking: L6 incoming, L5 system, L4 outgoing, L3 app, L2 stateful, L1 stateless. “It is just all inputs and outputs.” L81
  • Test mix: E2E for the happy path plus one or two sad paths, then ~12–20 high-value tests with concrete examples, parameterized. L81
  • Library mocks only for trivial stubs (a logger). Stateful dependencies are indirect inputs, so use fakes covered by contract tests. L81
  • React hooks “really force you to completely mangle your code”. Use a plain observer store and extract a routing service. L81

Best Q&A exchanges

Q: Should these tests run locally via Husky? Devs can turn hooks off and push broken code, so run tests in the pipeline (GitHub Actions). A student’s rule, endorsed: fast things pre-commit, slow things in CI. The minimum is that you can deploy and the E2E tests run. L81
Q: When we mock the use case’s repo, devs feel “we’re just testing what we put into the tests”. That feeling is a symptom of missing contracts. Run one integration spec over every repo implementation, fake and prod, so if one breaks they all break. L81
Q: What if the repo has complex filters and aggregations that are hard to fake? Pull the filtering into its own abstraction or subdomain (e.g. search). If the DB does the heavy lifting, test the contract and “let the external tool do the external tooling”. L81
“You’re testing the contract, not the implementation.”L81
“If you could deploy, and if you can run the E2E tests, and the E2E tests run, you’re good.”L81
“Raise the level of abstraction of what it is you’re looking at to test.”L81

Where this is covered: Contract Tests · Walking Skeleton · Deployment & Delivery · 4-Layer Acceptance Tests · Guess Points as Test Levels

Aug 15, 2023: New Q&A Structure + Frontend Architecture 1 of 2 L90

This session introduces the new format: topics proposed in the office-hours channel and voted on. Frontend architecture beats high-value unit testing, and Khalil draws the whole frontend architecture on an iPad.

Top insights

  • Two mental models (feedback loop + abstraction), tied together by systems thinking: “If you understand those things that is the entire course really.” L90
  • Architecture’s goal is scalability, meaning all three roles win (users, customers, developers). You achieve or lose it through the four pillars. L90
  • Bad design example: packaging by infrastructure (routes/, controllers/). Structure should “progressively move inwards”. L90
  • Coupling is the enemy of testing. Insert a contract between two clumps (one implements it, one relies on it) and repeat to isolate smaller clumps. L90
  • Framework patterns map to agnostic patterns (Redux store, single-file components → DTO, controller, presenter, observer, gateway, view model), which derive from the six RDD stereotypes. L90
  • Read path: gateway/API client → cache → observer/coordinator → presenter → view model → component, bound via useEffect or MobX. L90
  • Write path: component → controller (use cases/command handlers) → domain object (e.g. RegistrationForm) → repository → gateway. Any state-changing command should pass through a domain object first. L90
  • Component state (ephemeral, useState) is separate from app state (the cache). L90
  • Strategy: small and medium frontends start with E2E tests. Carve out the pure middle (the high-value unit test zone) only when complexity justifies it. L90

Best Q&A exchanges

Q: What’s the goal of frontend architecture? Students offered easy to change, many devs on one codebase, easy to navigate. Khalil abstracted all of them into scalability: all three roles winning, via the four pillars. L90
Q: Don’t React Query or Apollo abstract all this? They handle fetching, caching and hooks. At responsibility-first you see their doings and knowings, map them to stereotypes, and either vet the tool or compose the missing responsibilities yourself. L90
Q: Is it OK to share models between frontend and backend? Yes. Share value objects and their validation from a shared package. Frontend-only domain objects like RegistrationForm still exist. L90
Q: Is this necessary for small or medium companies? Often no. Start with E2E per the ideal workflow, and decouple only when internal complexity grows. “This is why I cannot prescribe to you a single approach.” L90
“Scalability is when one two three are winning.”L90
“Coupling... is the enemy of testing.”L90
“The presenter’s whole job is to build the view models.”L90

Where this is covered: The 3 Roles · The 4 Pillars · Horizontal Decoupling · Value-First Test Strategies · Read Side · Write Side

Aug 22, 2023: Final Course Structure L91

Khalil shows his topic map, built on the abstraction prism and his North Star for re-recording the course. He derives advanced topics from the two mental models, then walks the final phase plan.

Top insights

  • The topic map is a walking skeleton for the curriculum: goals → capabilities → features → acceptance criteria, linked “almost like a context”. It means less rework. L91
  • Every essential stems from abstraction or the feedback loop. Derived live: sagas (state machines chained by events) and composition (layering = abstraction; encapsulation as a constraint that aids feed-forward). L91
  • “No more room for it depends”: systems thinking tells you what it depends on. Short on time? E2E on the main things, then high-value unit tests. Weird Stripe API? More outgoing tests. L91
  • Why only 12: horizontal decoupling alone has a dozen synonyms (hexagonal, onion, ports & adapters…). Learn the 12 and map new jargon onto them (CQS → vertical slicing). L91
  • Capability ≠ choice: the course gives you the ability; whether to use it is a strategy decision. L91
  • Final phases: Code First → Best Practice First (E2E, 4-layer infra, walking skeleton) → Pattern First (decouple; result → communication → contract tests; state machines and sagas) → Responsibility First (custom abstractions: LoadingState, router, unit of work) → Value First (FA²STR, guess points) → Bridging the Gaps (long live-coded builds). L91
  • Three-step RDD: list responsibilities → assign roles → define collaborations; then find tools that implement those roles. L91
  • Flaky E2E tests are usually a symptom of missing the four-layer structure. L91
  • Mocks without contracts create two divergent code paths. Production and test code should follow the same path. L91

Best Q&A exchanges

Q: Our managers say there’s no time for tests. How do we apply this at work? Fast/good/cheap is a strategy trade-off, and “I don’t have time” is really a value decision. Customers make business decisions and developers make development decisions. Your professional responsibility is to tell them the consequences, ideally in advance. Practice new techniques on your own time (the car-tire analogy). L91
Q: How do two mental models explain advanced topics like sagas? Apps are states (sign up = nonexistent → “just signed up”). Sagas chain those state machines with events, e.g. Amazon’s place order. They’re taught at the stateful domain modelling guess point. L91
Q: I learn best by watching someone reason through designing a whole system. That’s Bridging the Gaps: ~2-hour live builds, top to bottom, with strategic decisions (test types, how much decoupling, DB choice) made out loud. L91
“There’s no more room for it depends now.”L91
“There’s a difference between not being able to do something and not doing something.”L91
“If you understand the doings and knowings, you could design anything.”L91

Where this is covered: Phases of Craftship · The Big Map · Mapping Jargon onto the Essentials · “No Time to Test” · Contract Tests · Working in Teams & Companies

Aug 30, 2023: Frontend Architecture 2 of 2: Structure, NFRs & Test Strategies L92

Part 2 revises Khalil’s own earlier structure advice, demos discoverability on DDD Forum, explains how to choose a frontend architecture, and contrasts two complete test strategies.

Top insights

  • Organize by feature, not by pages and components (Khalil retracts his earlier advice). Features are where all three roles meet on the abstraction prism: feature → story → scenario → acceptance criteria. L92
  • Drive work outside-in from the customer boundary. Building a component library or small functions first is “a fundamentally flawed approach”. L92
  • Three north stars for structure: key developer use cases, customers decide, and 1–2 second discoverability starting from the README. L92
  • modules/ vs shared/: essential complexity (the customer’s) vs accidental complexity (the developer’s: base classes, drivers). Ask this for every new abstraction. L92
  • Tree vs network: the folder tree holds features, modules and slices. Inside a module, objects follow the stereotypical architecture. L92
  • Choosing a frontend architecture is an architecture-guess-point decision driven by NFRs (speed/bundle size, SEO, security, availability). The main lever is moving responsibilities between client and server (SSR, pre-rendering). L92
  • Stop the bleeding: in a messy codebase, wrap everything in E2E tests first (the tailor pinning the fit), then refactor to patterns. L92
  • Two test strategies: (A) E2E + high-value unit tests, or (B) incoming (contract) tests + high-value integration tests. Judge them by confidence, and mix freely. L92
  • Incoming test: mock the app behind the application interface and verify the controller extracts and validates the request, then calls the right use case. L92
  • Automated testing is an investment, and the customer decides. A friend’s four-tier E2E with reusable page objects made new features “plug and play”. L92

Best Q&A exchanges

Q: So use cases define features, which define modules, which define sub-modules? “That’s precisely it.” But feature vs use case (account management vs registration) takes constant philosophizing about cohesion. L92
Q: Which frontend architecture should we choose? Decide it at the architecture guess point: list functional requirements and NFRs, decompose with RDD, assign roles, then pick tools. A multiplayer “join game” is a trivial slice functionally; the NFRs are “where the real complexity lies”. L92
Q: I’m a junior dev in a messy codebase with no seniors. How do I do what’s best? You can’t fully yet, because it takes experience. Get reps on your own project: kill designs, redo them (Luigi got hired this way). “You’re structuring your consciousness now.” L92
Q: Aren’t unit and integration tests of business logic more important than E2E? E2E tests “suck” to write but give customer confidence like little else. For task-based UI apps, start with a few E2E tests and carve inward. Either strategy is valid. L92
“It’s almost like this modules folder is for the customer. And this folder is like for the developer.”L92
“Just stop the bleeding… It’s the end to end test, man.”L92

Where this is covered: Vertical Slicing · The Abstraction Prism · Value-First Test Strategies · 4-Layer Acceptance Tests · Architecture Guess Point · Structure & Choosing an Architecture · Frontend Testing Strategy · Modules as Mini-Applications

Nov 7, 2023: Introducing the 12 Essentials L93

The first live Q&A after a months-long break. Khalil walks the FigJam board of all 12 essentials (“the ubiquitous language of software essentialism”), then reviews a student’s slot-booking plan and another student’s composition roots.

Top insights

  • Abstraction is essential #1, and it has a direction: role → goal → features → stories → acceptance criteria → examples → code. Working from code up “always results in a mess”. L93
  • A test is “a flag post in the future”. Self-check while coding: can you link what you’re doing to a role’s goal? If not, you’re “thinking forwards”. L93
  • The highest theoretical abstraction in code is the feature file: stories, acceptance criteria and a concrete-examples table. L93
  • Vertical slicing: features should be visible from the folder structure. There are two slice types: the module/bounded context and the operation (an API call). L93
  • Horizontal decoupling has two parts: know the buckets and where each line belongs, then practice decoupling to gain control (fast CI tests). Quiz: await this.repo.save(post) belongs in the application service/use case. L93
  • Temporal coupling (a chain of awaited side effects after “job posted”) is “only solvable… from the very start”. Go event-based from day one: start with a coordinator and keep the flow unidirectional. L93
  • Composition: if (env === 'prod') is a smell. Wire swappable components in a composition root, and move to a DI container only when it gets messy (Mark Seemann). L93
  • Strategic design, Khalil’s four abilities: stereotype components quickly, build them, integrate them (glue code = RDD), and prioritize core/supporting/generic. L93
  • Deployment & delivery: make it very hard to ship negative value. L93
  • You need all 12; you don’t pick them per use case. They’re a practicable layer below the four pillars. L93

Best Q&A exchanges

Q: Is there an order to the 12 essentials when starting a project? No, they’re skills. The order comes from the ideal developer workflow (a checklist that starts with the theoretical guesses) and FA²STR. You can be “2 out of 10” on one essential and still follow the workflow. L93
Q: My slot-booking system notifies ~7 services after a booking. Where do I start? Walk the guess points: impact mapping → big-picture event storming → process modeling of one story → problem decomposition (screens, data, speed) → architecture (event-based from day one?) → walking skeleton. L93
Q (Eric): I build repos at request time to avoid long-lived DB connections. Good idea? The code is clean, but async builds invite a forgotten await, and per-request connections cost handshakes and cold starts. Create one DbConnection at bootstrap and inject it into thin repos via the composition root. L93
“We always need to start from the top and go downwards.”L93
“Writing tests is just setting a flag post in the future to explain what we are about to realize.”L93
“If you can’t see your features from the folder structure alone, there’s a good chance maintainability is under pressure.”L93

Where this is covered: The 12 Essentials at a Glance · Working Top-Down · Temporal Decoupling · Composition · Strategic Design · Deployment & Delivery · Code Placement Quiz

1-on-1 Part 1: Category Theory, Frontend Architecture, Metaphysics & RDD L94

Undated. Student Lucas is building a canvas drawing app like Excalidraw or Figma, and his canvas object is being passed to and changed by everything. Khalil goes down to first principles, then runs upfront FA²STR on a “zoom in/out” feature.

Top insights

  • Diagnosis: clarity and overwhelm. “Camera service” is too big and vague a building block; “everyone calls everything a service”. L94
  • Phases: code-first → pattern-first → first principles. The gateway to first principles is RDD, where responsibilities (doing/knowing) are the smallest building blocks (an idea from Scott Bellware). L94
  • Metaphysics chain: essence → actor/role/goal → purpose → form. For drinking coffee, the mug’s hole is essential and “printable” is not. A stone is a toy, a weapon or a tool depending on who uses it. L94
  • Essence of software: computing solves problems through sequence, selection and iteration. A problem = state A → state B. Transition = behavior, event = the fact it happened, data = initial state + events, namespacing = abstraction for understanding. L94
  • “The correct architecture is the event-based one”, because it works with the grain of reality. Event sourcing and CQRS strip away everything but that essence. L94
  • Pick the guess point first. Zoom is most likely level 3 (application), since it involves coordination and control. L94
  • Stereotypes assigned: Canvas = interfacer; MouseEvent = information holder; app events observer = coordinator; CameraController = controller (delegates the change); Camera = structurer (≈ aggregate); the math = likely service provider. L94
  • Control center = coordinator + controller. Take it back from React and push React to infrastructure, and ~90% of core use cases become testable without starting React. L94
  • Match rigor to product stage. Ship fast in React until the value is validated, then play defense. “There’s no right tests always.” L94
  • Frontend state: delegated (watch specific objects) or centralized (a Redux-like application data model). Both have trade-offs. L94

Best Q&A exchanges

Q: Is the camera an entity rather than a service? Partly right: it has rules. But the “service” should break into several smaller objects linked by stereotypical rules, for testability and fast extension. L94
Q: Isn’t abstraction essential to computing, since even reading voltage as binary is abstraction? “Good point.” Abstraction is the first of the three metaphysical essentials, and understanding may be the essence of everything. L94
Q: Does the controller make the change itself? Usually not. It orchestrates, and a stateful updater (a “camera repo”, like a repo saving a post) performs it. L94
“You should be writing no code unless you’re very clear on who plays what role and why do they need that.”L94
“Vagueness does not compile.”L94
“You can actually test out 90% of the core use cases without ever even starting react.”L94

Where this is covered: Essence → Role/Goal → Purpose → Form · Phases of Craftship · FA²STR · Responsibility-Driven Design · Object Stereotypes · Worked Example: Zoom

1-on-1 Part 2: Reviewing the Upfront Design & Next Steps L95

Undated. A Loom-style review of Lucas’s upfront RDD diagram for the zoom use case, following Part 1. Most of his decisions are confirmed; one is corrected.

Top insights

  • Core-value, granular problems (canvas manipulation) need RDD. Blocky or library-first thinking gets you part of the way, then breaks as use cases grow. L95
  • Objects playing more than one stereotype is normal. A canvas service that adds caching becomes structurer + interfacer. L95
  • Design without infrastructure first. Sending delta-Y to a backend adds reconciliation and offline concerns, so postpone it: “lead with the guess, but make small guesses”. L95
  • Roles confirmed: window API = interfacer (like Express’s network handler); application observer = control center; ZoomController ≈ DDD application service; Camera = information holder (origin, zoom factor); CanvasService = stateless service provider. L95
  • One transaction vs after-the-fact: changing the zoom factor is the vertical slice. Updating the canvas projection on ZoomUpdated is a separate feature, which is temporal decoupling. L95
  • The correction: controllers and use cases don’t subscribe. Put an intermediary subscription/event-handler object between events and side-effect use cases. L95
  • State management is the root of most complexity: where data belongs, who operates on it, which namespace. L95
  • Pedantic placement serves subject/system verification. Keep IO at the ports, out of the application layer. L95
  • Next step: move from upfront (theoretical) to emergent (physical) by writing an application-level Gherkin use-case test for the dominant zoom use case. L95

Best Q&A exchanges

Q: Several stereotypes seem right for one object. Which is correct? Usually more than one. Choosing is abstraction design and a coupling/cohesion call; “there is no statically right answer”. L95
Q: Is updating the canvas projection part of the zoom use case? No. Zoom ends at updating the zoom factor and emitting ZoomUpdated. The projection update is a separate, temporally decoupled feature. L95
Q: What next? Relax on certainty: this is all upfront. Write the first test at the application guess point for the dominant use case, and skip subscriptions and outside coordination for now. L95
“It’s very rare that an object plays exactly one stereotypical role.”L95
“Controllers, use cases, they don’t normally subscribe to things. They’re normally just called upon.”L95

Where this is covered: Temporal Decoupling · Vertical Slicing · Subject/System Verification · From Theoretical to Physical · Critique & Next Steps

AI-era lens · Copilot

Which Q&A ideas matter most when agents write much of the code:

  • Contract tests across fake and real implementations (Jul 27, Jun 7). Agent-generated fakes and adapters drift quietly; a shared spec catches the drift at once.
  • Walking skeleton + commit/acceptance pipeline. This is the gate that turns high-volume generated code into deployable code without shipping negative value.
  • Own the control center and the application interface (May 5, May 25, 1-on-1). Agents can then verify features with fast level-3 tests, with no browser or server.
  • Top-down specs: role → goal → feature file → examples. “Vagueness does not compile” applies to prompts too. Khalil’s own view is that AI shrinks decision logic but you still supply the inputs, outputs and goalpost. L89

Glossary

Course vocabulary A–Z. Where lessons define a term differently, the definitions are merged into one entry. Each entry links to the lessons that define it (up to five) and to the section of this guide that covers it best. Use search to filter rows.

A–C

TermCourse definitionLessonsSee
12 EssentialsThe 80/20 of testing, design, architecture and strategy. They come in three groups: metaphysical (abstraction, feedback loop), theoretical (value identification, domain discovery, strategic design) and physical (vertical slicing, horizontal decoupling, temporal decoupling, composition, subject/system verification, walking skeleton, deployment & delivery). The course calls them its “ubiquitous language”.L1L13L93Essentials overview
AAA backwardsWrite the test Assert-first: state the desired outcome, then the Act, then the Arrange. It is thinking backwards applied to a single test, usually together with programming by wishful thinking.L51L75AAA backwards
Abstract classHalfway between real and not real. It has a partial implementation plus abstract members that subclasses must define. Example: React's Component, where you implement render and the rest already exists behind the scenes.L79L84Levels of realness
AbstractionThe root principle of design, where design means discoverability and understanding. Abstraction separates the theoretical from the physical: it expresses what we want without defining everything, keeps what's essential and removes what isn't. It gives the highest-level picture (getting from here to there) plus concrete, discrete steps, with lower-level steps hidden. High level = contract, type, declarative. Low level = concretion, implementation, imperative.L14L79L91L93Abstraction
Abstraction designerThe developer's real role: taming complexity by describing the reality (metaphysics) of what things are inside the computer.L14L62Abstraction
Abstraction layers“Buckets” for where abstractions go while coding. They are also where guesses get implemented.L14L15Abstraction in practice
Abstraction prismA diagram with theoretical questions at the top that narrow down to code at the bottom: Vision → Roles/Goals → Capabilities → Features → Stories → Acceptance criteria → Concrete examples → code.L14L21L26Abstraction prism
Acceptance criteriaThe things that must be verified as working, such as form state, validation, a spinner and errors. They get encoded in the outer-loop acceptance test.L15L27Value identification
Acceptance phaseThe deployment-pipeline phase that deploys to production-like (staging) infrastructure and runs the E2E tests there.L25L81Deployment & delivery
Acceptance test (outer-loop test)A concrete example (Given/When/Then) derived from a user story, written in the user's language and put straight into the codebase to drive the work. It is the E2E/system-level test and a shared executable specification for all platforms and teams (frontend and backend).L26L40L82L87Acceptance tests
Accidental complexityCode needed to build the thing that isn't about the problem itself, e.g. a RESTful API driver or a use-case base class. It goes in shared/ or core/.L92Structure & NFRs
ActorThe real thing that plays one or many roles, e.g. Khalil as brother, coach and musician. In event storming, it's whoever performs a command: a person/role (Author, Pre-reader) or the System.L10L69L79L94Roles & actors
Adapter layer“Describing how outside world stuff can integrate with our core code.” It defines the ports (e.g. repositories). Hexagonal/clean architecture is layered architecture plus this adapter layer.L37L84One architecture
Aggregate“The data that we're doing work against.” It's the minimum information needed to perform a command and evaluate its rules, and the result is saved into an event. It is not necessarily the input data. Khalil also calls it a transaction boundary: the state change either happens or it doesn't, which keeps the app consistent. It may be a logical boundary rather than a code construct. The student view, “objects that enforce invariants”, was accepted.L69L88L89Aggregates
Analysis paralysisA perfectionist need to explore everything, which prevents action.L5Clarity strategies
Anemic domain modelAll logic (parsing, rules, persistence) crammed into an infrastructure controller, so there's effectively no domain model. Typical of code-first.L84L85Q&A: FDD
Anti-visionThe negative future you want to avoid. Use it alongside a positive vision to stay motivated.L6Motivation
API designDesigning the shape and usage of anything that others (or you) will consume. Per Khalil, that's pretty much everything you write.L51AAA backwards
Application boundaryThe inner boundary around application logic. Work doesn't start here, but much of it happens here.L92Structure & NFRs
Application concernAnything that deals with the outside world: external services, receiving requests, and deciding when to call level-2 domain concepts (including time).L89Q&A: aggregates
Application interfaceA pure object/API that says “everything that your app can do”. The app implements it, and delivery mechanisms such as a web server use it.L88Application interface
Application ruleInput data that isn't a domain invariant but is needed to operate, e.g. an authorId to connect back to the author.L70Refining the process model
ArchitectSomeone who makes the smart, large-scale decisions at the start of a project.L32The architect's role
Architecture (pillar)Whether the structure supports the long-term goals of the three roles. Also: the large-scale decisions made mostly very early in a project.L12L23Four pillars
Architectural componentAny library, framework, tool or platform that helps piece the architecture together.L23Strategic design
Big ball of mudA codebase whose team doesn't know its core domain. It's a mess and can't be changed.L88Q&A: decoupling
Bespoke designDesigning your own abstractions instead of applying off-the-shelf patterns. Taught in Responsibility-First.L33RDD
Best-practice-firstPhase 2 of craftship. Start from an acceptance test, add E2E tests, deploy, build a walking skeleton and use a monorepo. Most vertical-slicing work happens here.L16L24L28L82Phases of craftship
Boundary (squiggly line)Khalil's drawing convention for the line between code we write and code we don't (e.g. React). A solid line means “uses”.L90Control center
Bounded contextA grouping of subdomains into a major domain inside which the same language is used. It places a boundary around the language allowed within one sphere of the domain. Where to draw the line is “incredibly subjective”. In code, it maps to a package-by-domain module.L65L66L67L68Bounded contexts
Builder (test)An object that encapsulates setting up the initial state (fixture), so tests stay clean and can start from a named, prepared state. See GOOS.L78L86L88Fixtures & builders
Cache (frontend)Infrastructure storage for fetched data. It is global/app state, persisted across screens.L90Frontend state
CapabilityA high-level thing a role will be able to do (profile management, friending, settings). Capabilities map to modules.L21L29L93Role → goal chain
Characterization testA test written after the fact to “characterize what it is that our code is doing”. It's a black-box test that “pins” legacy code in place, like tailor's pins, before you carve into it. Approval tests were mentioned as possibly the same thing.L81L84L87Q&A: FDD
ChoreA technical enabler task, as opposed to a user story.L89Q&A: aggregates
ChunkingThe mind can only take in so much at once, so work is broken into chunks. This is the reason for vertical slices and functional decomposition.L28DDD as code-first dev
Clarify before you verifyGet clear on the input/output objects and on how each responsibility will be verified before you write the tests.L58Stats calculator
ClarityKnowing where you're going and how the pieces fit. It's the first step to mastery and the antidote to anxiety.L5Clarity strategies
Clock abstractionAn abstraction of time injected into the domain, so the domain never touches system time.L88L89Q&A: aggregates
Code-firstPhase 1 of craftship. The goal is to “make things work to solve problems with code”. It leads to thinking about the code and tools, throwing technology at problems, anemic domain models and building-block thinking. The tools shape how you think. A code-first developer “might not know how to craft but you can build.”L1L14L15L42L85Phases of craftship
Code pathEach branch introduced by a conditional. More branches mean more paths to test.L47FizzBuzz
Cognitive dissonanceMental resistance, like having your foot on the gas and the brake at once.L4Obstacles & flow
CohesionHow well things belong together, i.e. which category something is more cohesive with. A class is SRP-compliant when its responsibilities are cohesive.L67L68Bounded contexts
Co-locationKeeping state and behavior together in the same file or place. This is how the functional approach achieves encapsulation.L60L71Military time
CommandAn action written in the imperative form of its event (“Create pre-reader invite”). It is performed against an aggregate and produces an event (createUser → UserCreated). In CQS, it's an operation that changes the system.L16L69L88Event storming
Commit phaseThe first pipeline phase after a merge: lint, build, unit tests and packaging. It produces the release candidate (Dave Farley).L81L82Deployment & delivery
Communication verificationVerifies that the subject interacts correctly with its collaborators, i.e. its indirect inputs and outputs. Example: it called the notification service. Done with mocks, stubs or spies, without real network calls.L20L53L64L84L91Verification types
Compensating eventsEvents created to handle failures in decoupled operations, e.g. “charge failed”.L18Temporal decoupling
Component (frontend)React code below the boundary: “just the view”, “just the presentation”. It renders from a view model.L90Control center
Component stateShort-lived local state (e.g. form input) managed with useState. It's gone when you leave the screen and isn't part of the cache.L90Frontend state
CompositionConsciously linking lower-level parts into a network of collaborating abstractions, by passing in the required dependencies and their dependencies. Linking unconsciously leads to circular dependencies.L19L93Composition
Composition rootThe object that encapsulates the work of linking everything together.L19L82L93Composition
Conceptual modelAn abstract model built during design, “not a real one yet”. It's a tool for understanding that allows fast communication through symbols and ideas.L66L90Mental models
ConcretionA fully implemented class or object, the “most real” level of abstraction.L79Levels of realness
ConstraintSomething that narrows the set of things you can do. The deployment pipeline is one.L25Deployment & delivery
Context mappingSeparating contexts, applying namespace boundaries, and drawing how bounded contexts talk to each other (conversations and dependencies, e.g. customer–supplier or upstream–downstream).L22L68Consolidating contexts
ContractAn abstraction placed between components: one side implements it and the other depends on it, which allows isolated testing. At the level of realness, it's an actor playing a role via implements/extends.L79L90Levels of realness
Contract testOne test suite run against every implementation of an interface (e.g. the in-memory and the real repo) to keep them in parity. It's a level-4 integration test. It keeps production and test code on the same path, whereas plain mocks create “two divergent code paths”. The term also covers incoming/outgoing adapter tests.L81L87L89L91L93Contract tests
Control centerThe coordinator and controller objects where the main decisions are made: coordinating (receiving requests and routing them) and controlling (“do this, do this”).L94L95Frontend control center
Controller (stereotype)An object that tells other objects to do work and executes use cases. It is either a single use case or holds many use cases as methods, ≈ a DDD application service / command handlers. On the frontend it handles state-changing operations.L90L94L95Object stereotypes
Coordination and controlThe responsibility of running the show and orchestrating use cases. It belongs in your application layer, not in React. A view library “becomes a framework” once it coordinates and controls.L87Control center
Coordinator / observerAn object that lets others subscribe to events and notifies them on change. “Global state… fundamentally it is an observer” (e.g. Redux).L90L94Frontend state
Core code“The heart of your app”: the domain, application and adapter layers. It doesn't touch infrastructure, so it's pure, fast to test, and where the value is.L81L84Code placement
Core subdomain (core domain)What makes the business unique and most important to it (for essentialist.dev: education). You build it yourself.L65L66L88L93Subdomains
CouplingHow tightly classes, features, components or modules are intertwined, i.e. one component relying on another. It's bad when something depends on a thing it isn't related to.L12L18L67L90Horizontal decoupling
CQSCommand–query separation: there has to be a read path and a write path. Khalil files it under vertical slicing.L16L32L91Vertical slicing
Customer boundaryThe outermost boundary. The customer decides what gets built.L92Structure & NFRs
Customer goalIncrease revenue or protect revenue.L11Three roles

D–F

TermCourse definitionLessonsSee
DataWhat comes in from the world and goes out of the model. In stateful terms, it's the initial state plus events: each transition produces a new version of the data.L53L94Essence, purpose, form
Dependency inversionCreate a contract that describes a dependency (e.g. persistence) and depend on that abstraction, not on the concrete DB. This lets you isolate exactly the layers you want to test.L17L88Horizontal decoupling
Dependency ruleHigher-policy layers (domain, application) must not depend directly on lower-level details or infrastructure. Example: an entity shouldn't call a repository or the console.L32L68One architecture
Deployment pipelineA constraint that forces a single path to production and makes sure code meets a minimum quality standard. Phases: commit, then acceptance.L25L81L82Deployment & delivery
Design (pillar)Discoverability and understanding: how easily developers can find and understand how to carry out the key developer use cases.L12L16L30Four pillars
Design storyThe upfront problem narrative given with each assignment. You extract domain knowledge and rules from it.L65FeedBook problem
Developer goalKeep users and customers in benefit at the same time, while keeping the key developer use cases easy to perform again and again.L11Three roles
DiscoverabilityHow easy it is to find what you're looking for. The discoverability gap and the understanding gap are the two gulfs between a goal and knowing whether you achieved it.L12L30Getting better at design
DistillationRefactoring toward patterns and distilling domain language into the code (Eric Evans).L81Q&A: walking skeleton
Doing / knowingThe two kinds of responsibility. A doing is an action (setName, validatePassword). A knowing is knowledge implied by a rule (getName, “knows passwords without a digit are invalid”).L52L61L94RDD
DomainThe big problem: “literally everything involved in me operating this business.”L66Subdomains
Domain discoveryGetting very clear on the language used, and making sure everyone understands it, through a shared mental model, domain model, subdomains, context mapping, event storming and event modeling.L22L93Domain discovery
Domain-driven design (premise)Working from a shared understanding (mental model) of the problem leads to higher-quality code. DDD patterns carve out an architecture that makes room for the domain layer.L22L28DDD as code-first dev
Domain eventSomething that happened, written in the past tense (e.g. “Pre-reader invite created”).L69Event storming
Domain knowledgeFacts about the conceptual reality you're creating: what's true, how things interact, what belongs where, what happens before what. It's locked in domain experts' heads.L65L66FeedBook problem
Domain layerThe layer where the shared understanding of the problem is fully embedded in code. It's “what really matters” and should be highly stable.L22L28Domain discovery
Domain model“Anything tasked with representing your data, your rules, your processes and your relationships.” It's the shared understanding, continually refined, and then codified as abstractions with agreed names and behavior. It covers the systems, knowledge, language, processes and symbols used to solve a problem.L22L65L76L84L93State machines
Domain object (frontend)The decision maker that validates input (value objects/entities) and decides whether a request should go ahead, e.g. RegistrationForm.L90Write side
Domain serviceThe DDD pattern that matches the service-provider stereotype. It's an input → output system that works across entities for complex domain processing, e.g. syncing a task list with a calendar (two state machines).L88L89Object stereotypes
DomainErrorAn abstract base error with a type and a message. It is returned, not thrown. Subtypes: MissingValueError and ValidationError.L77PreReaderInvite
DTO“Data in a certain shape.” It only carries data and has no behavior. It is not an aggregate.L89Q&A: aggregates
E2E testInput-output testing of “the entirety of the system” as a black box (level 5). Use result verification only.L31L81L84Test strategies
Emergent designDesign that comes out of Specify/Test/Refine (red–green–refactor), on the fly. Compare upfront design.L54L55L63FA²STR stateless
EncapsulationKeeping data together with its related behavior while protecting the data, in order to protect the way the model changes. In OOP: private constructor, static factory method, limited getters/setters. In FP: co-location.L71L74L86State machines
EntityAn object compared by identity. A level-2 domain concept (e.g. PreReaderInvite).L77L89PreReaderInvite
EssenceWhat a thing is: all of its properties and attributes. Form is the subset of those needed for a purpose.L94Essence, purpose, form
Essential complexityCode about the problem itself. It goes in modules/.L92Structure & NFRs
Essentialism / software essentialistFinding the few things that matter and produce most of the results, then refining them. A software essentialist is an 80/20, value-focused developer who seeks skills that last and masters the ones that gained leverage.L3L12Four mindsets
EventA piece of data meaning “we just moved to this state”, i.e. the fact that a transition happened. One is created on every transition and named after it (e.g. “gathered clothes”).L74L86L94State machines
Event busA component where anyone can register and subscribe to events. It lets modules talk to each other.L71FeedBook architecture
Event handler / subscriptionInfrastructure that listens for an event (e.g. OrderPlaced) and calls new vertical slices. It links one event type to any number of later side effects, which can be extended.L18L95Temporal decoupling
Event modelingAdam Dymitruk's technique, similar to event storming, that views the system as inputs, outputs and state changes.L22Domain discovery
Event sourcingSaving events instead of overwriting state. Current state is derived from the events.L94Q&A: RDD
Event stormingBig picture: clarify the current problem, what the business does and how it solves it today. Process level: lay out domain events (past tense), commands (imperative), actors and aggregates, plus Given/When/Then examples.L21L69Event storming
Eventual consistencyDoing secondary updates (sequence numbers, track-list IDs) later instead of in the same request.L89Q&A: aggregates
Examples (concrete)Concrete input/output instances of responsibilities, often written as Given (starting state) / When (actions) / Then (expected outcomes). They are the lowest rung of the theoretical prism.L52L69L82Worked example
Executable specificationA test file informed by a Gherkin feature file. It reads like a table of contents for the feature.L14L82Acceptance tests
Execution guess pointThe guess point where code actually runs in production and users can use it. After deployment you check whether KPIs (usage, sales) are being hit.L24L81Guess points
FA²STRThe six-step design method: Find (concrete examples: problem + solution guess points), Architect, Automate (test infrastructure/pipeline), Specify, Test, Refine (= red–green–refactor, nth looping). It abstracts the ideal developer workflow. As a metacognitive tool, it makes the upfront and emergent parts of problem solving visible.L27L52L54L63L86FA²STR
Fake / in-memory repoKhalil's preferred umbrella name for test doubles, whatever the spy/stub/mock flavor. The in-memory repo is a fake repository implemented as an array, a name that sidesteps the “category theory around fakes, spies, stubs, mocks”.L73L87Test doubles
Fake itThe simplest TDD transformation: return exactly what the test asks for (e.g. return "Fizz") or add a hard-coded branch, until the rule of three calls for a refactor.L44L45L63FizzBuzz
Failing for the right reasonRed because the logic is wrong, not because of a compilation or import error.L45L49Palindrome
FeatureA unit of value to the customer and user, described by a user story that takes someone from A to B through many operations (API calls). It groups use cases and is where “stuff should begin becoming code”. Also called a workflow (submit claim → … → notify customer).L16L29L92L93L94Vertical slicing
Feedback loopFeed forward → feedback → learn/refine → a faster, better next attempt. It starts from recognizing that every action is a guess, and you refine one system before moving on.L15L91L93Feedback loop
FeedBookThe demo app for the theoretical guess points. It helps authors test manuscripts with pre-readers through feedback cycles.L65FeedBook problem
First principlesUnderstanding how and why something works, not just pattern-matching its use. The “first principles effect” is reaching enough depth that you stop diverging and converge on the right things.L5L91Clarity strategies
FixtureThe initial state for a test: setting up the state of the world so you can test the functionality you want.L78L86L88Fixtures & builders
Flow stateA state of extreme focus, concentration and presence, where space and time blur. It's blocked by anxiety (challenge beyond your skill or clarity) and by boredom (work that doesn't feel relevant).L4Obstacles & flow
FormThe essential properties a thing needs for its purpose.L94Essence, purpose, form
Four pillarsArchitecture, design, testing and strategy. Together they achieve scalability, where all three roles win.L12L90Four pillars
Four-tier architectureView / controller / service layer / database. You get it by carving a service layer out of fat controllers.L82Q&A: best practice
Functional decompositionStepping down from problem / solution / architecture / deployment / system to the level of functions.L28DDD as code-first dev
Functional programming (as framed)Start from the desired state B and apply steps/events as composable functions to build a slice: data in, result out.L34Books

G–L

TermCourse definitionLessonsSee
Game theoryThe study of how and why active agents make decisions while trying to reach goals. It frames the three roles.L11Three roles
Gateway / API clientThe infrastructure component that sends requests to the backend (e.g. via axios or an HTTP adapter).L90Write side
Generic subdomainSomething you can pay for, download or integrate instead of building, e.g. identity & access management, auth or email sending.L65L66L88Subdomains
Gherkin fileA file that documents a feature and its scenarios. It informs the executable specification.L14Abstraction in practice
Guard / GuardResultA stateless (level-1) utility that checks preconditions (null/undefined, validation). It returns a GuardResult that can report hasErrors() and getFirstError().L77PreReaderInvite
GuessAnything we implement (a feature, an edge case, an API call, the belief that users want it). It stays unverified until feedback arrives.L15L93Guess points
Guess points“Our problem decomposition technique”: the value creation system seen as a series of systems, each with questions to answer. Theoretical: problem, solution, architecture. Physical feedback levels: stateless (1), stateful (2), application (3), outgoing adapter (4), system/E2E (5), plus incoming adapters. Execution comes after deployment.L1L7L15L81L87Guess points
Hexagonal / clean architectureLayered architecture plus an adapter layer that decouples core code from infrastructure code.L37One architecture
High-value integration testKhalil's name for testing from the controller (incoming adapter) “all the way to the database”, through to real outgoing infrastructure. It verifies real integration but isn't E2E.L64L92Test strategies
High-value unit testA fast, pure test at the application/use-case level (level 3), with use cases wired to a fake database. It covers the edge cases of each acceptance scenario, makes up about 80% of tests and gives about 80% confidence. Also called a use-case, controller, application or developer test.L25L28L64L82L87Test strategies
Horizontal decoupling(1) Putting the correct abstractions in the right layer. (2) Decoupling them strategically so you can isolate and bound the parts you want to verify. It's like a gradient from the “what” down to the database, getting more technical at each layer.L17L82Horizontal decoupling
Idempotency (as used in the course)The system could fail at any step, be brought back up, and still be in a consistent state: “either this whole thing works or none of it works”. Idempotent tests can be run over and over. (The standard meaning is that repeating an operation has the same effect as doing it once. The course's phrasing is closer to atomicity.)L18L70L82L88Temporal decoupling
Ideal developer workflowA way to combine the 12 essentials to move from theoretical to physical, based on what experts do (GOOS). Clarify theoretical guesses, then outer-loop acceptance test → inner-loop tests.L26L87Ideal workflow
Impact mappingA technique that puts the impact front and center: why you're doing it, the goal, who's involved and who benefits.L66Subdomains
Incoming adapterAnything that needs to use your system: web frontend, desktop, mobile, or an external system via webhooks (REST/GraphQL/SOAP).L88Application interface
Incoming (adapter/contract) testAlso called an API or driver test. It checks that calling the API/controller extracts and validates the request and invokes the correct use case, using a test double for the application so no use cases run. It checks that routes and request shapes haven't broken clients.L64L81L92Contract tests
Indirect input / outputData the subject gets from a dependency (e.g. fetching a user via a repo), and effects it sends to dependencies (saving via the repo, the mail service). Compare direct input/output of a pure function (string in, boolean out).L20L81Subject/system verification
Information holderAn object stereotype that only holds data, the place where information belongs (e.g. a camera's origin coordinates and zoom factor).L94L95Object stereotypes
Infrastructure codeCode you don't own that touches real things: databases, file system, network, system clock, random number generator. It lives in the infra layer (Express, React, ORMs, Firebase).L84Code placement
Inner-loop testsDeveloper-focused tests of internals: unit tests and incoming/outgoing contract tests.L26L40N loops
Integration testTesting from the application through outgoing infrastructure (database, services), i.e. a little infra plus parts of the application and domain. The definition is widely debated.L20L31Test strategies
InterfaceA description of what a role should do. A purely abstract concept that can't be instantiated.L79Levels of realness
InterfacerAn object that crosses over to infrastructure and the outside world (React components, Express handlers, a window wheel listener, the canvas API). It fills a responsibility gap by using an external API.L14L17L94L95Object stereotypes
Internal representationWhat comes to mind when you meet a word or concept. Code creates internal representations in its readers.L8Mental models
Invalid transitionA move between states that the rules disallow (e.g. gathered clothes → clothes clean).L74L86State machines
InvariantA rule, which is really business logic, about which states your domain concepts may be in and what you can and can't do. It is enforced to prevent invalid transitions. Example: a washing machine can't be off while settings are selected.L74L86L89State machines
Key developer use casesWhat developers do with features: discover, understand, test, add, change, execute.L11L29Large codebases

TermCourse definitionLessonsSee
