Object stereotypesThe stereotypical kinds of object that “everything tends to be” (RDD): controller, coordinator, information holder, interfacer, service provider, structurer.L94L95Object stereotypes
Obvious implementationWriting the real logic right away instead of faking it. Along with fake it, it's one of the two TDD strategies. It's fine when it's already the simplest option, but it can skip past simpler transformations.L47L62L63Boolean calculator
Open–closed principle“Express your code in such a way that if you need to add something new, all you have to do is add on top of it”, without duplicating code.L60Military time
OperationA thin input → output vertical slice below a feature, effectively one API call. It is either a command (changes the system, e.g. create user) or a query (get profile details).L16L93Vertical slicing
Outgoing adapter / contract testA level-4 test verifying that external infrastructure still behaves as expected (e.g. the DB returns data in the expected shape, a drag-and-drop library works).L81L92Contract tests
Package by domain / feature (screaming architecture)Folders that follow features, goals or bounded contexts: one folder per context module.L14L68Structuring codebases
Package by infrastructureTop-level folders named after technical parts (controllers/, routes/, models/, frontend components/). It's a code-first habit that hurts discoverability and understanding and is “generally bad”.L14L16L68L90Structuring codebases
Page objectA frontend protocol driver that exercises the UI.L82Acceptance tests
ParameterizationExpressing several examples of one behavior as a data table (it.each) run against a single test body, with %s substituted into the name.L55Password validator
Pareto principleAbout 80% of results come from 20% of the effort.L3Four mindsets
PatternA mental/conceptual model: an abstraction and shortcut that speeds up understanding and solving problems by piecing things together.L30L90Getting better at design
Pattern catalogAn upcoming pattern-first artifact. For each frontend or backend pattern it covers the bucket, collaborations, how to test it and the state types.L92Q&A: frontend 2
Pattern-firstPhase 3 of craftship: working with named building blocks such as entities, value objects, aggregates, use cases, domain events, repositories and external services. DDD enters here.L28L85Phases of craftship
Phases of craftshipThe staged apprenticeship path from building to crafting, where the 12 essentials get refined. Code-First → Best-Practice-First → Pattern-First → Responsibility-First → Value-First. The phases are also levels of thinking.L1L8L13L28L85Phases of craftship
PhronimosA developer who is where you'd like to be in design, architecture and testing. The course studies these masterful developers (phronesis = wisdom/mastery).L5L13Clarity strategies
Physical essentialsThe essentials for writing and running actual source code (the physical realm): vertical slicing, horizontal and temporal decoupling, composition, subject/system verification, walking skeleton, deployment & delivery.L13L24L93Physical essentials
PolicyA rule that reacts to events: “only when this happens / under this circumstance”.L18Temporal decoupling
Polymorphism“The ability for your code to take on different shapes.”L19Composition
PreReaderInviteThe FeedBook aggregate/entity: author ID + invited email, with an initial status and an accept transition. It connects an Author to a Pre-reader. It takes raw string input and holds typed state (value objects + status).L70L77PreReaderInvite
Pre-renderingRender the first requested page on the server and return it, then run client-side afterwards. Used for quick SEO.L92Structure & NFRs
PresenterSubscribes to changes and builds view models for components (“the correct shape for the component”) using selectors. Its API looks like presenter.load(). Khalil calls “facade” a conflated term for this.L87L90Read side
ProblemBeing in an undesirable state A and wanting a desirable state B.L9L94Systems thinking
Problem decomposition“The main skill”: breaking a problem or design challenge into steps you can act on. Khalil defines the developer as a problem decomposer.L1L27L93Main skill
Programming by wishful thinkingImagining the code already exists and writing it as if it were real, even though it won't compile yet, to feel out the API design.L51AAA backwards
Protocol driver“An abstraction that is going to act almost as if it is the user talking to the system.” Acceptance tests use it.L82Acceptance tests
Psychic entropyHow much complexity you put into a reader's brain as they try to parse what you did. Also the overwhelm you feel without a consistent process.L62L93Boolean calculator
Pure function (course definition)Same input → same output, no side effects, and no variable declarations or assignments. It returns immediately and chains into other functions (railroad-oriented programming / piping).L50Palindrome
PurposeWhy something is used. It depends entirely on the actor/role/goal (“always up to the actor to decide”). A system's purpose is to reach a goal, going from state A to state B. Personal purpose is the antidote to boredom.L6L9L10L94Essence, purpose, form

Q–S

TermCourse definitionLessonsSee
Qualitative / quantitative analysisQuantitative: are there enough people, in enough pain, who want this? (“gaining a number”). Qualitative: a feel for the problem from talking with users and domain experts.L21Value identification
Quantum momentA moment during work that matters more than others: the decision made there can drastically change your results and send you down one path or another.L5L8L85Right action
Red–green–refactor (Specify–Test–Refine)The TDD cycle: a failing test, a transformation that makes it pass, then a refactor. Commit on every phase change so reviewers can follow. It's the S-T-R of FA²STR.L27L44L45Commits
Reducer / selectors (Redux)The reducer is effectively the cache/gateway, sitting on the infrastructure side. Selectors develop “reactivity to key parts of the cache” so view models stay in sync, much like repository queries.L87Frontend state
Reference experiencesConcrete hands-on experiences (e.g. from tedious TDD katas) that later abstract concepts attach to. Their depth matters more than a title.L3L85Four mindsets
RefactoringA change to the structure of code that adds no new functionality (green → green). In the refactor phase, look for duplication (three occurrences) and turn it into an abstraction, in both production and test code.L44L45L49FizzBuzz
Release candidateA deployable artifact created after the commit phase. It becomes production if the later stages pass.L82Deployment & delivery
RepositoryA contract (role, port) for persisting and retrieving, e.g. UserRepo.save(user). On the frontend, it takes valid domain objects and calls the gateway/API client.L84L88L90Code placement
ResponsibilityThe smallest building block in programming: something an object or function does or knows. For a system, these are its requirements (e.g. “can detect valid time”). A line of code's responsibility decides which layer it belongs in.L52L56L61L93L94RDD
Responsibility-driven design (RDD)Seeing software as responsibilities (doings and knowings) grouped into roles that collaborate. Objects and functions (actors) fill those roles.L23L79L94RDD
Responsibility gap (object design gap)A missing responsibility between components that must be filled to integrate them. Often an interfacer fills it.L23L95Strategic design
Responsibility specificationA test description that names a doing or knowing of the system (“it can calculate the minimum value”) without naming the specific example.L59Test naming
Responsibility-firstPhase 4 of craftship: the metaphysical, first-principles way of looking at code, and the deepest level of design (bespoke design).L33L85Phases of craftship
Result (type)An abstraction that returns a value of a given type marked as success or failure. Use it when “you're expecting more than one return type”.L77PreReaderInvite
Result verificationChecking only the output (the returned result) against the input, not the internals. It's the only form used at the stateless level and at E2E.L20L51L53L64L84Verification types
Right actionThe better action at a decision point (quantum moment). What counts as right depends on what you currently value.L85Right action
RoleA part an actor plays (brother, coach, programmer), and each role has a goal. In RDD, a job to be played: an abstract description (interface/type) of the shape an object must match, abstract until an actor plays it. The three roles are user, customer and developer.L10L11L57L79L94Three roles
Rule of threeRefactor duplication into a new abstraction only on its third occurrence.L44L45L84FizzBuzz
SagaState machines and events linked into a sequence that chains business steps (place order → later events).L91Q&A: course structure
ScalabilityThe state where users, customers and developers are all reaching their goals (“one, two, three are winning”). You get there through the four pillars.L11L90Three roles
Scoring a pointPushing out a feature that created value for somebody.L85Q&A: mastery
Separation of concernsGrouping similar categories of work (accepting requests, validation, business rules…) and keeping responsibilities out of the wrong places.L17Horizontal decoupling
Sequence of creationThe order in which pieces of state must come into existence (author → invite → user → pre-reader).L76State machines
Service (external)Minimal code wrapping an integration with an external API (Stripe, PayPal, mail, a window wrapper). A key pattern role.L84L95Code placement
Service providerA mostly stateless object (e.g. a class with static methods) that exists just to run behavior: maths or utility logic. Worth considering when names like validator.validate appear. A static factory method is a class's service-provider role.L56L57L77L95Object stereotypes
Side effect (as used)Creating state, e.g. with the assignment operator, or acting on external collaborators.L50Palindrome
Slice (of value)The smallest result that solves part of the problem. It's built incrementally, reaches production and is seen and used by stakeholders.L89Q&A: aggregates
Solution guess pointWhere you find features, stories, acceptance criteria and examples.L22L27Tools per guess point
Spec / scenarioOne test case for a feature: the success case or one of the many failure cases.L87Acceptance tests
Spy (hand-written)A test double you write yourself. It implements the collaborator's contract plus logic to record calls. “Mocks” are the library-made kind (Jest).L73L87Test doubles
SRPAt the problem/solution level: one bounded context for one subject with clear responsibilities. At the class level: a class whose responsibilities are cohesive.L68Consolidating contexts
StateA position the system can be in. Being in a state is itself a form of data.L74L86State machines
State machineThe high-level events/steps (“chapters”) needed to reach a goal: states, transitions and events, guarded by invariants.L14L74L76State machines
State verificationActing on a loaded model, then querying its internal state (e.g. the game object), for inputs that produce no output.L20L53L84Verification types
Stateful (domain modeling) guess pointFeedback level 2: problems with intermediate states, where you encapsulate the core of the software (the domain layer: entities, value objects, aggregates).L74L77L86L88Guess points
Stateless guess pointFeedback level 1: data in, data out, no state (a pure transformation such as palindrome). The subject is a function or a static method.L46L52L86FA²STR stateless
Static factory methodA static create on the class, used with a private constructor to enforce creation rules.L71L77PreReaderInvite
Stereotypical architectureThe recurring layered structure found on every platform (domain, application, adapters, system/infra) with fixed rules about what may talk to what. It makes any app testable and brings calm about where things belong.L14L87L88One architecture
Stereotyping a componentIdentifying which aspects, concerns and responsibilities a component helps implement.L23Strategic design
Strategic designFrom DDD: making smart decisions about how the architecture is pieced together. That means classifying core, supporting and generic subdomains (build, outsource, or build anyway), and choosing the platform, components, tools and external services before the walking skeleton.L23L32L93Strategic design
Strategy (pillar)Making the most effective use of contending and assistive elements: the right amount of architecture, design and testing, and which shortcuts to take.L12Four pillars
StructurerAn object holding essential data plus the rules for changing it, ≈ an aggregate.L94Object stereotypes
SubdomainA smaller part the problem breaks into: whatever category of the problem comes to mind, big or tiny, with no fixed grouping. Classified as core, supporting or generic.L65L66Subdomains
Subject/system verificationUsing tests to draw a boundary around the thing you want to verify, chosen according to the guess being validated, to tell whether it helps reach a goal. It comes in three types: result, state and communication.L20L53L82L93Subject/system verification
Subject (system) under testThe part of the collaborating system you actually test, how it works, and how you interact with it (inputs and outputs). At the stateless level, it's a function or a static method. The “first level of production code” is whatever gets called to start it.L52L53L54L61Verification types
Supporting subdomainNot the problem you're currently solving, but strategic enough that you build it yourself rather than buy it (e.g. reporting). You “don't want to have to build this but need to”.L65L66L93Subdomains
System“A model in some environment where there's an input and there's an output.” Its purpose is to reach a goal (state A → B).L9Systems thinking

T–Z

TermCourse definitionLessonsSee
Temporal couplingChained “after X do Y” logic that breaks when earlier steps fail.L93Temporal decoupling
Temporal decouplingDecoupling functionality with events instead of slotting new operations into existing ones. The transaction happens, an event is dispatched, and a subscriber runs another feature later.L18L95Temporal decoupling
Test doubleAnything that stands in for the real thing (“it's just something that's fake”). Use it as the umbrella term for fakes, mocks and stubs instead of arguing over the distinctions.L73L84Test doubles
Test parityThe fake and production implementations are verified against the same contract, so tests that use the fake reflect production.L81L87Contract tests
Testing (pillar)Defining ahead of time what the system does, and staying aware of whether it still does it.L12Four pillars
Theoretical essentialsEverything that happens before writing code (value identification, domain discovery, strategic design): getting clear on what you're trying to do, and who, how, capabilities, features, use cases and concrete examples.L13L93Theoretical essentials
Thinking backwardsDefine the desired future state, then work out the steps that come before it. Used in daily planning, in TDD (assert first) and in state machines.L75Thinking backwards
Tracer bulletsThe Pragmatic Programmer idea of firing a thin path through all components early to confirm they integrate. Equated with the walking skeleton.L81L86L87Walking skeleton
Trail of whysAsking “why?” repeatedly until you reach an emotionally charged reason.L6Motivation
Transaction scriptPutting every step of a feature into one procedural call (e.g. makePurchase). As a way of thinking, it treats work as “just adding code” to tiny scripts. Sometimes needed for speed, but risky for maintainability.L16L88Vertical slicing
TransformationA production-code change that goes from red to green. A refactor, by contrast, keeps green → green.L49L60Palindrome
Transformation Priority Premise (TPP)A table ranking transformations from simplest (return nil, return a constant) to most complex (multiple statements, conditionals, variables/mutation). Use it to limit how much code you write per step.L60Military time
TransitionThe behavior that moves the system from one state to the next (A → B). It's the functional part of a program in any paradigm, and every transition produces an event.L74L86L94State machines
TriangulationUsing examples to drive out behavior: one example per feature across many features, or many examples per feature.L57Password validator
Triple blindnessNot being aware of quantum moments, not knowing how to act on them, and not knowing what's possible.L5Clarity strategies
Ubiquitous languageThe shared language of a domain model. In “the ubiquitous language of software essentialism”, that language is the 12 essentials themselves.L22L93Jargon map
Upfront designDesign decisions made before coding: FA²STR's Find, Architect and Automate (e.g. choosing a table-driven test structure). Compare emergent design.L54L63L95FA²STR stateless
Use caseA developer-level object representing a feature (the “controller” stereotype). It takes input, talks to collaborators such as a repo, performs behavior and saves: data in → validation and application rules → state changes and events out. Physically, it's a sub-folder under a module.L84L92L94Code placement
User goalGet time back (saved) or have time enriched.L10Three roles
ValueCreated when someone moves from pain to benefit, or stays in benefit, over time.L10Value creation system
Value creation systemThe mental model that breaks work down from theoretical (high level) to physical (low level), from left to right, ending in a software artifact of value in users' hands. An artifact of value creates state changes in people over time (pain → benefit).L10L15L85Value creation system
Value differentialThe shift in what's valuable caused by tools like ChatGPT, which commoditize basic how-to content and front-end work.L80Differentiate yourself
Value-firstPhase 5 of craftship, and the most valuable level of thinking. FA²STR and the guess points are the main way to break down problems here.L8L15L27Phases of craftship
Value identification“The act of getting clear on what is valuable”: the problem guess point, covering vision, role/goal and capabilities (the who and the why).L21L93Value identification
Value objectAn object compared by value. IDs and emails are value objects, even though IDs identify things.L77L89PreReaderInvite
Vertical slicingBreaking work into manageable chunks: modules → features → operations, each a vertical slice through the architecture (layer 5 to layer 1). The test: can you spot the feature, e.g. a create user folder with what you'd expect inside? It's about design, understanding and discoverability.L16L82L87Vertical slicing
View modelThe data shape a component actually renders from. The presenter builds it.L90Read side
VisionWhether you can even picture what you want to build, i.e. what we're making. It's the top of the abstraction prism.L21Value identification
Walking skeletonThe smallest, most bare-bones slice of useful functionality: a drawn architecture plus one user story cut from the UI to the database, built and deployed end to end as early as possible. It connects all the main components before feature work begins. Same as tracer bullets.L24L40L81L87L93Walking skeleton
What vs howThe behavior a spec promises (higher-level behavior/feature, e.g. “detect multiple errors”) versus the implementation details that deliver it.L55L56Password validator
